The gameplay foundation stays true to the proven recipe: cartoon tracks full of bends, the sliding technique called drifting that gradually charges up a turbo boost, and an arsenal of destructive items ranging from shells to the dreaded blue shell that homes in on the lead racer. The DS version's big addition was a wealth of retro content that brought in remastered tracks from every previous game in the series, so nostalgia went hand in hand with the new stuff.

Development was handled by the internal division Nintendo EAD. The Nintendo DS gave racing two screens: the top one let the driver watch the track from behind the vehicle, while the bottom one displayed the map and the positions of rivals. The game also made use of local wireless play, letting several DS owners race together, with a single cartridge being enough for a mode with a limited roster of characters.

The cultural footprint is unmistakable. Online multiplayer via the Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection service was, for most players, their very first experience of internet gaming on a handheld, and an incredibly devoted community grew up around the game. Mario Kart DS became one of the console's best-selling titles and to this day is regarded by many fans as one of the most balanced entries in the entire series.

Beyond the classic races, the game offers a mission mode where you complete short tasks of increasing difficulty, as well as an elaborate system of battle arenas. It is precisely this variety that makes Mario Kart DS a title you come back to again and again, whether for five minutes or a whole evening.

**Why play:** Masterfully tuned kart racing that was the first to bring Mario to the starting grid of a worldwide online contest.

nds__super-mario-64-ds.article:
When Nintendo launched its new dual-screen handheld in 2004, it needed a strong flagship title, and it reached for the very cornerstone of three-dimensional gaming. Super Mario 64 DS is a remake of the legendary game that in 1996 practically invented the rules of the 3D platformer, this time significantly expanded and reworked for the new hardware.

This is no mere port. The game adds three new playable characters alongside Mario, namely Yoshi, Luigi and Wario, each with their own abilities needed to collect certain stars. The total number of collectible stars grew from 120 to 150, brand-new levels were added, touchscreen minigames appeared, and there is a standalone multiplayer mode for several players.

Development was handled by Nintendo in cooperation with the remake's developers, and the game shipped as one of the Nintendo DS launch titles. The controls proved the biggest challenge: the original relied on an analog stick that the DS lacks, so movement had to be handled via the touch pad or the directional pad. This compromise solution is one of the game's most debated aspects, even though the content itself remains exceptionally rich.

The cultural significance of the original is beyond question, as Super Mario 64 defined how a character should move in an open three-dimensional space and influenced practically every later 3D game. The DS version made that legacy accessible to a new generation and became one of the console's very well-selling launch titles.

For players who know the original, the remake offers plenty of new content and reasons to rediscover Princess Peach's castle. For newcomers it is a gateway into one of the most important games in history, albeit with the awareness that the controls on the DS take a bit of patience.

**Why play:** An expanded version of the pioneering 3D platformer with four characters and dozens of extra stars, ideal for discovering the classic on the go.

nds__mario-and-luigi-partners-in-time.article:
The second installment of the quirky Mario & Luigi series pushed its idea into unexpected dimensions: what if not only the adult brothers fought side by side, but also their own toddler versions from the past? Mario & Luigi: Partners in Time from 2005 builds its entire gameplay around time travel and the interplay of four characters at once.

The game system is a turn-based RPG with an emphasis on action inputs. Attacks and especially defense require pressing a button precisely at the right moment, so even in battles the player never just waits around. The presence of both the adult and the miniature brothers means each of the four heroes is assigned to their own button, and the game exploits this both in battle and in solving puzzles in environments where the small and the big cooperate.

Behind the series stands the studio AlphaDream, which developed these distinctive turn-based adventures full of humor for Nintendo. The Nintendo DS made it possible to split the action across two screens, and the game played with their layout, especially when moving between the present and the past. This time the story leaves the usual Bowser behind and introduces an alien threat in the form of mushrooms called the Shroob.

The cultural significance of the series lies in how it managed to combine the accessibility of the mainstream Mario brand with the depth of a Japanese RPG and its own unmistakable humor. Partners in Time was well received and cemented the series' position as a fixture on Nintendo's handhelds, followed by further installments.

Thanks to its lighthearted tone, witty dialogue and cleverly designed battles, the game is a great entry into the RPG genre even for players who otherwise shy away from turn-based combat. It is never overly difficult, yet always remains fun and inventive.

**Why play:** A witty and original turn-based RPG where adult and toddler brothers fight side by side across time.

nds__mario-and-luigi-bowser-s-inside-sto.article:
Most games in the Mario series cast Bowser as the villain to be defeated. Mario & Luigi: Bowser's Inside Story from 2009, however, turns the script inside out: the player controls not only both brothers but above all the King of the Koopas himself, and spends a considerable part of the adventure literally inside his body. Many fans and critics consider this game the pinnacle of the entire series.

The genius lies above all in the interweaving of two gameplay layers. Mario and Luigi move through Bowser's insides and solve puzzles from within, while Bowser himself fights and explores the world outside. What the brothers do inside affects Bowser's abilities outside and vice versa. The battles once again rest on precisely timed action inputs, with Bowser's fights offering monumental scale and humor alike.

Development was again handled by AlphaDream, and the game came out on the Nintendo DS, whose dual-screen layout was made for this concept: the bottom display often belonged to the brothers inside the body, while the top one showed Bowser in the outside world. Some battles also made use of touch controls and tilting the console.

The game's cultural significance is confirmed by its exceptional critical reception. Bowser's Inside Story is one of the highest-rated titles on the Nintendo DS, and its humor, writing and inventive battle design made it a benchmark of quality. It later received a remake on the Nintendo 3DS, which testifies to its enduring popularity.

The combination of sharp humor, catchy gameplay and an unconventional take on the series' most famous villain makes this game a must-have for every DS owner. It is funny, inventive and surprisingly deep.

**Why play:** The peak installment of the series where you play as both Bowser and the brothers at once, with brilliant humor and inventive battles.

nds__legend-of-zelda-phantom-hourglass.article:
When, after the breathtaking installment The Wind Waker, word came that Link would head to a handheld console, skepticism reigned. The Legend of Zelda: Phantom Hourglass from 2007, however, proved that the cult series could be transferred to a touchscreen without losing its soul. The game is a direct sequel to the story from The Wind Waker and shares its charming comic-book visual style.

The boldest decision was to build the entire control scheme around the stylus. Link moves wherever the player points, attacks are issued by touching an enemy, and the stylus also serves for solving puzzles, drawing boomerang paths, or jotting notes directly onto the map. This approach was controversial at first but proved surprisingly intuitive and natural for the DS.

Development was handled by the internal studio Nintendo EAD. The game cleverly uses both screens and other hardware features, including the microphone and closing the console, which is part of one of its best-known puzzles. Central to it is the mysterious Temple of the Ocean King, to which the player returns repeatedly, a design element much debated at the time.

The cultural significance lies in the fact that Phantom Hourglass was the first fully original Zelda entry designed from the ground up for touch controls. It became a great commercial success and ranks among the best-selling Zelda games ever, confirming that the series has a firm place on handhelds.

For players seeking an adventure full of sailing the seas, exploring islands and clever puzzles, Phantom Hourglass is an ideal choice. It is accessible, visually enchanting and, within the possibilities of touch controls, masterfully designed.

**Why play:** The first Zelda designed for the stylus, with enchanting graphics and inventive puzzles on a seafaring adventure.

nds__legend-of-zelda-spirit-tracks.article:
Link on a locomotive? Yes, and it works. The Legend of Zelda: Spirit Tracks from 2009 followed up on the success of Phantom Hourglass and put the hero at the throttle of a steam engine that races across a sprawling landscape along fixed tracks. This unusual premise gives the game a unique character within the entire series.

The gameplay rests on the proven touch controls from the previous installment but expands them with train travel, during which the player controls speed, switches the tracks and fends off attacks on the rails. An entirely new addition is a companion in the form of Princess Zelda, whose spirit can take over the stone guardians known as Phantoms. The player thus controls both Link and a Phantom at once, opening up entirely new possibilities for cooperative puzzles.

Development was again handled by Nintendo EAD, and the game runs on the Nintendo DS. Besides the stylus, it also uses the microphone, into which the player blows to play a special pan flute that serves to control the tracks and solve puzzles. Visually the game continues the comic-book style of its predecessor but moves the setting from the sea onto land.

The cultural significance of Spirit Tracks lies in its courage to experiment. Combining Zelda with a railway sounded crazy on paper, but the game extracted from it fresh mechanics and a surprisingly strong narrative built on the partnership of Link and Zelda, which is a rarity in the series. The title met with a positive reception and sold well.

Anyone looking for an adventure unafraid to go its own way will find in Spirit Tracks an inventive blend of classic Zelda dungeons, clever cooperative puzzles and a distinctive railway journey.

**Why play:** A bold Zelda on rails with inventive puzzles and a singular partnership between Link and the spirit of Princess Zelda.

nds__pokemon-diamond-pearl.article:
The fourth generation of Pokémon brought the beloved series to the dual-screen Nintendo DS for the first time, and with it the Sinnoh region, a new roster of pocket monsters and key changes that shaped the entire future of the brand. Pokémon Diamond and Pearl from 2006 and 2007 are a pair of mutually complementary versions of the same game, as is customary for the series.

The core stays true to the tried-and-true formula: as a young trainer the player travels the region, catches wild Pokémon, trains them in battles and gradually defeats the eight gym trainers in order to finally take on the Pokémon League. Diamond and Pearl, however, brought a fundamental mechanical change by splitting attacks into physical and special according to the specific move rather than its type, which profoundly deepened battle strategy.

Development was, as always, handled by the studio Game Freak. The Nintendo DS hardware enabled substantially richer online features via the Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection, thanks to which players could trade and battle each other remotely over the internet, a huge step for the series. The two screens and touch controls in turn made item management and the battle menu easier.

The cultural significance is immense. Diamond and Pearl are among the best-selling entries in the entire Pokémon series, and the Sinnoh region became one of the most popular among fans. The games later received an improved Platinum version and, in subsequent years, complete remakes on Nintendo's newer consoles, which attests to their lasting significance.

Whether you are a collector eager to complete the Pokédex, a competitive player hungry for online battles, or simply a nostalgic soul, Diamond and Pearl offer dozens of hours of catching, training and discovery. It is a classic Pokémon journey in its matured form.

**Why play:** A pivotal fourth generation that introduced online battles and trades and the Sinnoh region, one of the most beloved in the entire series.

nds__pokemon-platinum.article:
Sinnoh, but this time with real punch. **Pokémon Platinum** is the enhanced version of the Diamond and Pearl pair, and exactly as with the third versions of previous generations, this is the incarnation of the region you want to remember. The frosty, foggy atmosphere of the mountains, redesigned route layouts and, above all, the Distortion World, a surreal gravity-defying dimension where the final showdown with the legendary Giratina takes place.

The basic loop stays intact and sacred: you catch, train, evolve and send pocket monsters into turn-based battles in which knowledge of type weaknesses and timing decide the outcome. Platinum, however, adds a number of clever improvements. The Battle Frontier offers five specialized battle facilities for hardcore trainers, a significantly wider selection of Pokémon available already in the base game, and a brisker pace that addressed one of the main complaints about the slower Diamond and Pearl.

The game was developed by the studio Game Freak, the series' home creator, under the publishers The Pokémon Company and Nintendo. It came out in the fourth generation, which was the first to fully exploit the dual screens and touch controls of the Nintendo DS, including online features via the Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection for trades and battles with players around the world.

Culturally, Platinum confirmed that Pokémon on the DS had come of age. Generation four introduced the split of physical and special attacks according to the specific move, which profoundly deepened competitive play and to this day forms the foundation of modern mechanics. The Distortion World, moreover, became one of the most frequently recalled locations in the entire series for its bold, disorienting aesthetic.

For collectors and competitive players alike, Platinum represents the peak of the Sinnoh era, which the later Brilliant Diamond and Shining Pearl remakes could only struggle to approach. It is the version that fans still recommend as the definitive way through the Sinnoh region.

**Why play:** The definitive form of the fourth generation with the unforgettable Distortion World and a brisker pace than the original Diamond and Pearl.

nds__pokemon-heartgold-soulsilver.article:
A return to Johto that many consider the best Pokémon remake ever. **Pokémon HeartGold and SoulSilver** bring the second-generation classic from the Game Boy to the Nintendo DS with such polish that even players who know the original by heart discover the region as if for the first time. And then there is that legendary little touch: your Pokémon walks by your side, literally, always the first in the team, visibly following you across the whole map.

Mechanically it is traditional catching, training and turn-based battles, but Johto has a soul of its own, two generations of Pokémon and, after completing the main storyline, the entire second region of Kanto to explore, crowned by a battle on Mount Silver. This two-act structure makes HeartGold and SoulSilver one of the most content-generous games in the series.

The release was prepared by Game Freak in cooperation with Nintendo and came out as part of the fourth generation, so it adopts the modern battle system with the split of physical and special attacks. The package also included the Pokéwalker accessory, a small Poké Ball-shaped pedometer into which you could transfer a Pokémon and raise it during a walk in the real world.

Culturally, this pair reinforced Johto's reputation as one of the most beloved regions and showed what a respectful remake should look like, one that not only updates the graphics and controls but adds new content and preserves the soul of the original. The walking-companion feature became iconic, and fans wished for its return in every subsequent generation.

Among collectors, HeartGold and SoulSilver are among the most sought-after titles on the DS and frequently appear in rankings of the best Pokémon games of all time. They are proof that nostalgia and modern design can be combined without compromise.

**Why play:** A model remake with a walking companion, two regions and content that will keep you busy for dozens of hours.

nds__metroid-prime-hunters.article:
Samus Aran with aiming on a touchscreen, long before the mobile FPS was a given. **Metroid Prime Hunters** was an ambitious attempt to bring the three-dimensional action of the Prime series to a handheld and, above all, to prove that a stylus could replace a mouse. You turn by dragging the pen across the bottom screen, you shoot, you scan, and in the guise of the Morph Ball you roll through the corridors of a lost civilization's stations.

The core of the game rests on two pillars. The single-player campaign sends Samus after an artifact of the lost Alimbic race, while she is hunted by six rival bounty hunters, each with their own weapon and alternate form. The second pillar is the multiplayer, which was remarkable for its time, deathmatches for up to four players locally and online via the Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection, where you could pick any of the hunters.

Development was overseen by Nintendo, and the game was created by the studio Nintendo Software Technology in North America. The title built on the success of the console Metroid Prime trilogy and was meant to show that the brand had a place in your pocket, too. The stylus controls divided players: some appreciated the precision of aiming, others suffered hand cramps during longer sessions.

Culturally, Hunters worked as an important experiment at a time when people were still figuring out how to sensibly play a shooter on a touch device. It foreshadowed much of what later spread to smartphones, and its online multiplayer was among the best that the DS of the day offered in the field of competitive action.

Today Metroid Prime Hunters is more of a curiosity for fans, but still an interesting, atmospheric and technically bold one. It recalls a time when control schemes were still searching for their form and every piece of hardware fought its own battle with ergonomics.

**Why play:** A bold handheld FPS starring Samus that experimented with stylus controls and offered a surprisingly strong online multiplayer.

nds__castlevania-dawn-of-sorrow.article:
Dracula is dead, but his legacy lives on, and this time the lead role goes to a young man named Soma Cruz. **Castlevania: Dawn of Sorrow** is a direct sequel to Aria of Sorrow from the Game Boy Advance and the first entry in the series on the Nintendo DS. The ingenious soul system returns, in which you gain the abilities of defeated enemies and assemble your own arsenal of attacks, spells and passive effects.

The game is a pure-blooded metroidvania: you explore a sprawling, interconnected castle, gradually unlock new areas thanks to acquired abilities and battle a bestiary of demons. Dawn of Sorrow cleverly involves the touchscreen, at the end of boss battles you draw magic seals with the stylus to seal them away for good, and you also handle small puzzles.

Behind the game stand Konami and director Koji Igarashi, the architect of the series' modern era. It came out not long after the DS launch and brought one controversy, a markedly anime-styled look for the characters that replaced the gothic style of artist Ayami Kojima from previous installments. The music was composed by Michiru Yamane, whose melodies are among the finest ever heard in the series.

Culturally, Dawn of Sorrow confirmed that Castlevania's metroidvania format feels right at home on the pair of screens. Many critics and players to this day rank it among the best entries of the so-called Igavania era, that is, the games created under Igarashi's direction, and praise the depth of the soul system and the fluidity of the combat.

For the DS it became one of the defining titles of the genre and opened the way for two further installments of the series on the same console. Anyone wondering what set this generation of metroidvanias apart starts right here.

**Why play:** An excellent metroidvania with an addictive soul-collecting system and a soundtrack by Michiru Yamane, one of the peaks of the Igavania era.

nds__castlevania-portrait-of-ruin.article:
Two heroes, one whip, one book of spells and a castle that is really a gateway into dozens of painted worlds. **Castlevania: Portrait of Ruin** pushes the DS Castlevania formula forward with a bold idea: besides the main castle, you jump through portraits into separate themed areas, from Egyptian ruins through city streets to a circus, each with its own atmosphere and enemies.

The key novelty is a pair of controllable characters. Jonathan Morris, heir to the legendary whip Vampire Killer, and the sorceress Charlotte Aulin complement each other; you can switch between them at any time or have them fight together in paired attacks. This dynamic adds a new dimension to both combat and exploration of the sprawling castle and opens up puzzles that require the abilities of both.

The title was developed by Konami, again under the direction of Koji Igarashi, and came out as the second of the trio of Castlevania games on the Nintendo DS. It draws inspiration from the old installment Castlevania III and its idea of multiple playable characters, which it brings into a modern metroidvania form. The music was, alongside other composers, once again handled by Michiru Yamane.

Culturally, Portrait of Ruin showed that the series is not afraid to experiment with its own formula without losing its identity. The portrait system brought a variety of environments that a classic Castlevania confined to a single castle could not offer, and the paired mechanic foreshadowed some elements of later installments.

For fans of the genre it belongs to the solid trio of DS metroidvanias worth playing all the way through. It is an entry full of ideas that keeps a brisk pace and rewards players who love to explore every corner.

**Why play:** An inventive metroidvania with two playable heroes and portals into themed worlds that refreshes the classic formula.

nds__castlevania-order-of-ecclesia.article:
What if Dracula isn't the only hope for salvation, and that hope is a mysterious symbol carved into the back of a young warrior? **Castlevania: Order of Ecclesia** closes out the trio of DS entries in the series and is the darkest, the most demanding, and by many accounts the best of them. The lead role belongs to Shanoa, a member of the Ecclesia order, who wields glyphs, magical symbols absorbed from enemies and the environment alike.

The glyph system is the heart of the game. Instead of conventional weapons, Shanoa assigns glyphs to each hand and combines them into attacks, spells, and devastating Glyph Union abilities. The structure also differs from earlier entries: part of the game consists of standalone locations scattered across the countryside, and only later does the traditional sprawling castle open up. The difficulty is noticeably higher, and boss battles demand precision and patience.

Behind the game stands Konami and the team around Koji Igarashi. Order of Ecclesia returns to a more serious, more melancholic tone and places greater emphasis on challenge, as if answering the voices of fans who found the previous entries too forgiving. The artwork of both the characters and the environments ranks among the most visually accomplished of the entire generation.

Culturally, this entry reinforced the reputation of the DS Castlevanias as a refuge for fans of demanding, deeply crafted metroidvanias. Order of Ecclesia regularly appears in lists of the best games of the genre on the console and is often called the most mature of the Igarashi-era DS titles.

For players seeking a true challenge and a dense atmosphere, this is a clear choice and a dignified farewell to the era of hand-painted metroidvanias on a pair of screens.

**Why play:** The most demanding and most melancholic of the DS Castlevanias, with an original glyph system and a heroine you won't forget.

nds__advance-wars-dual-strike.article:
Turn-based warfare has never looked so clever and so adorable at the same time. **Advance Wars: Dual Strike** brings Nintendo's beloved turn-based strategy to the DS and uses both screens to play out battles on two fronts at once. You command units on a grid-based map, capture buildings, manage your finances, and send tanks, infantry, and aircraft against the enemy.

The key to the series lies in the commanders, the so-called COs, each of whom bends the rules in their own way: one lowers unit costs, another boosts firepower, yet another controls the weather. Dual Strike adds the option to deploy two commanders into battle at once and to combine their passive bonuses along with their devastating Super CO Power abilities. Meanwhile, the bottom screen can host a second battlefield, so keeping track of both is a strategic challenge in itself.

The series is developed by the Japanese studio Intelligent Systems under Nintendo, the same studio behind Fire Emblem. Dual Strike is the third main entry in the franchise and the first on the DS, following the successful titles from the Game Boy Advance. It offers an extensive campaign, a rich skirmish mode, and a War Room full of challenges for high-score hunters.

Culturally, Advance Wars earned fame as one of the most accessible yet deepest turn-based strategies for the everyday player, a genre that otherwise often feels aloof. Its clean rules, legible pixel graphics, and balanced mechanics made it a favorite of critics and the tactical-game community alike.

Today Dual Strike ranks among the most prized strategies on the DS, and the whole series enjoyed a comeback thanks to a modern remake of the first two entries. This, however, is the DS peak, where a simple concept became a master class in turn-based warfare.

**Why play:** An accessible yet deep turn-based strategy that cleverly engages both screens and a two-commander system.

nds__fire-emblem-shadow-dragon.article:
Where it all began, and for the first time in full form for Western players too. **Fire Emblem: Shadow Dragon** is a remake of the very first entry in the legendary turn-based strategy series from 1990, which originally never left Japan. Prince Marth, a character many in the West knew only from the fighting game Super Smash Bros., finally got his story into the hands of players around the world.

The heart of the series is unforgiving turn-based tactics on a grid-based map, where every unit has its class, range, and weaknesses in a rock-paper-scissors weapon system. The key element is so-called permadeath: fallen comrades stay dead for good, which turns every decision into a weighing of risk and reward. Shadow Dragon adds modern conveniences such as class switching and touch-based control of units with the stylus.

The game was developed by the studio Intelligent Systems under Nintendo, the very creators who have accompanied the series from the very beginning. The remake set the classic story into modernized graphics and supplemented it with optional side missions, which you can access only at the cost of sacrificed units, a harsh but thematically fitting mechanic.

Culturally, Shadow Dragon holds a special significance: it introduced the series' long history to a Western audience at precisely the time when Fire Emblem was gaining popularity, partly thanks to its heroes' appearances in Super Smash Bros. For many players it was the first chance to play where the entire saga of tactical fantasy began.

Compared to the later, more story-rich entries, Shadow Dragon feels austere and classic, but that is exactly where its charm lies. It is pure, hard tactics without embellishment, a textbook of the fundamentals on which the series built its name.

**Why play:** A modernized remake of the very first Fire Emblem that finally brought Marth's original story and its harsh permadeath to the West.

nds__chrono-trigger.article:
There are games that age. And then there's Chrono Trigger, which the years seem to give a wide berth. When Square released this title on the Super Nintendo in 1995, it assembled the so-called Dream Team: writer Hironobu Sakaguchi (Final Fantasy), creative mind Yuji Horii (Dragon Quest), and artist Akira Toriyama (Dragon Ball). On the Nintendo DS it returned in 2008 in a carefully carried-over version that supplemented the original marvel with touch controls and two new dungeon locations.

The story follows a band of heroes who accidentally tumble through time and discover that in the distant future the planet faces destruction. Traveling through the eras isn't just scenery but the very heart of the game: an intervention in one century changes the world in another, and the characters visit prehistory, the Middle Ages, and a post-apocalyptic future. Battles play out without a transition to a special screen, right there in the field, and their highlight is the Techs, combined attacks in which two or three characters join their spells into flashy displays of teamwork.

The hallmark that keeps Chrono Trigger remembered with reverence to this day is its system of many endings. The game can be finished at various stages, and depending on when and how you defeat the final enemy, you get one of many epilogues. Tied to this was the then-unusual New Game Plus mode, which let you start over with your accumulated experience. This willingness to experiment made the title a textbook example of how playful and generous the JRPG genre can be.

The artistic side carries Toriyama's unmistakable signature, and Yasunori Mitsuda's music ranks among the most-cited soundtracks in gaming history. The DS version also brought translated dialogue and a polished localization, thanks to which the game reached a new generation of players. For many critics and players it is one of the best JRPGs ever made, and the handheld version is today regarded as one of the most approachable ways to reach it.

Chrono Trigger, in short, remains a benchmark. It showed that a story-driven game can be both dense and lighthearted, technically daring and humanly warm. And that a trio of geniuses, when you give them a free hand, can create a work that outlives its creators and the consoles it was made for.

**Why play:** One of the highest-rated JRPGs of all time, on the DS with touch controls and bonus content. An ideal gateway into the genre and a treasure for veterans.

nds__final-fantasy-iv.article:
When Final Fantasy IV came out in 1991, it advanced JRPG storytelling by a great leap. Here Square fully committed for the first time to characters with their own motivations, betrayals, and redemption, instead of merely having the player lead a nameless party from one boss to the next. The main hero Cecil, a dark knight yearning to atone for his own deeds, underwent a transformation that game stories had until then scarcely known. On the Nintendo DS this classic returned in 2007 (in Europe 2008) in a completely reworked 3D form.

The DS version isn't a mere port but a full-fledged remake. The original two-dimensional graphics gave way to three-dimensional models, voice acting was added to key scenes, and the whole game received a new coat while preserving the original story and the music of Nobuo Uematsu. Square Enix also nudged the difficulty upward, so even players familiar with the old version ran into a fresh challenge.

The heart of the battles is the ATB system, Active Time Battle, which Final Fantasy IV introduced as the very first entry in the series. Battles don't play out purely turn by turn; instead, an action gauge fills in real time, so decision-making has pace and tension. Each of the many playable characters has a firmly defined role, from white and black magic to the summoner Rydia to the twins capable of joined spells, and the game deftly rotates them according to the drama of the story.

The DS remake also added a unique layer in the form of augments, abilities that can be assigned to characters and that unlock in part according to how you treat your companions. This gave veterans a reason to explore the game anew. The visual execution was among the best the DS saw in the genre, and it proved that a small screen can bear even an ambitious 3D RPG.

Final Fantasy IV is today rightly named one of the milestones on which the genre grew. The story of betrayal, sacrifice, and hope resonates even after decades, and the DS version delivers it in a form that respects the original spirit while speaking the language of the modern generation. It is a work that showed a game can move you as much as a film or a book.

**Why play:** A full-fledged 3D remake of the legendary JRPG that was the first to bring the ATB system and mature storytelling. A classic in a form that holds up to this day.

nds__dragon-quest-ix-sentinels-of-starry.article:
Dragon Quest is a phenomenon in Japan that surpasses even Final Fantasy in popularity, and the ninth entry, Sentinels of the Starry Skies, was released directly and exclusively for the Nintendo DS. With this Square Enix made a bold move: it entrusted the biggest Japanese RPG brand to a handheld console and bet on what the DS did best, namely the wireless connection of players. The game came out in 2009 (in the West 2010) and became one of the best-selling titles in the series.

Compared to older entries, the ninth brought a fundamental change: for the first time the player creates their own hero and party members, choosing their vocation, appearance, and equipment. The story follows a celestial guardian who, after falling to earth, loses his divine essence and must recollect the lost fragments. The turn-based battles stayed true to the series' tradition, with the characteristic monster design from the workshop of Akira Toriyama, whose slimes are among the most recognizable icons of the gaming world.

The greatest charm, however, lay in the multiplayer. Up to four players could join a single party at any time and traverse dungeons together, which made Dragon Quest IX a genuine social event in Japan. Tied to this was the StreetPass system, where consoles exchanged data merely by players carrying them around in their pockets. Lines formed outside shops, people gathered over rare treasure maps, and the game lived far beyond the bounds of its own story.

There is an enormous amount of content in it. After finishing the main line, players are met by an extensive endgame with generated dungeons, collecting missions, and tougher bosses, so dozens of hours easily stretch into hundreds. The vocation system with the possibility of reassignment gives room for experimentation and for building your own ideal party.

Dragon Quest IX became a commercial hit and ranks among the most successful games of the entire DS console. It showed that a big traditional brand can be both modern and sociable without losing its soul. For fans of turn-based RPGs and for those seeking a game for long shared evenings, it is one of the defining titles of handheld gaming.

**Why play:** An extraordinarily extensive turn-based RPG with your own party creation and cooperation for up to four players. One of the best-selling and most-played titles of the entire DS library.

nds__world-ends-with-you.article:
Few games look and play as unmistakably as The World Ends with You. In 2007 (in Europe 2008) Square Enix sent out into the world a title that has nothing to do with swords and dragons but with the streets of modern Tokyo, fashion, mobile phones, and teenage loneliness. It takes place in the Shibuya district, which the creators captured with a love of detail, from graffiti through clothing brands to the music pulsing in every menu.

The story follows the withdrawn teenager Neku, who wakes up in the middle of a mysterious Game of survival. Together with his partners he must complete tasks over seven-day cycles, or else erasure awaits him. This existential premise of alienation and the necessity of opening up to others gives the game a surprising emotional depth beneath its layer of stylish pop culture.

The battle system is a marvel devised directly for the DS's two displays. The player controls Neku with the stylus on the bottom screen using so-called pins, badges with various abilities, and at the same time steers a partner on the top screen with buttons. Both battles play out simultaneously, and synchronizing them requires a genuine division of attention. It is one of the boldest attempts to use the DS hardware to the fullest, and nothing like it was created before or since.

Over everything hovers the artistic style of Tetsuya Nomura and a soundtrack mixing hip hop, rock, and electronica that became cult-favorite in its own right. Fashion, moreover, isn't just cosmetic: clothing brands have an effect in the game, individual Shibuya districts favor different trends, and so the player indirectly follows a kind of street-fashion simulation.

The World Ends with You earned enthusiastic reviews and gradually gained the status of a cult classic. It received ports to newer platforms as well as a full-fledged sequel and an anime adaptation, confirming that its bold vision had staying power. For the DS it remains one of the most original titles of all, a game that proved an action RPG can look and sound like nothing else on the market.

**Why play:** A stylistically unmistakable action RPG with a unique battle across two displays and a cult soundtrack. An original that uses the DS hardware to the fullest.

nds__kirby-canvas-curse.article:
When Nintendo got its hands on a console with two displays and a stylus, it asked itself how to use the pen differently than as a mere pointer. Kirby: Canvas Curse, released in 2005, was one of the first and most elegant answers. Here you don't control the pink hero directly, but instead draw with the pen the paths along which he rolls like a helpless little ball.

The premise is delightful: the evil witch Drawcia turns the world into a painting and robs Kirby of his legs. The player must therefore help him by drawing rainbow lines on the touchscreen that serve as ramps, bridges, and protective walls. Tapping Kirby sends him rolling; tapping an enemy stuns it. The whole game plays out purely with the pen, without a single button for movement, which makes it a textbook example of design tailored to the hardware.

Across the levels Kirby swallows enemies and gains their abilities, from fire-breathing to turning into stone, so the heart of the classic series remains here. But drawing the paths adds a wholly new layer of puzzle and dexterity: a limited amount of ink forces you to plan your moves, save lines for key jumps, and improvise when a chasm or trap appears in front of Kirby.

Visually the game leans on a painterly motif, with richly colored backgrounds resembling canvas and brush strokes all around. Reviewers praised how naturally the touch controls play and how inventively the whole concept is developed all the way to the boss fights. Canvas Curse joined the titles that showed skeptics that the stylus isn't just a marketing gimmick but a tool for entirely new gaming ideas.

Within Nintendo it was an important proof that even an established brand like Kirby can bear a radical experiment with controls. The studio HAL Laboratory later followed up on this idea with further titles featuring a drawing mechanic. For DS owners Canvas Curse remains one of the games for which the console essentially existed, namely to do things that weren't possible elsewhere.

**Why play:** An inventive platformer controlled solely by drawing with the pen, tailored directly to the DS touchscreen. Proof that Kirby can endure even a bold experiment.

nds__kirby-super-star-ultra.article:
Some games deserve a second life, and Kirby Super Star belongs among them exactly. The original Super Nintendo title from 1996 was prized as a collection of several standalone adventures in one package, a so-called game full of games. In 2008 HAL Laboratory and Nintendo brought it to the Nintendo DS under the name Kirby Super Star Ultra, in an enhanced form with new modes and a reworked presentation.

The concept stayed true to the original: instead of one long campaign, the game offers several shorter stories each with its own focus. One is a classic platformer, another a grand epic battle, yet another a race against time or a treasure hunt. This structure makes the game an ideal title for a handheld console, because you'll always find a bit for a few minutes as well as a longer expedition for the evening. The DS version added entirely new episodes that weren't in the original.

Kirby's main hallmark, namely the ability to swallow enemies and take over their powers, is developed here into a rich palette. Kirby transforms into a sword fighter, a fireball, an ice knight, and dozens of other forms. Super Star also became famous for its Helper system, where the player can create from an absorbed ability a helper controlled by a second player, so the whole game can be played cooperatively.

The DS remake replaced the original 2D graphics with sharper reworked sprites, redid the interludes, and added touch-controlled minigames using the bottom display. For veterans it was pleasant nostalgia in a better coat; for newcomers a comfortable gateway into one of the most beloved classics of the pink icon.

Kirby Super Star Ultra confirmed why the series is so loved: it's accessible even for the youngest players, yet hides enough content and playfulness to entertain seasoned veterans too. The variety of modes, cooperative play, and the characteristically lighthearted atmosphere make it one of the most rewarding platformer titles on the DS and proof that a good idea holds up across console generations.

**Why play:** An enhanced remake of the cult collection of many games in one, full of abilities, co-op, and new content. A varied and accessible platformer for everyone.

nds__professor-layton-and-curious-villag.article:
What if an entire game were just a fairy-tale-drawn village full of people who, instead of a greeting, toss you a puzzle? From this simple idea grew Professor Layton and the Curious Village, a title from the studio Level-5 that in 2007 (in the West 2008) kicked off one of the most endearing brands on the Nintendo DS. It combines an elegant detective story with dozens of logic puzzles and does so with such charm that it won over even people who otherwise don't play games.

The main hero is the gentlemanly archaeologist and puzzle lover Professor Layton, accompanied by his apprentice Luke. Together they arrive in the mysterious village of St. Mystere to unravel a mystery surrounding the inheritance of a deceased baron. The investigation, however, unfolds in a peculiar way: every character you meet offers you a puzzle instead of information, and only by solving it does the story move forward. The puzzles range from logic riddles through sliding objects to deceptive word problems.

It's precisely this variety that makes the game a little treasure. Many of the puzzles are taken from the work of the Japanese riddle author Akira Tago and require wit and a moment of thought rather than fast fingers. But the game never punishes: it offers a hint system, so when you get stuck, you can gradually unlock clues without having to peek into a walkthrough.

Visually Curious Village enchants with a hand-drawn aesthetic and animated cinematic interludes that lend the game the atmosphere of a European fairy tale. Pleasant jazz music and the kind tone of the narration make it an ideal game for quiet evenings. The stylus serves both for jotting down notes and for solving the puzzles themselves, which again makes excellent use of the DS's capabilities.

Professor Layton became both a commercial and critical success and founded a long, beloved series with many sequels and even a feature-length animated film. The first entry remains where it all began, and to this day it counts as one of the best examples of how a logic game can be at once clever, kindly, and captivatingly story-driven.

**Why play:** A magical combination of a detective adventure and dozens of logic puzzles with hand-drawn charm. The start of one of the most endearing DS series, ideal even for non-gamers.

nds__phoenix-wright-ace-attorney.article:
Objection! This single word can bring a smile to the faces of game fans, and Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney is to thank for it. Capcom originally released the game in Japan back in 2001 for the Game Boy Advance, but the real breakthrough came with the Nintendo DS version from 2005, which reached the West and unleashed an avalanche of popularity. It's a courtroom drama in interactive form, where the player becomes a rookie defense attorney fighting for his clients' innocence.

The game divides into two phases. In the investigative one you examine crime scenes, talk to witnesses, and gather evidence. The real tension, however, comes in the courtroom, where witnesses testify and your task is to find contradictions in their claims. When you notice that testimony doesn't match evidence in your case file, you raise that famous Objection and present the incriminating piece of paper. But the wrong evidence at the wrong moment costs you the judge's patience, so it's a game of attention and logic.

The series' magic lies in the writing. The cases are full of absurd humor, eccentric characters, and surprising twists, yet they can also be tense to the point of held breath. The gallery of figures, from the domineering prosecutor to eccentric witnesses, sears itself into memory, and the final entry of the original trilogy ranks among the most-cited moments of game storytelling ever.

Compared to the original GBA game, the DS version added a fifth, entirely new case that used specific functions of the console: in it the player examines evidence in 3D, uncovers clues by blowing into the microphone, and uses the touchscreen. These elements helped the game stand out on the new platform and gave even veterans a reason to buy it again.

Phoenix Wright kicked off the extensive and still-living Ace Attorney series with many sequels, spin-offs, and collector's collections. It proved that the genre of the visual novel and detective logic can entertain a mass audience, and it became one of the symbols of what the DS was: a console on which even unconventional, text-driven games succeeded. For lovers of stories it's a must.

**Why play:** A funny yet tense courtroom drama where you hunt for contradictions in testimonies and shout the famous Objection. The start of the cult Ace Attorney series with a bonus case for the DS.

nds__ghost-trick-phantom-detective.article:
You wake up dead. That's an opening situation scarcely any other game in the world will offer you. The hero named Sissel has neither memory nor body, but he does have one day to find out who killed him and why. And he has a single tool: the ability of a ghost to enter objects, manipulate them, and in the last four seconds before someone else's death, rewrite fate. Ghost Trick is one of the most original titles ever to come out on the Nintendo DS.

At its core the game is a logic adventure built around a mechanic called „Ghost Trick“. Sissel jumps between objects in the environment, sets them in motion, and triggers chains of reactions to save people who have just died. He turns time back a few seconds and the player must rearrange the events in the scene so as to prevent the tragedy. The individual mysteries fit together with the precision of clockwork and gradually assemble into one grand, surprisingly emotional story.

Behind the game stands Shu Takumi, the creator of the Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney series, and his signature is evident at every step. It came out under the Capcom banner and is distinguished by absolutely remarkable character animation. The developers used motion capture and hand-tuned fluidity of movement, so even the tiny figures on the DS's lower screen seem to come to life. The visual style, music, and dramaturgy form an exceptionally tight whole.

Culturally Ghost Trick joined the titles that critics loved but that commercially didn't reach big numbers. Over time, however, it built up the status of a cult classic and a devoted fan base that recommended it for years as a hidden gem of the DS library. The game later received a remastered version for modern platforms, which brought it a deserved second wave of attention from a new audience.

What makes Ghost Trick exceptional is the way it weaves witty humor, a tense detective plot, and clever puzzles into one breath. The story of lost identity and a fate that can be rewritten builds toward a conclusion that ranks among the very best in the genre of narrative adventures. It's a game you'll finish practically in one sitting and remember for a long time afterward.

**Why play:** A completely original puzzle-adventure with an unforgettable story about death, time, and identity, from the creator of Ace Attorney.

nds__elite-beat-agents.article:
Someone has a problem. A truly serious problem. And the only ones who can help are a team of three sharply dressed agents who, instead of weapons, wield rhythm and dance. Welcome to Elite Beat Agents, one of the craziest and at the same time most addictive rhythm games ever released on the Nintendo DS. You tap the stylus against the screen in time with the music and literally save the world through groove.

The mechanics are brilliantly simple yet deep. Numbered targets appear on the touch screen, and you have to tap them at the exact moment a shrinking ring lines up over them. Some sequences require dragging the stylus along a path, others tracing a spiral. Everything is tied to popular songs and comic-book-style vignettes in which your accuracy decides whether the character in the story succeeds or fails.

The game was created by iNiS and published by Nintendo in 2006 in North America. It was a Western adaptation of the Japanese hit Osu! Tatakae! Ouendan, where instead of agents, a squad of male cheerleaders rallied people in distress. For the Western market the concept was reworked into secret agents, and the playlist features cover versions of well-known pop and rock hits, from Avril Lavigne to Deep Purple.

Culturally, Elite Beat Agents became a critical darling and proof that the DS touch screen could be a full-fledged musical instrument. The stories of the individual songs range from comical to surprisingly touching, earning the game a reputation as a title that will make you laugh and move you to tears alike. The mechanics of this series later strongly influenced community rhythm games such as Osu!, which draw directly from it.

What makes Elite Beat Agents so unforgettable is the sheer shamelessness with which it combines absurd humor, energetic music and a surprisingly deep emotional charge. It is a game that makes you tap the screen with a smile on your face while, during some of the more dramatic songs, it may even bring a lump to your throat. It belongs in the essential collection of every DS owner who loves rhythm.

**Why play:** A wild, addictive rhythm game that makes full use of the DS touch screen, packed with humor, emotion and catchy music.

nds__sonic-rush.article:
The blue hedgehog was always about one thing: speed. And Sonic Rush is perhaps the purest distillation of speed that Sega ever put on a handheld. Spread across both screens of the Nintendo DS, the game hurls Sonic through tunnels, loops and vertical leaps at such a cadence that it occasionally takes your breath away. After years of awkward 3D experiments, the series returned here to its roots.

The gameplay combines classic 2D platforming with a modern take on speed. Sonic tears through the levels, collects rings and fills up a meter called the „Tension Gauge“, which charges as you pull off flashy maneuvers and lets you unleash a speed boost. The game uses both DS screens to render long vertical stretches where the hedgehog falls or shoots upward across both displays at once. Alongside Sonic, a new character is playable too, the girl Blaze the Cat, who has her own parallel campaign.

The game was developed by Dimps in collaboration with Sonic Team and released in 2005. Dimps had rich experience with 2D Sonic from the Game Boy Advance era, and that craftsmanship confidence shows in Sonic Rush. The soundtrack was composed by Hideki Naganuma, whose funky, hip-hop beats known from Jet Set Radio give the game its unmistakable energy and style.

Culturally, Sonic Rush marked an important moment: it reminded everyone that Sonic can be great when he sticks to what he does best. Critics received the game warmly as one of the best portable entries in the series, and it sold well commercially. It became the foundation for the sequel Sonic Rush Adventure and, with its approach to high-speed 2D Sonic, influenced later titles such as Sonic Colors and Sonic Generations.

What makes Sonic Rush so gripping is the utterly fluid sense of motion and the clever use of both screens for passages that would be impossible on a single display. It is a game that rewards courage and quick reflexes while staying accessible. For any fan of classic Sonic, it is a fixed point in the otherwise shaky history of the modern series.

**Why play:** High-speed 2D Sonic at its finest, with a superb soundtrack and clever use of both DS screens.

nds__mega-man-zx.article:
The blue bomber transformed into something new and surprisingly bold on the Nintendo DS. Mega Man ZX took the long-running action series and infused it with the lifeblood of an open, interconnected world. Instead of a linear run through levels, the player explores a sprawling map, returns to visited areas with new abilities and gradually uncovers the threads of a larger story. For fans of the series it was a refreshing change of course.

The core of the game remains what Mega Man does best: brisk, precise action and platforming with an emphasis on mastering demanding boss fights. The novelty is the „Live Metal“ Biometal system, thanks to which the hero transforms into various combat forms, each offering different weapons and movement abilities. On top of that, the game employs a metroidvania structure, where new abilities open up previously inaccessible paths and encourage thorough exploration.

Mega Man ZX was developed and published by Capcom in 2006 as the successor to the popular Mega Man Zero series from the Game Boy Advance. The team built on the darker, more narratively ambitious tone of that line and pushed it into a new hardware generation. The characteristic anime visuals and high difficulty were preserved, which has long defined the series.

Culturally, ZX joined the ranks of titles that critics praised for their courage to experiment with form, though the game did not escape criticism for the sometimes confusing navigation of its expansive world. It received a direct sequel, Mega Man ZX Advent, and today it is part of the Mega Man Zero/ZX Legacy Collection, which made the series accessible to modern audiences on current platforms.

What makes Mega Man ZX interesting is precisely that blend of proven hard action and an unconventional, more open structure. It is a game for players who love a challenge and are not afraid of serious difficulty, while also appreciating a series that refuses to stand still. In the context of the DS library, it is one of the more distinctive action platformers for the demanding.

**Why play:** A demanding action platformer that combines classic Mega Man with a more open metroidvania structure and transformations.

nds__contra-4.article:
Sometimes the best way forward is the way back. Contra 4 is a declaration of love for the eight-bit and sixteen-bit era, when run & gun shooters knew no mercy and death came from a single hit. The game was released on the Nintendo DS and cleverly used both screens to render gigantic levels and bosses stretching across the two displays. For fans of classic Contra it was a dream come true.

The gameplay is pure and uncompromising: you advance through the level, shoot everything that moves, collect weapon upgrades and dodge a torrent of projectiles. The novelty is a grappling hook that lets the heroes swing between the top and bottom screens, extending the action vertically in a way the single-screen entries never allowed. The difficulty is legendarily high, and the game offers several difficulty levels along with rich unlockable content.

Contra 4 was developed by WayForward and published by Konami in 2007. WayForward, known for its love of classic 2D games, poured evident reverence for the series' legacy and precise pixel-art craftsmanship into the project. The game serves as a direct continuation of the storyline following Contra and Super C, and it even includes emulated versions of both those classics as a bonus.

Culturally, Contra 4 became a celebrated reboot of the brand after years of more awkward entries. Critics praised how faithfully it captured the tough spirit of the originals while adding clever modern touches. For many reviewers it was one of the best run & gun games of its time and proof that the old school still has plenty to offer, as long as it is approached with respect.

What makes Contra 4 unforgettable is that pure, adrenaline-fueled difficulty and the satisfaction of slowly earned mastery. It is a game that will kill you again and again until you learn every enemy pattern by heart, and therein lies its charm. For devotees of hardcore old-school action, it is a must.

**Why play:** An uncompromising old-school run & gun that cleverly uses both DS screens and is a written love letter to classic Contra.

nds__grand-theft-auto-chinatown-wars.article:
A top-down view, a handheld console for kids, and a brutal drug gang warring for dominance over Liberty City. Grand Theft Auto: Chinatown Wars is one of the boldest and most unexpected pieces in the history of the series. Rockstar took its controversial brand, returned it to the isometric view of the original entries and crammed a full-fledged crime epic into a Nintendo DS cartridge. And the result surprised absolutely everyone.

The game combines the classic GTA formula, that is free-roaming an open city, completing missions and causing chaos, with mechanics tailored to the DS touch screen. With the stylus you smash car windows while stealing them, assemble improvised explosives in the form of a minigame, and even run a full-fledged drug-trade system where you track prices and hunt for the most lucrative markets. The story follows Huang Lee, who arrives in Liberty City to avenge his father's death.

Chinatown Wars was developed by Rockstar Leeds in collaboration with Rockstar North and released in 2009. Visually it bets on a fresh cel-shading-inspired style that gives the isometric world a comic-book sharpness. The game was later ported to the PSP and the iOS and Android mobile platforms, finding an even wider audience.

Culturally it was an unexpected critical triumph. Chinatown Wars reaped excellent scores and ranks among the highest-rated games on the entire Nintendo DS. Many reviewers called it one of the best portable games of its generation and proof that a sprawling, mature game could be brought to handheld hardware without compromising the fun. Commercially it was not a bestseller, but its critical reputation remains unshakeable.

What makes Chinatown Wars exceptional is the incredible density of its content and the cleverness with which the creators adapted a big game to a small screen. It is a full-fledged GTA with everything included, just in pocket format, while retaining its own distinct identity. For any fan of the series and of handheld games alike, it is a small miracle.

**Why play:** A full-fledged, critically celebrated GTA in a pocket isometric rendition, one of the best games on the entire DS.

nds__scribblenauts.article:
Write anything and it comes to life. That simple sentence sounds like every child's dream, and Scribblenauts turned it into a genuine playable mechanic. You take the stylus, write a word in your notebook, and the game instantly conjures the object right into the game world. Need to cross a chasm? Write „bridge“. Or would you rather have a „jetpack“? Or straight up a „dragon“ to fly across on? The possibilities are dizzying.

At the heart of the game is a giant database of thousands of nouns that can be created and used to solve puzzles. Each level presents a logical riddle whose goal is to obtain a star called a Starite, and there are almost infinitely many ways to solve it. The game actively rewards creativity and experimentation, and it even offers challenges where you must beat the same level three times in a row without repeating the same object.

Scribblenauts was developed by 5th Cell and published by Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment in 2009. At the heart of the whole project is a proprietary database of terms called „Objectnaut“, which allowed the game to recognize a staggering number of words, including mythological creatures, animals, tools and more abstract objects. It was precisely this breadth that made the game a phenomenon even before release.

Culturally, Scribblenauts became one of the most talked-about games at the E3 show, where it earned several awards and enormous attention from a media fascinated by its interface. After release, part of the criticism did point out the sometimes clumsy control of the main character's movement, but the central idea itself was received as ingenious. The game kicked off a whole series, including the improved sequel Super Scribblenauts and later entries.

What makes Scribblenauts unforgettable is that pure sense of childlike wonder when you discover that the game really does know even the unexpected word that just popped into your head. It is a toy and a game at the same time, a space for experimentation limited only by your imagination and vocabulary. In the DS library it represents one of the most original ideas of all.

**Why play:** A brilliantly creative puzzle where you conjure any object you write and solve the riddle in literally infinitely many ways.

nds__animal-crossing-wild-world.article:
No enemies, no ending, no score. Just a little village inhabited by cute animals, a debt to a raccoon named Tom Nook, and the flow of time that runs in real life even when you turn the console off. Animal Crossing: Wild World is the game that defined the genre of laid-back life simulations on a handheld and became a daily ritual for millions of players. A few minutes a day are enough, and the village lives a life of its own.

The gameplay is deliberately unhurried and open. You catch fish and insects, plant trees, furnish your own house, pay off your mortgage, write letters to your neighbors and collect furniture and clothing. The game's internal clock mirrors the real time and date, so in the morning you encounter different goings-on than in the evening, and in every season the nature, holidays and available creatures change. There is no goal except the one you set for yourself.

Wild World was developed and published by Nintendo in 2005 as the portable sequel to the GameCube original. The key novelty was the use of the Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection feature, which for the first time made it possible to visit friends' villages over the internet and play with them online. This ability to connect with friends at a distance was absolutely groundbreaking for its time.

Culturally, Animal Crossing: Wild World became one of the best-selling titles on the entire Nintendo DS, with sales on the order of more than ten million units. The game contributed fundamentally to popularizing the „cozy“ simulation genre and helped expand the DS audience far beyond the boundaries of traditional gamers. Its principles led directly to the series' later megahits, especially the phenomenon Animal Crossing: New Horizons.

What makes Wild World so special is the feeling that you have your own little corner of the world that waits for you and evolves even in your absence. It is a game about calm, collecting and small everyday joys, ideal for moments when you just want to unwind. For many DS owners it was a game they returned to day after day for years.

**Why play:** A tranquil life simulation running in real time that you will return to every day, with groundbreaking online visits to friends' villages.

nds__nintendogs.article:
You flip open the lid of the Nintendo DS, touch the stylus to the fluffy little head of a puppy on the bottom screen, it tilts its ears and looks straight at you. In that moment it is decided. Nintendogs was not just another game, it was a small miracle that convinced millions of people, including those who had never held a console before, that a living animal lived on the display.

The basics are brilliantly simple. You choose a breed, give it a name, and from that moment on you take care of it. You feed it, bathe it, brush it, throw it a ball and, above all, train it. And this is where the trick came in that felt like magic back in 2005: the puppy responds to the microphone. You say the chosen name, it comes running. You teach it commands and it remembers them. Touch controls and voice input were not a gimmick here but the core of the whole experience, a perfect demonstration of why the Nintendo DS had two screens and a microphone.

The game was developed and published by Nintendo itself, and it was one of the first titles to fully demonstrate the console's philosophy from 2004. Under the guidance of creators connected to the legacy of Shigeru Miyamoto, a product was born that aimed far beyond the boundaries of the traditional gaming audience. It came out in several versions differing in the selection of available breeds, which was, incidentally, a clever business move to sell more cartridges into a single household.

The cultural impact was enormous. Nintendogs became one of the flagship titles of the so-called casual boom, the wave that, together with Brain Age and Wii Sports, brought grandmothers, mothers and children to gaming who had until then passed consoles by. It became one of the best-selling games on the entire platform and a symbol of the era when Nintendo managed to convince the world that truly anyone can play.

When you look at Nintendogs today, you might object that it lacks challenge, a goal, a score. But that is precisely the point. It is digital calm, therapy in your pocket, a game you cannot finish because it cannot be finished. You open it in the morning, the puppy wags its tail, and that is enough.

**Why play:** If you want to understand why the Nintendo DS conquered the world, sit down with the microphone and stylus and let your own puppy come trotting up to you. It is a touchingly timeless example of games that warm the heart.

nds__brain-age.article:
How much is seven times eight? And now say it out loud into the microphone, quickly. Welcome to Brain Age, the game that in the mid-2000s turned the Nintendo DS from a children's toy into a daily ritual for adults around the world and unleashed a veritable brain-training phenomenon.

The concept is disarming. Instead of a story and enemies, you get a series of short exercises. You calculate chains of simple problems against the clock, read texts aloud, draw from memory, solve Sudoku. The game measures your performance and converts it into a so-called brain age, a number you try to push as low as possible toward the ideal twenty. It was precisely this playful metric that was the driving force of the whole game. People competed against themselves and their families, returned day after day and watched themselves improve.

Brain Age is built on a concept inspired by the work of Japanese neuroscientist Professor Ryuta Kawashima, whose stylized polygonal head guides you through the exercises and comments on your results. The game was developed and published by Nintendo and cleverly used both of the console's key features: you hold the console upright like a book, write directly on the touch screen with the stylus, and speak your answers into the microphone. Handwriting and voice recognition did misbehave at times, but even that became part of the folklore around the game.

Commercially it was one of the greatest triumphs of the era. Brain Age sold tens of millions of units around the world and, together with Nintendogs and Wii Sports, formed the holy trinity of so-called casual games that won Nintendo an entire generation. It also kicked off a wave of imitators, a genre of educational and brain-sharpening titles that flooded the stores and became a category of its own for a few years.

Is Brain Age truly science, or cleverly packaged entertainment? The debate over the real benefits of brain training continues to this day. Either way, one thing is certain: as an addictive, short and surprisingly satisfying workout for the mind, it works great even years later.

**Why play:** Short daily doses of arithmetic and puzzles that fit into five minutes or an hour alike. The ideal title when you want something other than action from your console and yet cannot tear yourself away.

nds__tetris-ds.article:
There is a game that truly everyone knows, and then there is Tetris DS, the version that wrapped this immortal classic in Nintendo nostalgia and sent it onto two screens. The falling blocks that defined the very concept of a video game meet Mario, Zelda and Metroid here, and the result is simply irresistible.

The core remains sacred and untouchable. You assemble four-part shapes, clear rows, speed up, panic. But Tetris DS adds several game modes that freshen up that good old formula. The standard mode is accompanied by variants inspired by specific Nintendo games, where retro scenes play out on the top screen and your stacking below influences what happens above. There is a mode where you knock down blocks, a mode with a pushing wall, and other ideas thanks to which the game has something to offer even hardened veterans.

The title was developed and published by Nintendo, which cleverly bet on its two strongest cards, the bottomless depth of Tetris and the love for its own classic brands from the eight-bit era. The visuals and music draw directly from games like Super Mario Bros., The Legend of Zelda and Metroid, so each mode is a small tribute to a piece of Nintendo history. The console's two screens are not there for their own sake but serve the overall experience.

Where Tetris DS truly excels is multiplayer. The console from 2004 offered wireless connectivity, and the game made full use of it. Player-versus-player battles, where you make each other's lives harder by sending over rows, are among the most addictive things Tetris has ever offered in handheld form. For many fans it remains to this day one of the best portable versions of the entire series.

Tetris is a game you never truly beat, you only postpone the inevitable end. And that is exactly why we keep coming back to it. Tetris DS adds colors, memories and clever ideas to that perfect loop without touching what makes Tetris Tetris.

**Why play:** Immortal gameplay wrapped in Nintendo nostalgia and with excellent multiplayer. If you own a DS, this is a must.

nds__mario-party-ds.article:
Friendship is a precious thing, and Mario Party can be its most effective solvent. Mario Party DS brought the notorious party series to a handheld and proved that you do not have to miss out on that chaotic, unfair and gloriously fun competition for stars even when you do not have a TV and four controllers on hand.

Even those who have never played Mario Party know the format. You move your character across a board game by rolling a die, collect coins, buy stars and try to make your opponents' journey as unpleasant as possible. Between rounds you play minigames, short and inventive battles that decide who gets rich and who loses everything. And the minigames are the heart of the whole thing. On the DS they make full use of the touch screen, the microphone and holding the console upright, so you blow, draw, tap and twist the hardware.

The game was created by Hudson Soft, the series' longtime in-house developer, in collaboration with Nintendo, which published it. The story framework sends the familiar quintet led by Mario into a shrunken form after the treacherous Bowser turns them into little crumbs with a spell, which elegantly explains why you suddenly toddle across giant tables and board games. The single-player campaign here is surprisingly substantial and serves as excellent training for the main event, playing with more people.

Multiplayer is precisely why Mario Party exists. Mario Party DS made it possible to play four-player via wireless connection, and crucially, often a single cartridge was enough while the others downloaded the necessary data. This accessibility made the game an ideal title for travel, school and parties, where friends became mortal enemies for a few dozen minutes.

Mario Party was never about fairness. It is about that last roll of the die that turns victory into farce, about the random star that thwarts a perfectly thought-out strategy. And it is precisely this fickleness of fortune that keeps the series alive to this day. On the small DS screen it works just as reliably as on the television.

**Why play:** A pocket party full of chaos and minigames where, thanks to data download, you can play four-player from a single cartridge. The perfect friendship destroyer for the road.

nds__jump-ultimate-stars.article:
Imagine a crossover where Goku meets Luffy, Naruto and dozens of other heroes from Shonen Jump magazine on a single screen. Jump Ultimate Stars from 2006 offers exactly that: a celebration of the legendary Japanese comic magazine in the form of a fighting game for the Nintendo DS.

The game is the successor to Jump Super Stars and pushes the concept even further. At its core is the so-called comic system, where you place blocks representing characters onto a panel arranged like a manga page. Battle characters you control directly, support characters you summon into action, and helper characters provide passive bonuses. The fights take place in multi-layered arenas with an emphasis on fast action and clever team building, so the depth lies not only in the combat but also in constructing your roster.

Development of the game was handled by Ganbarion, and behind it stands enormous licensing work: Jump Ultimate Stars includes dozens of characters from many Shonen Jump magazine series, from Dragon Ball through One Piece, Naruto and Bleach to older and lesser-known titles. This breadth makes the game a literally interactive encyclopedia of Japanese manga and is the main reason for its cult reputation.

Culturally it is a phenomenon above all in Japan, where Shonen Jump is an institution. The game never officially released in the West, which made it a sought-after import title among fans outside Japan, often accompanied by fan translations. For manga connoisseurs it is a dream come true.

Jump Ultimate Stars remains one of the most ambitious crossover fighting games of all time and proof of how rich the tradition of the magazine that shaped generations of readers is. Even years later it is a title that collectors and anime fans still seek out.

**Why play:** A giant crossover fighting game with dozens of characters from Shonen Jump, a dream come true for every fan of manga and anime, albeit at the cost of importing it.

nds__need-for-speed-most-wanted.article:
Police lights in the rearview mirror, the engine at its redline, and a single thought: get away. Need for Speed: Most Wanted is one of the most legendary entries in EA's racing series, and its 2005 Nintendo DS version brought the adrenaline of street chases to a handheld console.

Most Wanted became famous for fusing illegal street races with high-stakes police pursuits. The goal is to climb the list of most wanted racers, beat your rivals and at the same time escape an ever more aggressive police force. The DS version adapted this formula to the possibilities of the handheld, tapping into the touch screen and other features of the console to deliver a racing experience on the go, albeit on a more intimate scale than the big console release.

In terms of development, Most Wanted belongs to the era when EA was churning out Need for Speed titles for every imaginable platform and trying to make each main game available to handheld players as well. The DS version was thus created alongside the major release for home consoles and PC, which became one of the most commercially successful entries in the series ever and remains one of the most beloved Need for Speed games in history to this day.

Culturally, Most Wanted defined the era of street racing in the middle of the last decade, when tuning and the culture of illegal races were at the peak of their popularity. The atmosphere of fleeing from the police etched itself into the memory of an entire generation of players, and the Most Wanted brand later even got a reboot.

On the Nintendo DS, it is a solid way to enjoy street chases on the road. It is not the full-fat experience of the big platforms, but as a pocket-sized dose of Need for Speed adrenaline, it serves its purpose.

**Why play it:** A pocket-sized portion of the cult street chases from the police out of one of the most beloved Need for Speed entries, ideal racing for the road.

nds__mario-and-sonic-at-olympic-games.article:
After decades of stubborn rivalry in the console wars, the unthinkable happened: Mario and Sonic, gaming history's two greatest rivals, lined up at the same starting line. Mario & Sonic at the Olympic Games from 2007 is historically the first game where both mascot icons met, and on top of that under an official Olympic license.

The game is a collection of Olympic disciplines ranging from athletics through swimming and gymnastics to shooting, which on the Nintendo DS the player controls mainly via the touch screen. These control schemes, where you scratch the stylus into a run or draw strokes for individual disciplines, are the core of the experience and turn the game into a brisk party affair. You can compete as characters from both worlds, from Mario and Luigi to Sonic, Tails or Knuckles.

In terms of development, it was a groundbreaking collaboration between Nintendo and Sega under the auspices of the International Olympic Committee, tied to the 2008 Summer Olympic Games in Beijing. For players who grew up in the nineties on the rivalry of both brands, the mere meeting alone carried enormous symbolic weight.
