On the small Game Gear screen it's of course a more intimate experience than on a big TV, but the principle of fast, adrenaline-fueled shooting in tight levels remains legible and fun.

The original Gunstar Heroes from 1993 was the debut of the Treasure studio, founded by former developers from Konami, and it instantly became a cult title and one of the technical showcases of the Mega Drive. The studio built a reputation as creators who wring the maximum out of hardware and aren't afraid of an over-the-top amount of effects and enemies on screen. That reputation is tied to the Gunstar brand to this day.

The pocket version for the Game Gear is interesting mainly as context: it shows how the popular titles of the time were ported across platforms to appeal to owners of weaker hardware too. For fans of the series it's a chance to experience the familiar world and characters in an unusual format and to compare what all fit onto Sega's handheld and what had to give way to technical limits.

Gunstar Heroes as a brand is one of the pillars of the nineties action genre, and its influence can be felt in countless later shooters. Even the pocket edition thus bears the mark of one of the most respected names of its era and is a pleasant reminder of a time when people played wherever a battery and a small backlit screen would fit.

**Why play it:** Adrenaline-fueled run & gun action in pocket format, bearing the name of one of the most acclaimed action brands of the nineties.

game-gear__ax-battler.article:
Golden Axe was one of SEGA's biggest arcade hits, so it's no surprise that its world tried to conquer pocket hardware too. Ax Battler: A Legend of Golden Axe for the Game Gear, however, isn't a plain copy of the arcade brawler. It's a surprisingly ambitious attempt to fuse the Golden Axe fantasy world with elements of action RPG and adventure, tailored for gaming on the go.

Instead of a pure beat 'em up, the game sends you into a side-viewed world where you travel across a map, complete quests and switch into action sequences during battles. Gradually you learn new combat moves and spells, collect equipment and grow stronger. It's a mix that tries to give a pocket title depth and longer longevity than the simple arcade original offered. So instead of one concentrated bout of action, the player gets a little adventure with elements of character growth.

Development-wise, Ax Battler is part of the wave when SEGA was stretching its successful brands across platforms and genres. Golden Axe as a phenomenon gave rise to sequels and spin-offs on various consoles, and this Game Gear version is one of the bolder experiments, because it dared to depart from the original gameplay toward an action RPG.

For players today it's an interesting piece of pocket gaming history: a demonstration of how creators tried to fit a more expansive adventure into a limited format and appeal to an audience hungry for content on longer journeys. Fans of the Golden Axe brand will find familiar motifs in it, but delivered differently than they'd expect from an arcade brawler.

Although it's a title that today is more of a collector's and nostalgic affair than a widely known hit, it represents a valuable reminder of an era when pocket consoles experimented with genres and searched for ways to engage players for longer than just a few arcade minutes.

**Why play it:** An unusual fusion of the Golden Axe world with an action RPG that turns an arcade brawler into a little pocket adventure.

game-gear__world-series-baseball.article:
The pitcher winds up, the batter grits his teeth, and the whole stadium holds its breath - **World Series Baseball** brings America's national pastime to the Game Gear's pocket screen in a form that can win over even players who don't fully understand baseball. This game proves that even a small display can conjure up the tension of a big match.

At its core it's a baseball sports simulation, where you alternate between offense and defense. At bat you wait for the right pitch and try to hit the ball as far as possible; in the field you control the pitcher, catch hits and run between bases to stop your opponent from scoring. The game is built on tactical role-switching and gradually building a lead across individual innings, which makes it a title that rewards patience and awareness.

**World Series Baseball** was released under the SEGA label and followed a series of baseball games aimed at recreating the sport as faithfully as possible. On the color handheld Game Gear, SEGA's answer to the monochrome Game Boy, the title enjoyed the advantage of full-color display - on a portable console from the first half of the nineties, that was no small edge.

The Game Gear positioned itself as a technically more advanced handheld than the competition, and sports titles like this one were exactly the kind of games that showed off its color screen. World Series Baseball offered a portable serving of America's pastime for players who wanted to enjoy the sport anywhere and anytime - albeit at the cost of the notoriously fast battery drain the Game Gear was famous for.

Culturally the title fits into the broader wave of sports games with which both SEGA and Nintendo tried to reach American audiences in the early nineties. Baseball, as one of the most popular sports in the USA, was a logical choice, and the portable version expanded where and how you could play it.

**Why play:** For a color pocket serving of American baseball that shows what the Game Gear's screen could do against its monochrome rivals.

atari-lynx__chip-s-challenge.detail: The Lynx's flagship puzzle game and a launch title: as the nerd Chip you solve 149 puzzles (collecting chips, keys, pushing crates, building bridges) against a time limit to impress Melinda. Every level has a single solution, so it calls for experimentation. It became a cult classic and was ported elsewhere (later even to Windows). Depth and content unusual for a 1989 handheld.
atari-lynx__chip-s-challenge.article:
A brilliant puzzle isn't measured by its graphics, but by how long a single room you simply can't solve keeps you up at night. **Chip's Challenge** did exactly that — and it did it back in 1989, tucked inside a portable console remembered today more with fondness than with the respect it deserved.

The story is delightfully eighties: you're Chip, a likeable nerd who wants to impress a girl named Melinda, and to get into her exclusive club you must work through a series of logic rooms. Out of this came a game of **149 levels** where you collect chips, hunt for colored keys, push crates into water to build bridges, and dodge monsters and deadly floors. Each level has its own time limit and — crucially — usually just one correct solution, so progress is a blend of logic, spatial imagination and honest trial and error.

For a handheld of the time this was unusual depth and volume of content. Where other pocket games made do with a few repeating screens, here was a genuine building-block puzzle game of growing complexity, where new mechanics are introduced gradually and combine into ever more devilish puzzles. The studio **Epyx**, which was also behind the Lynx hardware itself, included the title among the launch games — and did well, because it was this game that proved the color handheld didn't have to be only about action.

The cult around **Chip's Challenge** outgrew its original platform. The game later reached other systems including Windows, where it was remembered by a whole generation of players who had never heard of the Atari Lynx. The community around it lives on to this day — fan-made level editors and sequels appeared, remarkable longevity for a puzzle game from the late eighties.

What makes the game timeless is the purity of its design. No needless clutter, no distractions — just you, the grid, the clock and one correct move after another. It's the type of game where you tell yourself "just one more level" and suddenly it's midnight.

**Why play:** A pure-bred grid puzzle with incredible depth for its era, one that hooks you with its simplicity and won't let go thanks to its devilishly clever levels.

atari-lynx__california-games.detail: A launch title and one of the first "summer extreme sports" games in your pocket (skateboarding, surfing, BMX, footbag). Epyx brought its computer hit to the Lynx with color. Laid-back multiplayer fun; a symbol of the console's early library.
atari-lynx__california-games.article:
Sunshine, a board under your feet and a wave waiting to be ridden — **California Games** was a digital postcard from California long before "lifestyle" became a marketing cliché. And on the Atari Lynx, in color no less, it felt like a slice of summer that fits in your palm.

Instead of classic disciplines like running or the long jump, the studio **Epyx** bet on the then-young "extreme" sports: skateboarding, surfing, BMX and footbag (hacky sack). Each discipline has its own controls and rhythm — the surfer has to read the wave and time tricks, the skateboarder must master the half-pipe, while BMX rides on speed and daring. It's not a simulation, it's an arcade full of style, all about flair, timing and competition.

The game originally shone on home computers, and Epyx ported it to the Lynx as one of the console's launch titles. The handheld's color and backlit display let the Californian beaches and graffiti aesthetic stand out in a way the competing black-and-white handhelds of the era simply couldn't offer.

But **California Games** hands out the most fun in a group. Taking turns at each discipline, jeers over a botched trick and the drive to beat a friend's record — that's exactly what turned this game into a social event. It's a title that builds not on the depth of any single discipline but on variety and a light, carefree mood.

Today the game is remembered mainly as a symbol of the Lynx's early library and as proof that Epyx knew how to capture the spirit of the age. It's no technical miracle nor a title to keep you busy for weeks, but as a pocket ticket to eighties California it still works.

**Why play:** A laid-back multi-discipline arcade packed with eighties style, perfect for quick contests with friends and a sip of digital summer.

atari-lynx__blue-lightning.detail: A launch rail shooter inspired by the film Top Gun — you fly a fighter jet into the screen, shoot down enemies and dodge mountains. It showed off the Lynx's hardware scaling (objects realistically grow larger) and was an impressive technical calling card.
atari-lynx__blue-lightning.article:
When you want a single game to prove what your new hardware can do, you don't show charts — you drop the player into a fighter cockpit. **Blue Lightning** was exactly that kind of calling card for the Atari Lynx: a fast, loud and visually confident rail shooter meant to convince at launch that a pocket console could work miracles.

The Top Gun inspiration is impossible to miss. You fly a fighter jet deep into the screen, shooting down waves of enemy aircraft, dodging mountains and guiding missiles onto ground targets. It's a classic rail shooter — your route is fixed, your task is to survive, aim and time evasive maneuvers — but the pace and spectacle made it a small sensation in 1989.

The star here is the hardware scaling the Lynx boasted. Objects grow realistically as you approach them, so enemies and terrain rise up out of the depth of the screen and create a pseudo-3D sense of speed that other handhelds of the era couldn't imitate. The studio **Epyx**, author of the console and its first games, meant this to literally take shoppers' breath away in every store.

As gameplay, **Blue Lightning** is more of a flashy ride than a deep challenge — anyone who knows the rail shooter genre knows what to expect: learn the route, avoid the crash, shoot down whatever flies at you. But precisely as a technology demo and launch draw it did its job to perfection and became one of the titles most often associated with the Lynx.

Today it's mainly a historically interesting piece — the moment a portable console first showed off an effect that belonged more in the arcade than in your palm.

**Why play:** A flashy rail shooter that shows off the power of Lynx scaling and delivers brisk, cinematic Top Gun-style action.

atari-lynx__zarlor-mercenary.detail: The two best original shooters on the Lynx. Zarlor Mercenary is a vertical shmup with upgrade purchases and co-op, Gates of Zendocon a horizontal one with dozens of bizarre portal levels. Solid Lynx exclusives for fans of the genre.
atari-lynx__zarlor-mercenary.article:
You know a proper shmup by the fact that the moment you lose you're already reaching for another try — and **Zarlor Mercenary** triggered exactly that reflex. It's among the best original shooters ever released on the Atari Lynx, and for fans of the genre it's one of the reasons to try the console at all.

It's a vertical shmup in which you fight your way through waves of enemies up the screen, dodging fire and reaping rewards. What lifts it above ordinary shooting is its upgrade-purchase system — with the money you earn you strengthen your weapons and abilities between missions, so there's a point to planning your progress and building an arsenal gives the game momentum. Co-op play also works splendidly, turning a lonely slog into a shared effort.

The studio **Epyx**, the company behind the Lynx itself, showed here that pocket hardware could handle even a hectic genre demanding precision and fluidity. Zarlor isn't just a technical exercise — it's a cleverly balanced shooter where the rhythm of shooting, dodging and upgrading merges into an addictive whole.

Because it's a Lynx exclusive, the game also carries the mark of something special. It's not an arcade port you can play anywhere — it belongs to the titles that gave the console its own identity and that its library could show off to owners of rival handhelds.

For shmup enthusiasts, then, it's a mandatory stop. The pace, the upgrades and the co-op make **Zarlor Mercenary** one of those games where "just one more run" stretches into a whole evening.

**Why play:** An addictive vertical shooter with upgrades and co-op, one of the best original Lynx exclusives for fans of the genre.

atari-lynx__gates-of-zendocon.article:
There are shooters that entertain you with their perfection, and then those that entertain you with how bizarre they are — and **Gates of Zendocon** clearly belongs to the second category. This horizontal shooter for the Atari Lynx bet on inventiveness and weirdness instead of stark seriousness, and that's exactly how it earned its place in the Lynx library.

You fly from right to left across dozens of levels, yet not linearly — the game is famous for its system of portals through which you switch between utterly different, often peculiar worlds. Each gate can dump you into a level full of unexpected enemies and curious environments, so there are far more routes here than you'll see in a single run. This structure lends the game an air of exploration you wouldn't expect from an ordinary "fly and shoot" title.

As one of the console's early titles it showed what the pocket hardware could do in a genre that relies on smooth movement and swarms of enemies. The feel of flying, shooting and collecting upgrades is brisk, and both the contemporary press and players ranked it alongside other solid Lynx shooters.

It's not a title that tries to be the most precise or most demanding shooter of its time. Its charm lies in variety and playful imagination — in the fact that you never quite know what awaits you beyond the next gate. That makes it a fun ride for anyone who enjoys a game that can surprise them.

Today **Gates of Zendocon** is one of those Lynx exclusives worth trying precisely for its distinctiveness — a reminder of an era when creators could afford to be thoroughly quirky.

**Why play:** A brisk and inventive horizontal shooter full of portals and bizarre worlds, entertaining through exploration and a distinctive imagination.

atari-lynx__todd-s-adventures-in-slime-w.detail: Exploratory action close to a metroidvania (you freely explore interconnected slimy caves and collect samples), famous for its early "gross-out" humor. It supported co-op via ComLynx. An interesting, ambitious title for its time.
atari-lynx__todd-s-adventures-in-slime-w.article:
Not every game from 1990 had the courage to be so grossly entertaining — **Todd's Adventures in Slime World** wasn't afraid of dirt, slime and humor that many an animated series would be proud of today. And beneath that gelatinous shell hid a surprisingly ambitious exploratory action game.

As the hero Todd you push your way through interconnected slimy caves, collecting samples and looking for a way out. The structure is close to a metroidvania — instead of linear progress you freely explore branching corridors, backtrack and gradually uncover the map. Slime isn't just scenery: it sticks to you, dirties you and you have to get rid of it, which gives exploration a distinctive mechanic and the typical "gross-out" charm that earned the game its reputation.

The studio **Epyx** also built in support for co-op play via the **ComLynx** cable, so you could wade through the caves as a duo — a remarkable feature on a pocket console in the early nineties. Linking two Lynxes to explore a slimy world together was something the competition couldn't boast at the time.

For its era this was an unusually ambitious title. Instead of a single repeating screen there was a sprawling interconnected world to discover, its own atmosphere and humor that pulled no punches. That made **Todd's Adventures in Slime World** one of the more distinctive games in the early Lynx lineup.

Today you'll appreciate it mainly as a bold experiment — proof that even at the dawn of color handhelds there were creators who wanted to offer more than just fast action and bet on exploration, mood and a hearty dose of slime.

**Why play:** Ambitious exploratory action with a metroidvania flavor, distinctive gross-out humor and co-op via ComLynx — one of the most distinctive early Lynx titles.

atari-lynx__rygar.detail: Considered by many the best port and one of the best Lynx games ever. It draws on the arcade classic but adds a story (a prophet and Rygar's quest against Ligar) and your main weapon is a yo-yo shield. Smooth, fair action with no cheap deaths; a visual gem. "A master class from start to finish."
atari-lynx__rygar.article:
There are ports that leave you reminiscing about the original, and then those that quietly surpass it. **Rygar** on the Atari Lynx belongs to that second, rarer group — many consider it the best port and one of the best games ever released on the console.

It draws on the arcade classic, but doesn't settle for a mere copy. It adds a narrative anchor — a prophet, the hero Rygar's quest and his campaign against the evil Ligar — and above all plays with your iconic weapon: the yo-yo shield you launch at enemies, which gives combat a unique rhythm and reach. The action-platformer progression here is smooth and fair, with none of the cheap deaths players so often complained about with less honest titles of the era.

For what the Lynx can do, **Rygar** is a visual gem. Colorful, detailed environments, clean animation and a brisk pace rank it among the console's technical high points. **Atari** worked on the port in collaboration with **Tecmo**, holder of the original brand, and the care for detail shows in every passage — one review aptly called it "a master class from start to finish."

What elevates the game is its balance. It's not frustrating, but neither is it trivial; every fight and every jump feels like you're in control, and death is almost always your mistake, not the ugliness of the design. It's precisely this fairness that makes playing a joy and keeps bringing you back.

For anyone who wants to learn what the Atari Lynx was capable of in the right hands, **Rygar** is an obvious choice — proof that even a pocket console could produce action worthy of the big screen.

**Why play:** Smooth, fair and visually gorgeous action-platformer considered one of the best Lynx games ever — a must for every owner of the console.

atari-lynx__roadblasters.detail: A port of the 1987 arcade game: you race down a track shooting other vehicles and helicopters while dodging obstacles. Extremely fast and often cited as proof of the Lynx's technical superiority — "it looks like a Sega Genesis," not a handheld. A great showcase of the machine's power.
atari-lynx__roadblasters.article:
If in 1990 you wanted to prove to someone that a pocket game didn't have to look like a pocket game, all it took was putting a Lynx running **RoadBlasters** into their hands. "This can't possibly run on a handheld" — that was exactly the reaction this title collected.

It's a port of the 1987 arcade game, and the principle is beautifully straightforward: you race down a track, shoot other vehicles and combat helicopters, dodge obstacles and try to get as far as possible before your fuel runs out. The adrenaline comes mainly from the speed — the track hurtles toward you at such a pace that there's no time to think, and every corner and enemy tests your reflexes.

But the talk was mostly about the technical side. **RoadBlasters** is often cited as proof of the Lynx's hardware superiority: thanks to scaling and color, the sense of speed and depth felt so convincing that players and press alike compared the result to the home console Sega Genesis rather than to a pocket machine. Seeing this on a backlit display in the early nineties was a small revelation.

The studio **Atari** thereby not only expanded the console's library with another arcade gem, but above all handed owners ammunition for the endless debates over whose handheld was technically ahead. And on that front, **RoadBlasters** spoke clearly.

As a game it's pure arcade riding — no complications, just the pedal to the floor, a finger on the trigger and the drive to get farther than last time. Exactly the type of title you switch on for five minutes and get up from half an hour later.

**Why play:** A blazingly fast arcade ride with shooting that fully shows off the Lynx's technical power — feeling like you're holding a home console in your palm.

atari-lynx__s-t-u-n-runner.detail: A port of an arcade game whose only home conversion was made specifically for the Lynx — you hurtle through a futuristic tunnel at supersonic speed and shoot. The Lynx's scaling delivers a superb sense of speed. A unique piece for fans of arcade action.
atari-lynx__s-t-u-n-runner.article:
A supersonic tunnel, a futuristic vehicle and speed that blurs the picture before your eyes — **S.T.U.N. Runner** was arcade adrenaline in its purest form, and on the Atari Lynx in a version you couldn't get anywhere else. This conversion is, after all, the only home port of the game ever made.

The principle combines racing and shooting into a single experience. You hurtle through a twisting tunnel at supersonic speed, dodging obstacles, collecting speed boosts and shooting at everything in your way. It's not about careful planning — it's about reflexes, about reading the track in the last fractions of a second, and about the courage to floor it even more.

The key to the experience is, once again, the Lynx's hardware scaling. It's what creates that dizzying sense of speed, where the tunnel rushes toward you and the surroundings grow and vanish at such a pace that you've got your hands full keeping the vehicle on the track. On a pocket console this was an effect the rivals simply couldn't imitate, and **Atari** made full use of it here.

Because it's the only home conversion of this arcade game, the Lynx version holds special value for collectors and fans. Anyone who wanted to play S.T.U.N. Runner at home had no other choice — and got a version that captured the spirit of the original surprisingly faithfully.

It's a genuine one-off: a piece of arcade history that survived precisely and only thanks to this console. For lovers of fast, purely reflexive action it's one of the most tempting reasons to pull out the Lynx.

**Why play:** The only home port of supersonic arcade racing with shooting, which thanks to Lynx scaling offers an intoxicating sense of speed — a unique piece for fans of arcade action.

atari-lynx__xybots.detail: A pseudo-3D maze shooter from a behind-the-hero view (Metroid-style aliens), a forerunner of the style of later 3D shooters. Technically impressive in your pocket for 1991. Co-op via ComLynx.
atari-lynx__xybots.article:
A view from behind the hero's back, a maze full of aliens and pseudo-3D that on a pocket console in 1991 seemed almost impossible — **Xybots** was one of those titles that make you wonder how it could ever have run in your palm.

It's a maze shooter from the unusual perspective behind the character's back as they push through cramped corridors and eliminate robotic enemies whose styling recalls the aliens from the Metroid series. The game combines action with spatial orientation — you have to track the map, find your way and at the same time react to enemies lurking around corners. In the way it works with perspective and movement through the maze, it foreshadows the style of later 3D shooters.

For 1991 and for pocket hardware this was a technically impressive piece. Creating a convincing impression of real-time movement through space on a portable console was no given, and **Xybots** was among the titles with which **Atari** showed that the Lynx could handle more ambitious forms than flat 2D.

Co-op via the **ComLynx** cable isn't missing either, so you could face the maze as a pair. Exploring corridors together and covering each other's backs added tension and a strategic dimension that solo play doesn't offer.

Today **Xybots** is interesting mainly as a bridge between the classic arcade shooter and the later era of 3D action — a reminder of the moment when developers were trying to pull the player into space, even before the hardware could do it comfortably. For fans of retro experiments it's a tempting stop.

**Why play:** A pseudo-3D maze shooter that impresses technically for 1991 and foreshadows later 3D action — with co-op via ComLynx on top.

atari-lynx__robotron-2084.detail: A port of the twin-stick shooter arcade legend (one stick moves you, the other aims). Endless replayability — every run different, pure reflexes and pattern recognition. It proved that a complex arcade game works even on a handheld. "Just one more try" in its purest form.
atari-lynx__robotron-2084.article:
Two sticks, thousands of enemies and a single goal: to survive one second longer. **Robotron: 2084** is the purest distillation of arcade action ever created, and its arrival on the **Atari Lynx** in 1991 was a small miracle of engineering. Williams' 1982 original was built on a brilliant control scheme no one else had at the time: one stick moves you, the other independently aims and fires. On a handheld this meant cramming two directional controllers into a single box under your thumbs, and the Lynx pulled it off surprisingly well.

The principle is brutally simple and all the more addictive for it. You find yourself in the middle of a screen flooded with hordes of robots trying to crush you, while the last human family runs around the edges, whom you try to save before the **Brains** convert or kill them. There's no story, no menu full of options, just pure reflex, peripheral vision and the ability to read the patterns of chaos. Every run looks different, because the enemies swarm dynamically and you learn when to dodge, when to shoot and when to sacrifice a civilian for your own survival.

It's precisely this endless replayability that makes Robotron a legend. The game has no ending in the traditional sense, just a growing number of waves and your personal score as the only measure. It's the embodiment of that famous **"just one more try"** feeling, when you die, pound your fist on the table and instantly hit the button for a new attempt. On a portable console, played in short bursts, it was the ideal format.

The Lynx version also showed something important for the whole platform: that a complex, fast arcade game needn't be the preserve of big cabinets in the arcades. That even in your pocket you could carry adrenaline capable of racing your heart. At a time when the rival Game Boy offered slower, more deliberate experiences, Robotron on the color Lynx was proof that Atari's handheld was aimed at players who wanted a real punch.

Today Robotron: 2084 is written into game-design textbooks as a model of purity and instant clarity. Its twin-stick mechanic influenced dozens of later titles from Geometry Wars to independent arcade shooters. The Lynx port isn't the most famous version, but it's a testament to the ambitions of a console that wasn't afraid to reach for the most demanding arcade jewels.

**Why play:** For genuine twin-stick action adrenaline in its purest form, where only reflexes and a cool head amid the chaos count.

atari-lynx__klax.detail: Atari's answer to Tetris: you catch falling colored tiles on a conveyor belt and arrange them into rows of the same color (horizontal, vertical, diagonal). Addictive, brisk; one of the console's best puzzlers.
atari-lynx__klax.article:
It's falling. It keeps falling. And you only have a few seconds to decide where to put it. **Klax** was Atari's answer to the Tetris fever of the late 1980s, and it arrived on the **Atari Lynx** in 1990 as one of the finest puzzle titles in the console's entire library. Its motto sounded half-joking, half-prophetic: "it is the nineties and there is time for Klax."

The mechanic is refreshingly different from Tetris. Colored tiles slide toward you along a moving belt and you catch them in a kind of paddle at the bottom of the screen. Then you set them down into a grid so as to form **klaxes**, meaning rows of three or more of the same color horizontally, vertically or diagonally. At the same time you have to make sure your stack of caught tiles doesn't overflow, and meet each round's goals, whether that's a certain number of klaxes or a points target. The result is a pleasant tension between catching and placing.

On the Lynx's small color display the game truly blossoms. The colors are bright and easily distinguishable, which is absolutely crucial for a puzzle that depends on telling shades apart, and the brisk pace can absorb you for long stretches of time. The gradually increasing belt speed turns what starts as a calm logic game into a test of reflexes and spatial imagination at once.

Klax was created at Atari Games as an arcade cabinet and quickly spread to countless platforms, because its concept was universally appealing. The Lynx version, however, is among the most accomplished precisely thanks to the display's color, which the monochrome competition simply couldn't offer. For console owners it was one of those titles you switched on "just for a moment" and put down an hour later.

Today Klax ranks among the respected classics of the "falling block" puzzle genre, alongside Tetris, Columns or Dr. Mario. It isn't as famous as its role models, but among connoisseurs it holds a firm place thanks to its original catch-and-place mechanic, which sets it apart from mere block dropping.

**Why play:** For addictive, colorful logic that will easily rob you of an evening and offer a refreshing alternative to eternal Tetris.

atari-lynx__xenophobe.detail: The Lynx version is considered the best version of the game ever. You clear space stations of aliens, and the large sprites look great on the small display. Up to four-player co-op (one player can even play as an alien) — a groundbreaking asymmetry for 1990. Epyx delivered a superb port.
atari-lynx__xenophobe.article:
Space stations infested with aliens, and three friends clearing them out together, room by room. **Xenophobe** on the **Atari Lynx** from 1990 is generally regarded as the very best existing version of this arcade classic, and for a port that is rare praise indeed. Where home conversions suffered from compromises, Epyx did work that is still remembered with respect today.

The premise is B-movie sci-fi and all the more fun for it. As an alien hunter you make your way through infested stations in a side view, exploring corridors and cabins, collecting weapons and eliminating the intruders before they take over the station completely. The large, detailed enemy sprites look surprisingly effective on the Lynx's small display and lend the action just the right dose of slimy horror that the genre demands.

The biggest asset, however, is **cooperation**. The game supports up to four players via the ComLynx console link, and what's innovative is that one of the players can even play as the alien itself and ruin everyone else's plans. This **asymmetry**, where one person plays against the rest of the group in the role of the monster, was an unexpectedly progressive idea for 1990, one that mainstream games only really discovered many years later.

The Lynx version benefits from the fact that the console was designed from the ground up for linking multiple units, so multiplayer wasn't an add-on crutch but a natural part of the design. Clearing stations together with friends was exactly the kind of experience Atari wanted to sell with its console, and Xenophobe delivered it better than most of the era's competition.

Xenophobe originated as an arcade cabinet from Bally/Midway, and its atmosphere clearly drew on the era's wave of space horror in the wake of the film Alien's success. The Lynx conversion by Epyx, a studio closely tied to the console's very birth, is prized among collectors today precisely as an example of what a well-made handheld arcade port should look like.

**Why play:** For the best version of the classic alien-blasting brawl and a surprisingly modern asymmetric co-op where one of the group can become the monster.

atari-lynx__ms-pac-man.detail: The Lynx version adds extra mazes over the arcade, a „speced boost“ power-up and the ported animated cutscenes. Only the two-player mode is missing. A charming and faithful port of the classic; ideal for „just one game“.
atari-lynx__ms-pac-man.article:
The most famous yellow lady in video game history returned to the **Atari Lynx** in 1990 in a version that has something to offer even seasoned fans of the original. **Ms. Pac-Man** was never just a cosmetic variation on Pac-Man; it was an improved, more dynamic game, and the Lynx port carries that legacy forward with grace.

The foundation remains immortal. You cruise through a maze, gobble dots, dodge the four ghosts, and the moment you swallow a big energizing pellet the roles reverse and you can set off after the frightened ghosts yourself. Ms. Pac-Man added several mazes instead of one over the original game, moving bonus fruit, and generally less predictable ghost behavior, so it couldn't be beaten with memorized patterns alone.

The Lynx version goes even further and enriches the experience with things the arcade didn't have. It offers **extra mazes** on top, a power-up in the form of a **speed boost** that briefly lets you escape the ghosts more easily, and it also carries over the cute animated interludes that told the tales of Mr. and Mrs. Pac-Man. The only thing that's noticeably missing is the two-player mode from some other versions; otherwise it's a generous package.

On the console's color display the game looks charming and clean. The bright colors of the mazes and characters make the Lynx an ideal platform for this kind of instantly comprehensible fun. It's exactly the sort of game you switch on "for one round" in a queue or on the bus and walk away feeling you've given your reflexes a proper workout.

Ms. Pac-Man is among the most successful arcade games of all time and its character became a cultural icon. The Lynx conversion is a faithful yet enriched tribute to the classic, one that proved even a time-tested concept can be freshened up on new hardware without losing its charm.

**Why play:** For a faithful and moreover enriched port of an immortal classic with extra mazes and a speed boost, ideal for a quick portion of nostalgia.

atari-lynx__shanghai.detail: Classic tile logic: you remove pairs of matching mahjong tiles from a pile until they all disappear. Calm, meditative, endlessly replayable. Highly rated among Lynx fans for its replay value.
atari-lynx__shanghai.article:
A pile of seemingly chaotically stacked tiles and before you a question: can you take it apart down to the last pair? **Shanghai** brought the ancient charm of mahjong solitaire to the **Atari Lynx** in 1990 in a form that fans of the console still praise today for its endless replayability.

The rules are elegantly simple, mastery of them decidedly not. Before you lies a pile of mahjong tiles stacked in several layers, and your task is to remove **pairs of identical tiles** until they all disappear. The catch is that you can only remove tiles that are "free," meaning uncovered from above and accessible from the side. Each move thus changes the structure of the pile, and the wrong order can lead you into a dead end where no valid move remains.

This makes Shanghai far more than a passive search for pairs. It's a **logic game about foresight**, where you have to plan ahead and decide which pair to sacrifice now so as not to block your path to later tiles. And yet the whole experience feels immensely calm and meditative, with no time pressure, no enemies, just you and the puzzle.

It is precisely this contemplative nature that makes it an ideal handheld title. Where other games pulse with adrenaline, Shanghai offers silence and concentration, a session during which you switch off your mind from the outside world. Among Lynx fans it's highly rated precisely for its **replay value**, because every new deal of the tiles is a new challenge and the game practically never grows stale.

Shanghai popularized the genre of computer mahjong solitaire and inspired countless imitators on every conceivable platform. The Lynx version brings this classic concept faithfully and comfortably into your pocket, becoming a quiet but persistent companion to anyone who enjoys stress-free puzzles.

**Why play:** For calm, meditative logic that never ages and that beautifully clears your head anytime, anywhere.

atari-lynx__crystal-mines-ii.detail: A „Lynx staple“ — a digging logic-action game (à la Boulder Dash/Repton) where, as a robot, you mine crystals, destroy obstacles and figure out how to get out, across dozens of levels. Huge amount of content and an addictive loop; one of the platform's darlings.
atari-lynx__crystal-mines-ii.article:
If there's one title that **Atari Lynx** fans utter with love almost automatically, it's **Crystal Mines II**. This digging logic-action game from 1992 became one of the platform's darlings thanks to a huge portion of content and a loop that's hard to step out of.

The concept follows the famous lineage of games like Boulder Dash and Repton. You control a small **mining robot** that digs through intricate levels, collects scattered crystals, destroys obstacles and searches for a way to the exit. But this isn't just simple digging, it's a puzzle: you have to weigh where to burrow so falling boulders don't crush you, how to skirt or eliminate enemies, and how to gather enough crystals to open the passage onward.

The game's charm lies in the tension between action and thinking. One hasty move can trap or crush you, so every step wants to be considered, and yet the pace is brisk enough to keep you on your toes. New kinds of obstacles, enemies and mechanisms gradually pile up, so the game keeps changing and won't let you get complacent.

On the Lynx the title's **enormous scope** particularly stands out. Dozens of elaborate levels mean there's content here for long hours, which in terms of value-for-fun made Crystal Mines II an exceptionally generous purchase. For a portable console, where people played in short bursts, it was an ideal structure where you could tackle a few levels and continue whenever you liked.

This combination of addictive, thoughtful gameplay and a generous amount of content earned Crystal Mines II a reputation as one of the console's defining games. It's neither a port of a famous arcade game nor a licensed blockbuster, and yet it managed to win a place in Lynx owners' hearts purely by the strength of its design, which is the best possible compliment for any game title.

**Why play:** For an addictive combination of digging logic and action with a huge helping of levels, one of the true darlings of the entire Lynx platform.

atari-lynx__double-dragon.detail: Often called the best beat 'em up on the Lynx. Billy Lee rescues a kidnapped girl from the Black Warriors gang. A solid port of the classic with smooth action; great for short sessions.
atari-lynx__double-dragon.article:
Your girl has been kidnapped by the Black Warriors gang and you have only two fists and a properly angry heart. **Double Dragon** arrived on the **Atari Lynx** in 1991 and many consider it the very best beat 'em up of the entire console, which for a genre so dependent on smooth action is no small thing.

The story is the archetypal 1980s brawler in its purest form. As **Billy Lee** you fight your way through streets full of thugs to free the kidnapped Marian from the clutches of a criminal gang. You advance from left to right, dishing out kicks and punches, picking up dropped weapons like a whip or a knife, and facing waves of enemies who harass you from every direction.

Double Dragon is today rightly regarded as one of the cornerstones of the entire beat 'em up genre. The arcade original by the Japanese studio **Technōs** in 1987 popularized cooperative screen-scrolling brawling and inspired a whole wave of imitators from Final Fight to Streets of Rage. Its influence on what arcades looked like at the turn of the 1980s and 1990s is enormous.

The Lynx port carries this classic over with solid, smooth action, which for brawlers is everything. On the small display the characters move briskly and the fights have the necessary punch, so the game suits short, intense play sessions where in a few minutes you thoroughly air out your reflexes and leave the day's frustration on the street hoodlums.

Although the most famous versions of Double Dragon were made in arcades and on home consoles, the Lynx conversion deserves recognition as one of the few truly successful handheld attempts to bring a fast brawler into your pocket. For genre fans and for those who want to taste a piece of history, it's an accomplished choice.

**Why play:** For a classic street brawler with smooth action, ideal for short, juicy doses of dispensing justice with your fists.

atari-lynx__ninja-gaiden-iii.detail: More of an action-platformer variation than an exact port of the NES game — multi-tiered levels, varied enemies, brisk ninja action. Smooth animation and good design; accomplished for action fans.
atari-lynx__ninja-gaiden-iii.article:
The name **Ninja Gaiden** evokes in players a respect mixed with a slight shiver down the spine, and rightly so. The version for the **Atari Lynx** from 1993, however, is not an exact imprint of the notoriously demanding NES game, but a distinctive action-platformer variation that goes its own way.

Instead of a faithful port, the Lynx offers **multi-tiered levels** through which the ninja slashes up and down, faces a varied palette of enemies and uses brisk, acrobatic moves to overcome traps. It's a design that draws more on the spirit of the series than it copies any specific installment, thereby avoiding the risk that the handheld couldn't bear the full complexity of the source.

Visually the game benefits from what the Lynx always had in abundance, namely **smooth animation** and colorful presentation. The ninja moves fluidly, his attacks have swing, and the whole action maintains the brisk pace that is key to the genre. The variety of enemies and environments then ensures that the gameplay doesn't grow stale and every tier brings something new.

The Ninja Gaiden series comes from the workshop of the Japanese **Tecmo** and became famous for two things: on the NES for cinematic interludes that pushed storytelling in games further, and in arcades for brutal difficulty. The Lynx version doesn't reach the renown of its predecessors, but as an action-platformer title it holds up and offers ninja action in portable form.

For fans of fast action and platformers this version is an accomplished, if somewhat overlooked, piece of the Lynx library. Don't expect an exact replica of the famous installments, but a standalone game that honors the name on the cover with solid design and a pleasant sense of movement.

**Why play:** For brisk ninja action with smooth animation and multi-tiered levels, an accomplished variation on a famous brand tailored for the handheld.

atari-lynx__desert-strike.detail: The Lynx version of the isometric helicopter action game (originally Mega Drive), where you complete military missions in enemy territory and watch your fuel and ammunition. Military themes were popular in the early 90s; a decent portable conversion.
atari-lynx__desert-strike.article:
A helicopter, a parched desert and missions you must not return from empty-handed. **Desert Strike** arrived on the **Atari Lynx** in 1993 as a portable version of the isometric military action game that originally made its name on the Mega Drive and caught the era's wave of interest in modern military conflict.

You take a seat in the cockpit of a combat helicopter and from an **isometric view** carry out a series of military tasks deep in enemy territory. You destroy targets, rescue allies and progress through missions that combine action with a pinch of tactical thinking. The game isn't about mindless shooting: you constantly have to watch your **fuel and ammunition** and return for supplies, or the desert will swallow you before the enemy does.

This very resource management set Desert Strike apart from ordinary shooters. It created a tension where you had to weigh every shot and every detour, because arriving with an empty tank meant the end. This layer of thinking gave the action depth and forced players to behave more like a prudent commander than a fearless Rambo.

Military themes were very popular in the early 1990s, among other reasons in the echoes of the era's conflicts, and EA's Strike series recorded a notable success at the time. The Lynx version brings this concept into your pocket as a decent portable conversion that preserves the core of the experience, though on a smaller screen it loses a little of the original presentation's grandeur.

For console owners it was a welcome expansion of the genre offering with something action-tactical that stood apart from simple arcades. Desert Strike on the Lynx isn't the most famous version of this game, but it represents an interesting piece of the era's wave of military games in a form you could take anywhere with you.

**Why play:** For isometric helicopter action with tactical management of fuel and ammunition, a portable portion of military tension from the early nineties.

atari-lynx__battlezone-2000.detail: A trio of arcade conversions. Battlezone 2000 is a vector tank shooter (a modernized classic), Hydra combat-boat racing, Checkered Flag Formula racing with surprisingly brisk controls. For fans of arcade action and racing.
atari-lynx__battlezone-2000.article:
Three arcade classics in one, from tank duels through boat racing to Formula cars. The Lynx offering around **Battlezone 2000** represents a trio of conversions that together show how varied arcade entertainment could be and how well the **Atari Lynx** managed to handle it.

The flagship is **Battlezone 2000** itself, a modernized version of the legendary **vector tank shooter** from 1980. You take a seat in a tank, look around a desolate battlefield and eliminate enemy vehicles from a first-person view. The original Battlezone was one of the first truly 3D experiences in arcades and its wireframe graphics went down in history; the Lynx variant dusts off this iconic concept for a new era.

The second piece is **Hydra**, races of armed fast boats where it's about a combination of speed and combat on the water's surface. The adrenaline here springs from drifting between obstacles while simultaneously fending off rivals, so it's not a purely racing experience but brisk action with a hearty dose of aggression.

The trio is rounded off by **Checkered Flag**, Formula racing that surprised on the Lynx with unexpectedly brisk and satisfying controls. The sense of speed and cornering managed to conjure real tension on a handheld of that time, and for fans of racing games it was a welcome piece for the collection.

Together this offering demonstrates the breadth of what the Lynx could handle, from historical vector action through water skirmishing to pure racing. For fans of arcade action and racing it's a varied package that reminds us Atari's portable console wasn't afraid to reach for the most diverse genres and faces of the arcade heritage.

**Why play:** For a varied trio of arcade classics from vector tank duels to brisk racing, a showcase of the Lynx console's genre breadth.

atari-lynx__hydra.article:
Picture a speedboat crammed with weapons hurtling across the water's surface while you deliver dubious packages to dubious clients. That's exactly what **Hydra** on the Atari Lynx is, a hybrid of racing and shooter that squeezed the maximum out of the console's capabilities.

The premise is simple and addictive. You move in a semi-pseudo-3D perspective, overtaking rivals while firing at obstacles and enemies that get in your way. For delivered packages you earn money, which you then spend on upgrades to your vessel, from stronger weapons to a better engine. This loop between driving, shooting and gradual upgrades gives the game a drive that wasn't a given on a pocket console from the turn of the 1980s and 1990s.

The Lynx was a technical marvel in its day. A color backlit display, hardware sprite scaling and a rotatable screen made it a markedly more capable machine than the rival Game Boy. **Hydra** is among the titles that liked to show off these capabilities: the speed effect, the enlarging of objects approaching the player and the smooth sense of movement over water looked striking on the small screen.

In genre terms the game fits into the wave of pseudo-3D arcade racers, where it wasn't just about finishing first but about surviving and getting rich. It's a title played in short, intense bursts, ideal for the nature of a pocket console. The difficulty grows, the wallet is forever empty, and you keep coming back for another try.

Today **Hydra** is more of a curiosity for collectors and Lynx fans than a broad classic, but that is precisely what makes it an interesting piece in the mosaic of what handheld gaming could do at the start of the nineties. It's proof of the ambitions of a platform that was ahead of its time but failed commercially.

**Why play:** For a brisk combination of racing and shooting that shows just how much the underrated Atari Lynx could mine out of a small screen.

atari-lynx__checkered-flag.article:
A racing game on a pocket console that wasn't afraid to try a real cockpit perspective was quite a piece of nerve in its year of release. **Checkered Flag** for the Atari Lynx offered exactly that and made use of the hardware tricks the console was proud of.

Instead of a plain top-down view, the game sat you in a pseudo-3D race from the driver's perspective. The Lynx's rotating screen, sprite scaling and the effort to create an illusion of depth were meant to evoke the feeling that you really were sitting behind the wheel, hurtling down the track. The goal is to drive the circuits, overtake rivals and deliver that proverbial checkered finish flag first.

The Lynx had an ace up its sleeve called ComLynx, a cable link between multiple consoles, and racing games were exactly the genre where shared play made the most sense. Competing with a friend on the console next to you had an entirely different charge than beating artificial intelligence.

It's fair to say that the ambition here sometimes outran the hardware's capabilities and the sense of driving wasn't always as smooth as a player might have wished. Even so, **Checkered Flag** remains an interesting testament to how seriously Atari took the Lynx's technical capabilities and how it tried to offer experiences the competition on monochrome displays couldn't.

Today it's a title mainly for platform enthusiasts and collectors who want to taste what attempts at realistic racing looked like on a pocket console at the start of the nineties. As a historical artifact it has its charm.

**Why play:** For a look into the cockpit from an era when pocket consoles weren't afraid to dream of real 3D racing, and the Lynx gave it a full-hearted try.

atari-lynx__rampart.detail: A hybrid of strategy and action: between rounds you repair and expand walls (Tetris-like piece placement), then position cannons and bombard the enemy in real time. An original loop, excellent in two-player.
atari-lynx__rampart.article:
What do you get when you cross Tetris with an artillery duel and a castle siege? You get **Rampart**, one of the most original gameplay loops of its time, and the Lynx brought its arcade version along for the ride.

The game's charm lies in its rhythm. First comes the building phase: under time pressure you assemble walls around your cannons from falling pieces, exactly as if you were placing Tetris blocks. Once your fortifications are closed off, the game switches into action and you bombard the enemy in real time, whether they're ships or a rival's castle. Then comes another building round in which you have to repair the damage and expand your territory, or it's over.

This loop of building, fighting and repairing is brilliantly simple and at the same time nerve-wracking. It constantly forces you to think ahead about where to place cannons and how to efficiently close off the walls before time runs out. Released by Atari in 1991, **Rampart** is among those games whose idea survived decades and saw many ports to the most diverse platforms.

On the Lynx the game benefits from the color screen, which helps quickly distinguish what's yours and what's the rival's, crucial in hectic moments. And as the description rightly notes, **Rampart** is excellent in two-player. Over the ComLynx link a friendly duel becomes a battle of nerves, decided by finger speed as much as tactical thinking.

It is precisely that hybrid nature, half puzzle, half action strategy, that makes **Rampart** a timeless title. It's not just a quick fix but a game with its own identity, one that still plays superbly today and hasn't aged the way one would expect from a title of the early nineties.

**Why play:** For an original loop of building walls and bombarding the enemy that brilliantly combines puzzle with action, and above all in two-player it's a small miracle.

atari-lynx__gauntlet-third-encounter.detail: A Lynx spin-off of the famous dungeon series featuring a lineup of unconventional classes (from a nerd to an android) and a fight through hordes of enemies. Co-op via ComLynx. Brisk hack-and-slash with loot collecting; a likeable Lynx take.
atari-lynx__gauntlet-third-encounter.article:
Step into the dungeon, hack through hordes of enemies, collect gold and food before your life runs out, that is the ritual the **Gauntlet** series burned into the memory of an entire generation. **Gauntlet: The Third Encounter** is a Lynx spin-off of this legend, and it does things its own way.

Instead of the classic quartet of warrior, wizard, elf and Valkyrie, a colorful and unexpected roster of classes awaits you here. You can play as anyone from a nerd to an android, which gives this version a quirky, almost humorous identity that defies expectations. The core of the game, however, stays faithful to the original: you battle your way through top-down mazes, mow down endless throngs of monsters, and your main enemy is your own dwindling life meter.

That feeling of constant pressure, where your health drains on its own and you have to rush toward the next meal and treasure, is what made **Gauntlet** so addictive. On the Lynx this adrenaline-fueled chase keeps its brisk pace, and the color screen helps you stay oriented amid the flood of enemies.

Released in 1990, the game is one of the titles that made use of the ComLynx link for cooperative play. And co-op is exactly where **Gauntlet** always shone brightest, with two players fighting their way through the dungeon at the same time, sharing the loot and occasionally, unintentionally, getting in each other's way. Cooperation and rivalry rolled into one.

In the end this Lynx version is a likeable and brisk representative of the brand. It is not the full-blooded arcade original, but a cleverly transplanted experience for the small screen, enriched by the choice of unconventional classes. For fans of dungeon brawlers, a pleasant surprise.

**Why play:** For the brisk battling through hordes of enemies with an unconventional choice of classes and ComLynx co-op that captures the spirit of the classic Gauntlet on the go.

atari-lynx__battlewheels.detail: Battle cars in an arena from a first-person view, with ComLynx multiplayer support. A game that „dangerously pushes the Lynx to its limits“ — technically ambitious. A curiosity for fans of vehicular combat.
atari-lynx__battlewheels.article:
Battle cars, a fight-to-the-death arena and a view straight from the cockpit, **Battlewheels** was a pretty bold idea for the year 1993 and a handheld console. And that is exactly how it played, like a title trying to squeeze the console down to its last byte.

You take the wheel of an armed vehicle and throw yourself into an arena where the only rule is to survive. From a first-person perspective you drive, maneuver and fire at opponents who crave exactly the same thing, to blast you to scrap. This blend of driving and combat, vehicular combat, was a genre that wanted to combine the adrenaline of racing with the satisfaction of destroying enemies.

The developers at Beyond Games reached for ambitions that, as a period description aptly notes, dangerously pushed the Lynx to its limits. Rendering a convincing cockpit view in real time on early-nineties handheld hardware was a technical nut to crack, and it is precisely this audacity that makes **Battlewheels** an interesting piece of the platform's history.

The game also supported ComLynx multiplayer, so arena battles could be fought against living opponents. And that was always the best way to experience a game like this, because nothing replaces the tension of a duel with a real person on the other console.

Today **Battlewheels** is more of a curiosity for fans of the battle-vehicle genre and Lynx collectors than a widely known classic. But as proof of technical courage and an effort to push the handheld beyond the boundaries of what was expected of it, it holds a firm place.

**Why play:** For technically ambitious battle-car combat from the driver's view that pushed the Atari Lynx to its limits, a treat for fans of vehicular combat.

atari-lynx__electrocop.article:
Handheld consoles usually settled for simple platformers, but the Atari Lynx had bigger ambitions, and **Electrocop** is a good example of that. An action title that tried to bring more to the small screen than just platforming basics.

You take on the role of a cybernetic cop whose task is to fight through an enemy complex. The game mixes action with elements of exploration and puzzles, so it is not just about shooting everything that moves, but also about finding your bearings in the environment and pushing deeper into the heart of the base. This combination gave the game more depth than many competing handheld titles of its era offered.

The Lynx could once again show off its strengths here. The color backlit display and its ability to work with sprites made it possible to render both the complex's environment and its enemies with a level of detail that owners of monochrome consoles could only envy. **Electrocop** was one of the titles meant to present the platform as a serious player in the field of handheld gaming.

By genre the game sits among action titles with a light touch of exploration, where the pace alternates with calmer moments of finding the way forward. It is not a mindless shooter, but an experience that also demands a bit of thought and patience from the player.

Today **Electrocop** is a reminder of the era when Atari tried to prove that a handheld console need not be just a toy for a brief moment. For enthusiasts of the platform and lovers of retro action, it is an interesting stop in the Lynx catalog.

**Why play:** For action with a touch of exploration that shows the Atari Lynx aimed higher than short arcade experiences, and the cyberpunk police setting suits it well.

atari-lynx__scrapyard-dog.article:
A dog on a journey to rescue its beloved pet, that is a premise that sounds like a cute fairy tale, but **Scrapyard Dog** hides behind it an honest platformer in the spirit of the genre's finest traditions. And on the Atari Lynx it was a welcome colorful addition.

You guide your four-legged hero through a series of levels full of enemies, chasms and obstacles. Platformers of this type stood or fell on the precision of the controls, a feel for jumps and clever level design, and it is precisely this classic recipe that forms the core of the experience. You jump, dodge hazards and search for the path to the end of each level.

On the Lynx the game benefits from the color screen, which was able to give the platformer a more cheerful and lively character than competing handheld machines offered. Colorful backgrounds and legible sprites help distinguish where it is safe to jump and where danger lurks, which is absolutely essential in a platformer.

The platformer genre was the royal discipline of the eight-bit and sixteen-bit era, and every platform longed to have its mascot and its flagship platformer. **Scrapyard Dog** fits into this tradition as a likeable representative that does not try to reinvent the wheel, but honestly delivers what you expect from a good platformer.

For Lynx owners and fans of retro platformers it is a pleasant title that reminds us handheld gaming of the early nineties was not just about shooters and racers, but also about classic jumping toward a simple, touching goal.

**Why play:** For an honest, colorful platformer with a sweet story about a dog's devotion that on the Atari Lynx delivers the best of the genre's classics.

atari-lynx__wyvern-tales.article:
You think a handheld console from 1989 is long dead? You only think so until you run into **Wyvern Tales**, a modern homebrew JRPG that proves the Atari Lynx still has something to offer even after decades, and that the community of enthusiasts never sleeps.

The homebrew scene around classic consoles is a fascinating phenomenon. These are developers who, out of love for the platform, create brand-new games for hardware that officially finished its journey decades ago. **Wyvern Tales** is one such fruit, a Japanese-flavored RPG adventure tailored to the Lynx's capabilities, created long after the console's commercial end.

The JRPG genre lures players with story, world exploration, a combat system and the gradual growth of characters. Bringing such an experience to late-eighties handheld hardware is in itself a small technical adventure that shows just how capable the Lynx was in its day, with its color screen and decent performance.

What makes homebrew titles like this one exceptional is precisely that context. This is not the product of a corporate plan, but pure passion, an effort to expand the library of a beloved platform with something new and meaningful. For collectors and Lynx fans, games like these are little holidays.

**Wyvern Tales** is thus more than just a game, it is testimony to the vitality of the retro community and to the fact that a good platform never truly dies as long as there are people willing to create for it. Enter a fantasy world that officially would never have come into being.

**Why play:** For a taste of a modern JRPG on classic hardware and for a fascinating demonstration of how the homebrew community keeps the Atari Lynx alive long after its official end.

saturn__nights-into-dreams.teaser: Dreamlike, flowing action from Sonic's creators; a visual poem.
saturn__nights-into-dreams.detail: Yuji Naka and Naoto Ōshima (the creators of Sonic) wanted to capture the feeling of flying in a dream. You control NiGHTS, a clown-acrobat, and collect points for the elegance and fluidity of flight through rings; it was also sold with an analog controller (the 3D Control Pad). A dreamlike, soothing visual poem. The console's flagship.
saturn__nights-into-dreams.article:
Close your eyes and remember that feeling from a dream, where you float, glide through the air and the laws of gravity cease to apply. It was exactly this fleeting experience that Yuji Naka and Naoto Ōshima, the fathers of Sonic, decided to turn into a game. The result is **NiGHTS into Dreams...**, a visual poem and the flagship of the SEGA Saturn console.

You control NiGHTS, an androgynous clown-acrobat, and fly through the dream worlds of child heroes. Instead of just getting from point A to point B, the game rewards you for elegance and fluidity. You collect points for how smoothly you fly through chains of rings, how gracefully you link one maneuver to another and how long you sustain your flight without hesitation. It is a game about rhythm, the beauty of movement and the satisfaction of a perfectly executed route.

Sonic Team bet on something entirely new here. **NiGHTS** was also sold with an analog controller, the so-called 3D Control Pad, which allowed more sensitive and fluid control of flight than the classic digital d-pad permitted. It was one of the important steps on the road to how we control games in three-dimensional space today.

The atmosphere is utterly distinctive. The music, colors and dreamlike aesthetic merge into a soothing, almost meditative experience that resembles nothing else. It is not a game about combat and frustration, but about the joy of movement and the effort to surpass yourself, to beat your own record, to fly a route a little more elegantly.

To this day **NiGHTS into Dreams...** is revered as one of the defining games of the Saturn and as proof that Sonic Team could do much more than just a blue hedgehog. It is a title that demonstrates games can be an art that touches emotions as much as reflexes.

**Why play:** For the unmistakable feeling of flying in a dream and the dreamlike visual poem from Sonic's creators, one of the most distinctive and beautiful games the SEGA Saturn ever offered.

saturn__panzer-dragoon.teaser: Rail shooter on a dragon's back; the atmosphere of another world.
saturn__panzer-dragoon.detail: A rail shooter where you sit on a dragon's back and fire in 360° in a melancholic post-apocalyptic fantasy world with its own invented language (Panzerese). The atmosphere of an utterly different world; one of the first games to take its setting so seriously. A cult series.
saturn__panzer-dragoon.article:
You sit on the back of a dragon, a crumbling post-apocalyptic world sweeps past beneath you, and all around you hear a language you don't understand, because no one ever spoke it before. Welcome to **Panzer Dragoon**, one of the most atmospheric rail shooters the SEGA Saturn ever hosted.

Mechanically it is a so-called rail shooter, where you move automatically along a predetermined path and your task is to shoot. The genius, however, lies in the fact that you can look around and fire in all 360 degrees around you. Enemies attack from the front, the back and the sides, so you must constantly turn your view, take aim and release volleys of homing missiles. What emerges is a tense ballet of attention and reflexes.

What elevated **Panzer Dragoon** above its genre competition, though, was its atmosphere. Team Andromeda created a melancholic fantasy world that feels like the remnant of a long-vanished civilization. The pinnacle of this devotion to detail is the invented language nicknamed Panzerese, which the characters speak. Few games of the era took their world so deadly seriously and built it with such care.

Released in the mid-nineties, the game was one of the titles meant to give the Saturn its own face and to show that the console could offer experiences with a soul and an artistic vision. The feeling of riding a dragon, the smooth leaning into turns and the melancholic music together form an unforgettable whole.

**Panzer Dragoon** became a cult series that earned sequels and a remake and is beloved to this day for its unique atmosphere. It is one of those titles that make fans remember the Saturn fondly, proof that even a commercially unsuccessful console can leave a lasting artistic legacy.

**Why play:** For the unforgettable feeling of flight on a dragon's back through a world with its own language and a melancholic soul, a cult rail shooter that took its atmosphere utterly seriously.

saturn__panzer-dragoon-ii-zwei.article:
Imagine cutting across the ruined landscape of a post-apocalyptic world on the back of a flying dragon, where every camera movement decides whether you survive. **Panzer Dragoon II Zwei** is the second installment of the cult rail-shooter series that Sega cultivated on its Saturn as a showcase of what its 3D hardware could do. The game builds on the concept of the original Panzer Dragoon and pushes it further in every respect.

The core of the experience remains what made the series famous: you fly forward along a fixed path, but you have full control over looking in all four cardinal directions. Enemies attack from behind, from the sides and from above, and you must constantly turn your view, target swarms of opponents with homing missiles and dodge fire. **Zwei** adds a key novelty compared to the first game — the dragon evolves over the course of the levels and changes form according to your play style, so every playthrough can look a little different. Branching paths across the levels further boost the motivation to play again.

Visually it was one of the proofs that the Saturn could set expansive 3D scenery in motion with breathtaking atmosphere. The world of the Panzer Dragoon series is among the most imaginative in the genre — melancholic, mysterious, full of organic-mechanical structures and its own invented language, which the game even uses in dialogue. This aesthetic cohesion made Panzer Dragoon more than just a shooter; it is a distinctive universe to which the developers returned again and again.

For players used to fast action titles the rail-shooter format may feel unusual at first, but it is precisely the tight choreography of the battles and the music underscoring the epic boss fights that make Zwei an experience that etches itself into memory. It is a game you enjoy in short, intense doses and that you gladly return to for higher scores and uncovering hidden paths.

Thanks to its reputation and its ties to the later, even more legendary installments of the series, **Panzer Dragoon II Zwei** ranks among the titles that defined the Saturn's identity as a console for demanding players and lovers of original worlds.

**Why play:** If you want to experience a rail shooter in its most atmospheric form and immerse yourself in one of the most original game worlds of the nineties, Zwei is a must.

saturn__panzer-dragoon-saga.teaser: A legendary, extremely rare JRPG; one of the holy grails for collectors.
saturn__panzer-dragoon-saga.detail: An action JRPG set in the same world with a unique combat system (you circle around the enemy into an advantageous position). It came out at the very end of the Saturn's life in a tiny print run (around 6,000 copies in the US), making it one of the rarest and most expensive games of all time — a complete copy goes for tens of thousands. The holy grail for collectors; the source code was reportedly lost.
saturn__panzer-dragoon-saga.article:
There are games that are expensive. And then there is **Panzer Dragoon Saga** — the holy grail for collectors, whose complete copies sell today for tens of thousands and about which a legend circulates that even the source code itself was lost. This action JRPG from 1998 is the peak that the studio **Team Andromeda** built under Sega's wing at the end of the Saturn's life — and paradoxically it was precisely this timing that made it one of the rarest titles in the history of gaming.

Saga abandons the series' purely rail-shooter roots and turns them into a full-fledged action RPG set in the same melancholic, post-apocalyptic world. The combat system remains unique to this day: on the back of your dragon you circle around enemies, trying to maneuver into an advantageous position from which your attacks penetrate deepest, while you yourself dodge fire from their vulnerable and armored sides. It is a tactical choreography of movement in real time, interwoven with the thoughtful use of the dragon's forms, which evolve according to how you play.

For its time it was an enormously ambitious project — spread across several discs, with a vast world, voiced dialogue in its own invented language, and a narrative that builds on the mythology of the previous installments and carries it to a climax. The atmosphere of abandoned ruins, flying cities and gigantic mechanical creatures is among the most powerful the era of 32-bit consoles offered.

Saga's legendary status, however, does not rest on quality alone. The game was released in North America in a tiny print run (according to available information on the order of around 6,000 copies) at a time when the Saturn was effectively dying in the West and Sega was pulling its forces toward the Dreamcast. The result is extreme rarity — complete copies are among the most expensive games of all time and it became a symbol of collector's desire and frustration alike. The myth is fed by the repeatedly mentioned fact that the source code was reportedly lost, which for many years complicated any thoughts of a re-release.

Panzer Dragoon Saga thus works today on two levels: as an exceptionally high-quality and original JRPG that was ahead of its time, and at the same time as one of the most legendary pieces of gaming history, spoken of more with reverent awe than as an ordinary game.

**Why play:** It is a unique JRPG with unmistakable combat and atmosphere — and at the same time a living legend that only a few will ever get to play.

saturn__guardian-heroes.teaser: A beat 'em up with RPG and branching; cult Treasure.
saturn__guardian-heroes.detail: A Treasure beat 'em up with RPG progression (experience, branching), three planes of combat you hop between, and a branching story with many endings. A superb versus mode for up to 6 players. Packed with ideas; one of the console's best titles.
saturn__guardian-heroes.article:
When you pour RPG progression, a branching story, three planes of combat and a six-player mode where you beat each other up into a beat 'em up, you get **Guardian Heroes** — one of the most packed titles that ever came out on the Saturn. Behind this 1996 game stands the studio **Treasure**, creators renowned for their ability to cram more ideas into a single game than the competition puts into a whole series, and Guardian Heroes is a shining proof of that.

The foundation is a classic side-scrolling brawler, but Treasure immediately enriched it with a system of experience and character upgrades, so you strengthen your heroes over the course of the game as in an RPG. The battlefield is divided into three planes between which you freely hop to avoid enemies or, conversely, to surround them — which gives the fights unexpected depth and spatiality. Add a mysterious animated skeleton that helps you, and a hectic alternation of attacks, magic and defense.

The biggest draw, however, is the branching story with many different endings. Your decisions over the course of the game change where the plot goes and whom you meet, which dramatically boosts the motivation to play again and again. Few beat 'em ups of the era offered such variability — and few dared to experiment so much with genre boundaries.

When the campaign is exhausted, a superb versus mode awaits you, one that handles up to six players and into which an incredible number of characters from across the whole game are unlocked. Guardian Heroes thus becomes a party hit and a solo challenge in one package — a combination that secured its firm cult status.

Thanks to this density, inventiveness and typical Treasure craftsmanship, **Guardian Heroes** remains to this day among the most frequently mentioned gems of the Saturn library and among the games that make fans remember the console fondly.

**Why play:** It is a beat 'em up packed with RPG depth, a branching story and insane multiplayer — the essence of why Treasure is a legend.

saturn__radiant-silvergun.teaser: The sacred grail of shmups; long unavailable, today a legend.
saturn__radiant-silvergun.detail: The sacred grail of shmups. A complex weapon system (seven types depending on button combinations), a story structure and depth that defined modern „score-based“ shooters. It came out only in Japan in a small print run, long extremely expensive (until the Xbox 360 port arrived). A legend of the genre.
saturn__radiant-silvergun.article:
For fans of vertical shooters there is no word that carries more weight than **Radiant Silvergun**. This shmup from the studio **Treasure**, from 1998, is the sacred grail of the genre — a game that for many years was almost unavailable, sold for exorbitant sums, and whose reputation grew in proportion to how few people owned it. And when you finally play it, you understand why the cult arose.

Unlike most shooters, where you collect power-ups and swap weapons, Radiant Silvergun is built on a fixed set of seven types of fire that you invoke with button combinations. Instead of random power-ups, the game emphasizes learning which weapon to use in which situation — and you gradually upgrade them all according to how you play. This turns the simple destruction of enemies into a deep strategic game in which mastering the system is as important as reflexes.

Into a genre that traditionally did not overflow with story, Treasure moreover brought a genuine narrative structure and depth. It elevated shooting down enemies of the right color, chaining combos and optimizing your score into an artistic discipline — Radiant Silvergun is often described as the game that defined the modern „score-based“ approach, where it is not just about finishing, but about the perfection of every playthrough.

The game was released only in Japan and in a small print run, so it quickly became an extreme rarity. For long years it was among the most expensive cartridges and discs of all time, and its unavailability surrounded it with the aura of an unreachable masterpiece. The situation was broken only by the later port to the Xbox 360, which finally made the game accessible to a wider audience and confirmed that a truly extraordinary design lay behind the legend.
