You play as Abe, a lowly worker of the Mudokon race in a gigantic meatpacking corporation, who discovers that the next product on the menu is meant to be his own kind. His escape turns into a rescue mission. The game is a puzzle-platformer where violence usually isn't the answer — you advance carefully, sneak through the shadows, and above all use **GameSpeak**: with the buttons you speak to other Mudokons, give them commands, lead them past traps, and open portals to freedom for them. You can also possess enemies and turn their weapons against them.

Visually it's an atmospheric masterpiece — pre-rendered backgrounds, industrial grime, and the unsettling design of the Oddworld universe radiate originality. Behind it all stands the vision of Lorne Lanning and the studio Oddworld Inhabitants, who wanted to tell a story with an ecological and anti-corporate undertone without losing humor or playability.

Exoddus, released soon after the first entry, refined the mechanics, added more companions to rescue, and noticeably expanded the content, including a Mudokon emotion system you can anger or calm. For many it's the better, more polished version of the same experience.

Together these two games form one of the most distinctive efforts of the era — funny, at times disturbing, and surprisingly grown-up in its message. No wonder Oddworld later received remakes and new installments.

**Why play it:** For an original puzzle-platformer with a conscience, an unmistakable atmosphere, and voice-command control of companions that has no equal.

playstation__tony-hawk-s-pro-skater-2.teaser: One of the highest-rated games of all time; a perfect gameplay loop.
playstation__tony-hawk-s-pro-skater-2.detail: Regularly among the highest-rated games of all time (Metacritic ~98). A perfect gameplay loop, the introduction of manuals for endless combos, and an iconic punk/hip-hop soundtrack. The definition of an arcade sports game; the 1+2 remaster is a hit today.
playstation__tony-hawk-s-pro-skater-2.article:
There are games that define a genre, and then there's **Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2** — a game that reviewers still rank among the highest-rated titles of all time. On Metacritic it holds a score of around 98, and anyone who's played it knows why.

The secret is the perfect gameplay loop. You ride out on your skateboard, you have limited time, a map full of objectives, and simple yet incredibly addictive trick controls. The most important addition over the first game was the **manual** — balancing on the front or back wheels, which links otherwise separate tricks into one endless combo. Suddenly the whole level turned into a single fluid chain, and the chase for a high score gained a completely new dimension.

Neversoft, under Activision's wing, built its level design around this mechanic to actively invite experimentation, packing the maps with hidden routes, secret areas, and objectives that force you to learn every last corner. Add to that the iconic punk and hip-hop soundtrack, which helped shape the atmosphere and became unforgettable for an entire generation of players.

For the arcade sports genre, Pro Skater 2 became the benchmark — the model against which fun, flow, and replayability were measured. It proved a sports game doesn't have to be a simulation to have depth.

That its magic hasn't faded was confirmed by the modern remaster Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 1+2, which brought the game to a new generation and earned rave reactions — proof that great design doesn't age.

**Why play it:** For one of the most perfect and addictive gameplay loops in the history of games, and a soundtrack that will stay in your head forever.

playstation__fifa-2005.teaser: FIFA for arcade thrills, ISS Pro (the ancestor of PES) for the connoisseurs; a football classic.
playstation__fifa-2005.detail: Two philosophies of football: FIFA is more arcadey and licensed, while ISS Pro Evolution (the ancestor of Pro Evolution Soccer) offered a more realistic model beloved by connoisseurs. FIFA 2005 was one of the last major PS1 games ever. A classic of weekend matches.
playstation__fifa-2005.article:
Weekend tournaments in front of a single TV, four controllers and one couch — for an entire generation of players, football on the PlayStation was a sacred ritual. And **FIFA 2005** belongs among its classic chapters.

At the end of the original PlayStation era, two philosophies of virtual football took shape. EA's FIFA bet on licenses — real clubs, real players, real competitions — and on more accessible, arcadey gameplay that even a complete newcomer could jump into. Facing it stood Konami's ISS Pro Evolution series, the forerunner of the later Pro Evolution Soccer, beloved by connoisseurs for its more realistic model of player movement and behavior on the pitch.

FIFA 2005 carries an interesting historical footnote: it was one of the last major games released for the original PlayStation, at a time when the PS2 had long since reigned. That it made it onto the aging hardware at all speaks to how vast and loyal a base football games maintained.

The magic of these games lay not so much in the graphics as in the social experience. It was about quick matches, bets on honor, one-liners at every goal, and the eternal argument over whether the arcadey FIFA or the more realistic ISS was better. Both sides had their die-hard fans, and both were right.

Today we remember FIFA 2005 as an honest football classic of its time — maybe not a revolution, but a reliable companion for countless evenings.

**Why play it:** For the nostalgia of weekend football battles, and as a reminder of an era when passionate FIFA versus ISS Pro arguments were waged.

playstation__iss-pro-evolution.article:
For football-game connoisseurs there was only one true choice — and it wasn't called FIFA. Konami's **ISS Pro Evolution** was the game for those who wanted to feel the real weight of the ball and a sense of tactics on the pitch.

Where the competition bet on licenses and instant fun, ISS Pro Evolution built on a more realistic model of movement. Players didn't move as if on strings; they had momentum, passes required timing, and battles for the ball felt believable. For many fans it was the most authentic football feel you could experience on the original PlayStation — a game you had to understand and learn, not just mash a button on.

The series' historical significance is enormous: ISS Pro Evolution is the direct predecessor of the **Pro Evolution Soccer** brand, the legendary PES that on next-generation consoles became FIFA's main and often superior rival. Here, at the twilight of the PS1 era, the DNA of one of the most beloved sports series of all time was being born.

This game's magic lay in its depth. The longer you played, the more you discovered — feints, pass timing, reading the defense. It rewarded patience and skill, and that's precisely why it built a devoted community that stayed loyal to it into later generations.

Today we view ISS Pro Evolution as a cornerstone of an entire gaming dynasty and proof that realism and fun need not be at odds.

**Why play it:** For a realistic football feel that was ahead of its time, and as the roots of the legendary Pro Evolution Soccer series.

playstation__gran-turismo.teaser: „The Real Driving Simulator“; enormous content and realism for its time.
playstation__gran-turismo.detail: „The Real Driving Simulator“ by Kazunori Yamauchi. A huge number of cars (GT2 over 600), realistic car handling, and a deep career mode with licenses and tuning. The first game is the best-selling PS1 game ever (over 10 million). The benchmark of the genre.
playstation__gran-turismo.article:
When Sony promised „The Real Driving Simulator,“ it sounded like a bold marketing slogan. But **Gran Turismo** fulfilled it completely and forever changed the notion of what a racing game on a console could look like.

Behind the vision stood Kazunori Yamauchi and his studio Polyphony Digital, who wanted more than just fast cornering. Gran Turismo offered a huge garage of real licensed cars, a physics model that took a car's behavior on the track seriously, and above all a deep career mode. You had to earn driving licenses, make money by racing, buy cars, and gradually tune them — from the tires to the engine. The player became not just a driver, but also a collector and a mechanic.

This combination of simulation realism and near-RPG progression proved immensely addictive. The second installment then inflated the content to absurd proportions — over six hundred cars and dozens of tracks — and raised the bar even higher.

The success was staggering. The first Gran Turismo became the best-selling game on the original PlayStation ever, with sales exceeding ten million copies. That placed it not only among commercial phenomena, but among the titles that helped define the very identity of the PlayStation brand.

Gran Turismo became the benchmark of the entire genre — the yardstick against which realism, content, and the feel of driving were measured. The series continues to this day and retains its reputation as one of the most serious racing brands in the world.

**Why play it:** For the foundational experience of the modern racing sim, an inexhaustible collection of cars, and a career mode that will pull you in for hours on end.

playstation__gran-turismo-2.article:
If the first Gran Turismo proved that a genuine driving simulator could exist on a console, **Gran Turismo 2** showed how far that idea could be pushed. It was bigger, richer, and in many ways more complete.

Polyphony Digital, led by Kazunori Yamauchi, bet above all on content, and on a scale that seemed unbelievable at the time — the lineup exceeded six hundred vehicles. From ordinary production cars to racing specials, all with carefully tuned behavior on the track. The game stayed true to its core concept: race, earn, buy and tune, collect licenses, and gradually build your dream garage.

The career mode was deep and satisfyingly addictive. Each championship you won pushed you closer to better cars and tougher challenges, so the „one more race“ loop kept players glued to the screen late into the night. Added to that were new tracks, including more demanding and varied environments.

The sequel thus expanded and refined everything that worked in the first entry, and confirmed Gran Turismo as the flagship of the racing-sim genre. For many fans this very episode remains the peak of the PlayStation era — the moment the series reached enormous scale without losing its soul.

Gran Turismo 2 is evidence that a sequel need not mean merely more of the same, but a genuine broadening of horizons.

**Why play it:** For the huge car roster, deep career mode, and refined driving feel that elevated the foundational first game to an even higher level.

playstation__ridge-racer-type-4.teaser: Stylish arcade racing; gorgeous presentation and music.
playstation__ridge-racer-type-4.detail: Stylish arcade racing with gorgeous presentation, a jazz/electronic soundtrack, and a distinctive drift. Visually and atmospherically the peak of the series on PS1; a lengthy career mode.
playstation__ridge-racer-type-4.article:
Not every racer wants to be a simulator — and **Ridge Racer Type 4**, often shortened to R4, knows that very well. This game isn't after realism, but after pure style, atmosphere, and the joy of drifting.

Namco bet on arcade gameplay built on its signature slide: you don't take corners with patient braking, but with a flashy drift that quickly becomes second nature. From this comes that characteristic flowing, dancing feel that set the Ridge Racer series apart from its more serious rivals. The game is fast, readable, and instantly fun.

Where R4 truly excels, though, is presentation. Visually it's the peak of the series on the PlayStation — elegant, colorful, and stylish from the menu to the finish straight. And then there's the music: an unforgettable jazz and electronic soundtrack that elevates every race into a little experience and remains among the most treasured game scores of that era.

There's also a surprisingly long career mode that guides you through a season with various teams and gradually unlocks cars. It gives the arcade core meaning and a reason to return, without burdening the game with needless complexity.

Ridge Racer Type 4 remains one of the most stylishly polished racing games of its generation — proof that atmosphere and the feel of driving can mean more than the number of faithfully simulated horses under the hood.

**Why play it:** For the unmistakable drift, dazzling presentation, and a soundtrack that turns every lap into a little celebration.

playstation__colin-mcrae-rally-2-0.teaser: The best rally sim of the era; demanding and satisfying.
playstation__colin-mcrae-rally-2-0.detail: The best rally sim of the era: a realistic driving model across various surfaces and a tense co-driver calling out corners ahead (pacenotes). Demanding and satisfying; it laid the foundation for the later DiRT series.
playstation__colin-mcrae-rally-2-0.article:
Rally isn't about the fastest car, but about courage, concentration, and trust in the voice beside you. **Colin McRae Rally 2.0** brought this tension to the screen like few games of its era — and for many it remains the best rally simulation of that time.

The studio Codemasters built the game on a realistic driving model that took the differences between surfaces seriously. Gravel, tarmac, snow, and mud — each demanded a different driving style, a different line, and a different degree of caution. The car beneath you was alive, sliding and reacting to the ground, so every special stage was a fight for tenths of a second and for keeping the car on the track at all.

But the heart of the experience was the co-driver. The pacenotes system, in which a voice calls out the upcoming corners and their severity ahead of time, turned the game into a tense dialogue between you and a track you can't see all the way ahead. You had to listen, trust, and react — and it was precisely this blind trust that made every stage a rush of adrenaline.

The game was demanding, but fair and immensely satisfying. Mastering a difficult stage without a mistake delivered a feeling of genuine driving triumph that more arcadey racers couldn't offer.

The significance of Colin McRae Rally 2.0 reaches beyond its time: it laid the foundations on which Codemasters later built the successful DiRT series. It is thus one of the pillars of modern off-road racing.

**Why play it:** For the authentic rally feel, the tense co-driver calls, and the demanding but fair driving that rewards precision.

playstation__driver-2.teaser: An open city behind the wheel before GTA III; cinematic chases.
playstation__driver-2.detail: An open city behind the wheel even before GTA III, with cinematic '70s-style chases (San Francisco, Rio). The sequel added the ability to step out of the car and steal another. Ambitious and influential, though right at the edge of the PS1's capabilities.
playstation__driver-2.article:
Imagine sitting behind the wheel in a living city where you can pick any street, shift into gear, and vanish from the police in your rear-view mirror long before the world discovered the shorthand GTA III. That's exactly what the Driver series offered, and its second installment raised the bar even higher.

**Driver 2** was created at the studio Reflections under the publisher Infogrames, building on the success of the first game that enchanted players with cinematic car chases in the spirit of '70s crime thrillers. The atmosphere of burnt rubber, Bullitt-style pursuits and The Taking of Pelham One Two Three wasn't just a backdrop here, but the very essence of the game. Reflections understood superbly how a car should hesitate in a corner with a slide and when the wheels bite back into the asphalt.

The sequel's key novelty was the ability to **step out of the car** and steal another. It sounds obvious today, but in 2000 it was an ambitious step on the PlayStation, pushing open cities closer to what we now consider standard. The player was no longer just a driver strapped to a single chassis, but a pedestrian who could decide which machine they needed for an escape right then.

Visually the game traveled through real locations like San Francisco, Havana, Las Vegas, and Rio de Janeiro. Each city had its own rhythm, its own intersections, and its own traps. That expansion to four metropolises and the addition of on-foot navigation, however, balanced right at the edge of the PS1's technical capabilities, so the game had to be split across multiple discs and at times struggled with rendering compromises.

Even so, **Driver 2** remains an important milestone. It showed that the concept of an open city driven by automotive action held enormous potential, and it indirectly paved the way for a genre that would later dominate the entire gaming industry. For those who remember it, it's a nostalgic ride full of drifts and police sirens; for students of gaming history, it's evidence of a small studio's courage to push the hardware past its limits.

**Why play it:** Cinematic chases and open cities across four metropolises at a time when that was still a rarity; a nostalgic classic that was ahead of its time.

playstation__crash-team-racing.teaser: The best kart racing outside Nintendo; deep driving mechanics.
playstation__crash-team-racing.detail: The best kart racing outside Nintendo, with deep driving mechanics (chaining boosts through slides) and a full-fledged adventure mode. For many, better than the Mario Karts of the day; a treasured remake (Nitro-Fueled).
playstation__crash-team-racing.article:
When you say kart racing, most people automatically picture a plumber in a red cap. Yet on the PlayStation in 1999 a rival appeared that not only matched Nintendo but, according to many, even surpassed it.

**Crash Team Racing**, affectionately known as CTR, comes from the studio **Naughty Dog**, then still at the peak of its career with the mascot Crash Bandicoot. And it was no lazy copy of the competition. Naughty Dog bet on unexpectedly deep driving mechanics whose heart is the boost system. When you slid, a gauge filled that rewarded you with a short burst of speed, and true masters could chain these boosts one after another in an unbroken stream of velocity. This skill ceiling made CTR a racer that rewarded practice and precision.

Beyond the usual cups and time trials, CTR offered a full-fledged **adventure mode** with a hub world, bosses, and item collecting. It wasn't a mere collection of tracks, then, but a kind of small campaign that gave racing meaning and context. That was unusually generous by the standards of the genre, and the game gained dozens of hours of content because of it.

The tracks themselves were imaginative and colorful, full of shortcuts, jumps, and traps, each of them demanding knowledge of the ideal line. Add to that sharp controls, a balanced arsenal of weapons, and superb multiplayer for a group of friends around one screen, and you have a recipe for one of the best racing games of its generation.

CTR's success was confirmed by the acclaimed remake **Crash Team Racing Nitro-Fueled**, which revived the original game in a modern coat and reminded a new generation how brilliantly the foundation was designed. The very fact that it received a full-fledged return after decades speaks for the quality of the original all on its own.

**Why play it:** The best kart racing outside Nintendo's world, with a boost mechanic that rewards skill and content that lasts far longer than a single afternoon.

playstation__tekken-2.teaser: The third game is often the best fighter of its generation; snappy and polished.
playstation__tekken-2.detail: The third game is often the best fighter of its generation: snappy, polished, with a varied roster and side-stepping. It sold over 8 million and had mini-games (Tekken Force, Tekken Ball). The second game laid the foundations. A must for fans.
playstation__tekken-2.article:
Before Tekken became synonymous with console fighting games, it had to build its foundations. And it was **Tekken 2** that firmly established Namco's series at the top.

The second installment took the solid concept of three-dimensional combat from the first Tekken and refined it into a far more playable form. It added new characters, tuned the controls built on independent buttons for each limb, and expanded the movement options. Tekken set itself apart from rival fighting games precisely through that intuitive system, where each button controls one arm or leg, giving the player a natural sense of control over their fighter.

Here Namco further developed the brand's signature traits: a varied roster of characters with their own fighting styles, story backgrounds for the individual combatants, and quality presentation. The combat was faster and more readable than that of many rivals, and the fighting system offered enough depth for tournament players and pleasant accessibility for Sunday brawlers alike.

The console version for the PlayStation ensured that the arcade attraction became a home evergreen. It was precisely the availability of quality 3D fighters at home that was a big draw in the mid-nineties, and Tekken became one of the console's flagships. It thus laid the foundations on which its successors would later build the reputation of one of the longest-living and most successful fighting series of all time.

Thanks to this installment, the series built a loyal fan base and a clear identity. Whether you're drawn to competitive play or just want to understand where today's legend of the genre came from, the second Tekken is an important stone in that structure.

**Why play it:** The installment that firmly established Tekken among the top console fighters and refined the intuitive control system based on individual limbs.

playstation__tekken-3.article:
There are games spoken of as the pinnacle of an entire generation, and **Tekken 3** unquestionably belongs among them. For many fans it is the finest fighting game ever to reach the original PlayStation.

Namco's third installment took everything the previous games offered and pushed it to a new level. The game was brisk, exceptionally polished and smooth, with controls that fit like a glove. The key innovation was the **sidestep**, the ability to dodge into the depth of the arena and slip past an opponent's attack, which brought an entirely new tactical dimension to the fights. In an instant, two-dimensional shoving turned into a spatial dance.

The roster of characters was varied and packed with iconic names, many of which still appear in the newest entries of the series today. Each fighter had a distinctive style, their own moves and personality, so every player could find a favorite of their own. On top of that, Namco added lighthearted **mini-games**, such as the Tekken Force beat-em-up mode or the quirky Tekken Ball, which extended the fun well beyond ordinary matches.

The quality was reflected in commercial success too. Tekken 3 sold more than eight million copies, placing it among the most successful titles of the entire PlayStation era and among the best-selling fighting games in history. Those numbers are no accident, but the result of superbly executed craftsmanship.

The combination of technical perfection, depth of the combat system and generous content made Tekken 3 the benchmark against which other fighting games were measured. Even today, after many years, the game keeps its gameplay surprisingly fresh.

**Why play:** Often called the best fighting game of its generation, brisk, polished and packed with content; a must for every fan of the genre.

playstation__mortal-kombat-trilogy.article:
What if all the characters, arenas and fatalities from the previous Mortal Kombat games came together in a single bloody collection? That is exactly the idea from which **Mortal Kombat Trilogy** was born.

This title is essentially a grand summary of the classic era of the famous fighting series. It combines content from the first three Mortal Kombat games into a single package and offers players one of the most stacked rosters the series had at the time. You will find both fighters from the base games and characters from the updated versions, so you can play as practically anyone you might have grown fond of back then.

Mortal Kombat was a phenomenon from the start, chiefly thanks to its digitized graphics, where characters were created by capturing real actors, and of course thanks to its notorious brutality and the finishing moves known as fatalities. It was precisely the controversy over the violence in the original games that ignited a society-wide debate at the time and indirectly contributed to the creation of age ratings for games. Trilogy proudly carries this raw identity onward and concentrates it into a single title.

For players on the PlayStation this meant the chance to savor nostalgia while having the entire classic battlefield on one disc. No switching between games, no compromises over which installment to boot up. Just a pure barrage of tournament fights, secret characters and iconic one-liners.

Mortal Kombat Trilogy is thus the ideal entry point for anyone who wants to understand why so much hype surrounded this series, or simply to relive the golden era of one of the most provocative fighting games of all. It is a celebration of everything that made classic Mortal Kombat so unforgettable.

**Why play:** A complete collection of characters, arenas and fatalities from the classic Mortal Kombat era on one disc, ideal for nostalgics and newcomers alike.

playstation__street-fighter-alpha-3.teaser: A rich 2D fighter; plenty of characters and styles.
playstation__street-fighter-alpha-3.detail: A rich 2D fighter with a huge roster (over 30 characters) and three styles (ISM) that change the mechanics. One of the most extensive classic SFs; the PS1 version had the most content.
playstation__street-fighter-alpha-3.article:
If there is a game capable of keeping a fan of two-dimensional fighters busy for weeks on end, it is **Street Fighter Alpha 3**. Here Capcom served up one of the most extensive classic portions from its legendary series.

The most striking feature is the massive roster, which counts over thirty characters. That makes Alpha 3 one of the richest classic Street Fighters ever released. You will find old familiar faces as well as less common fighters, so the room for experimenting with different play styles is virtually inexhaustible. Each character has their strengths and weaknesses, and finding yours is entertainment for long hours in itself.

The heart of the gameplay, however, is the system of three fighting styles, the so-called **ISM** (A-ism, X-ism and V-ism). Each of them fundamentally changes the combat mechanics, from the way you charge super attacks to your options for blocking and defense. Before a match, the player thus chooses not only a character but also an entire philosophy of how they want to fight. This layer adds unexpected depth and sets Alpha 3 apart from many other installments of the series.

The console version for PlayStation also became famous for containing the most content of all the versions at the time. Added characters, game modes and options made it the definitive release for home players who did not have to regularly visit the arcades.

Street Fighter Alpha 3 thus remains a celebration of everything that makes two-dimensional fighters so addictive. It combines a tremendous amount of content with thoughtful mechanics and a visual style that ages gracefully. For lovers of the genre it is a little treasure.

**Why play:** A huge roster of over thirty characters and three distinct ISM fighting styles give one of the most extensive classic Street Fighters depth to last for weeks.

playstation__bushido-blade.article:
Forget health bars that slowly drain with each blow. **Bushido Blade** arrived with a bold idea: a single well-aimed strike can end a duel instantly.

This fighting game from Squaresoft differed radically from anything the genre offered at the time. Instead of colorful super attacks and lives whittled away in small chunks, Bushido Blade wagered on realism and lethality. A hit to a vital spot meant instant defeat, while a lighter wound affected the fighter's mobility. The duel thus resembled a tense clash of master swordsmen more than a traditional arcade brawl.

The game took place without artificial arena boundaries, in free three-dimensional space where fighters could move across the landscape, retreat and seek an advantageous position. A range of bladed weapons with differing weight and reach was available, each requiring a different approach. This combination of freedom of movement and deadly precision created an atmosphere of tension that other fighters of the era simply did not have.

The emphasis on samurai honor and ethics was another distinctive element. The game guided the player to respect the rules of fair combat, and breaking the chivalric code had its consequences. In this way Bushido Blade touched on the cultural background of Japanese warriors far more deeply than was customary in the genre.

In a world where most fighting games bet on flashy combos and exaggerated moves, Bushido Blade was a refreshing exception. It was an experiment that prioritized tension and realism over spectacle, and that is precisely why it retains its reputation as a cult item to this day, one that veterans will hear no bad word about.

**Why play:** An original fighter where a single precise strike decides life and death; a realistic, tense duel with samurai honor of a kind you will not find elsewhere.

playstation__twisted-metal-2.teaser: A vehicular combat classic; destruction with humor.
playstation__twisted-metal-2.detail: The definition of vehicular combat: combat vehicles destroy each other in destructible arenas around the world, each with its own weapon and darkly humorous character (the clown Sweet Tooth). Great tracks and co-op. A classic of the subgenre.
playstation__twisted-metal-2.article:
A suicidal clown behind the wheel of an ice-cream van armed with rockets, who upon winning the tournament wants to fulfill a single morbid wish. Welcome to the world of **Twisted Metal 2**, where the roads turn into a battlefield.

This title from the studio SingleTrac under Sony's wing is essentially the textbook definition of the whole subgenre known as vehicular combat, that is, fighting in vehicles. The principle is ingeniously simple: you climb into an armored machine, head out into the arena and try to destroy everyone else before they destroy you. To that end you have machine guns, guided rockets and special weapons that each vehicle carries differently.

For its time it stood out especially for the variety of its environments. The arenas took place in real corners of the world, from Paris through Amsterdam to Hollywood, and were moreover destructible, so the surroundings reacted to your rampaging. Add to that a gallery of eccentric characters led by the infamous clown Sweet Tooth, whose motivations overflowed with black humor, and you get an unmistakable atmosphere.

Besides the superbly designed tracks, the game also offered a cooperative mode, so you could share the destruction with a friend. The fights were fast, chaotic and addictive, with an emphasis on mastering movement and timing special attacks. Learning the combinations for the powerful weapons was a discipline of its own that opened the game up to more experienced players.

Twisted Metal 2 became a benchmark of the genre and to this day counts as one of the best games of its kind. It combined easily graspable action, a witty and dark style and dense gameplay into a package that is hard to put down.

**Why play:** A textbook classic of vehicular combat full of destructible arenas, black humor and addictive fights; the benchmark of the entire subgenre.

playstation__command-and-conquer-red-ale.teaser: An RTS legend on console too; controls nailed.
playstation__command-and-conquer-red-ale.detail: An RTS legend in a surprisingly well-handled console port. An alternate history of the Cold War (Einstein killed Hitler, you wage war on the USSR), two campaigns and charismatic FMV scenes with live actors.
playstation__command-and-conquer-red-ale.article:
What if Einstein killed Hitler before the Second World War even began? From this crazy question grew one of the most beloved real-time strategies of all time, and what is more, one surprisingly playable on a console.

**Command & Conquer: Red Alert** from the legendary Westwood studio ranks among the pillars of the RTS genre. The story builds on an alternate history of the Cold War: when Einstein uses his time machine to remove Hitler, the resulting power vacuum is filled by the Soviet Union under Stalin's leadership and a red threat floods Europe. The player thus finds themselves in the middle of a conflict between the Allies and the USSR, with each side having its own campaign, units and strategy.

Controls were always tricky for real-time strategy on a console, because a mouse and keyboard offer a precision that a gamepad can hardly match. All the more remarkable, then, that the **PlayStation port** was handled surprisingly well and let console players too experience base building, resource harvesting and commanding armies of tanks, infantry and aircraft.

An inseparable part of the brand was the **FMV scenes** with live actors, which between missions told the story with wit and gusto. Charismatic officers, commanders and mysterious figures lent the campaign a cinematic atmosphere and a distinctive flavor that etched itself indelibly into the memory of fans. Together with the iconic music, it became an unmistakable experience.

Red Alert influenced the entire genre and grew into a rich series that kept a loyal audience for many years. Its combination of brisk gameplay, a wittily conceived alternate history and unforgettable presentation made it a classic that strategists are glad to revisit, as are those who simply want to savor a piece of gaming history.

**Why play:** A legend of the RTS genre in a surprisingly well-handled console port, with a witty alternate history of the Cold War and charismatic FMV scenes.

playstation__star-wars-episode-i-phantom.teaser: An action adaptation of the film; nostalgia.
playstation__star-wars-episode-i-phantom.detail: An action adaptation of the first prequel, where you walk through scenes from the film as Qui-Gon, Obi-Wan and others. A nostalgic period tie-in ride for fans.
playstation__star-wars-episode-i-phantom.article:
For an entire generation of fans, the year 1999 was magical, because Star Wars was returning to the screen. And along with the first prequel came an action game that let players walk through the film's most famous scenes firsthand.

**Star Wars Episode I: The Phantom Menace** from LucasArts in collaboration with the Big Ape studio is an action adaptation of the opening installment of the prequel trilogy. The player gradually takes on the roles of several heroes, among whom the Jedi master Qui-Gon Jinn and his apprentice Obi-Wan Kenobi are not missing, and passes through key moments of the story from the planet Naboo through the Tatooine desert to fateful confrontations.

The game combines lightsaber duels, the use of Jedi abilities and shooting, all while trying to convey the feeling that you are truly part of the film's events. You pass through familiar locations, meet characters from the screen and relive moments you saw in the cinema. For the fans of the time it was a tempting chance to extend the cinematic experience at home on the console.

Like many film adaptations of the era, this title too is above all a **nostalgic tie-in ride** aimed at fans of the brand. The game's strength lies chiefly in how it manages to appeal to lovers of Star Wars and offer them an interactive journey through a story they know by heart. The atmosphere and faithfulness to the film source were the main draw at the time.

Today the game is an interesting document of an era when a game adaptation was almost automatically tied to every big film blockbuster. For nostalgics and collectors it remains a pleasant reminder of the time when a galaxy far, far away once again ruled pop culture.

**Why play:** A nostalgic action adaptation of the first prequel, where as Qui-Gon and Obi-Wan you walk through key scenes of the film; a treat for Star Wars fans.

playstation__star-wars-rogue-squadron-cl.article:
A galaxy far, far away had never been so close on your television screen before. On the original PlayStation, Star Wars saw a whole series of titles that capitalized on the enormous wave of enthusiasm around the brand in the second half of the nineties, when Lucas's universe returned to the center of attention thanks to the special editions of the classic trilogy and the upcoming new saga.

Titles devoted to arcade action and aerial combat built on the most enticing thing Star Wars offers: the feeling of sitting in the cockpit of a fighter and hurtling among blasters and turbolasers. The player controls the iconic machines from the films, completes combat missions, destroys enemy positions and tries to survive against the odds. It was precisely the immediate action and the instantly recognizable settings that made these games rewarding material for fans who wanted to take the controls themselves rather than watch the heroes only from the screen.

As a platform, the PS1 had its limits, polygon models were angular, draw distance often short and textures blurry. The developers dealt with this in their own way: they compensated with pace, atmosphere and a soundtrack that borrowed from the films John Williams's iconic themes as well as the unmistakable sounds of blasters and hyperdrive. For many players at the time, that sound alone was reason enough not to let go of the controller.

Culturally, these games fit into a broader strategy of turning Star Wars into a multimedia phenomenon, where every platform got its own piece of the experience. Console versions bet on accessibility and instant fun, while more serious simulations and campaigns aimed rather at the PC. Together they helped keep the brand alive during the period between the original trilogy and the new films.

Today many remember these titles with nostalgia as the first chance to experience Star Wars with their own hands on a home console, with all the charm and roughness of the early 3D era.

**Why play:** If you want to experience Star Wars action in the authentic atmosphere of a nineties console, this is a nostalgic trip straight into the cockpit.

playstation__inuyasha-feudal-fairy-tale.teaser: An anime fighter; for fans of the series.
playstation__inuyasha-feudal-fairy-tale.detail: A 2D fighter based on the anime/manga with nice pixel-art graphics and characters from the series. Released late in the PS1's life. A delight for fans of InuYasha.
playstation__inuyasha-feudal-fairy-tale.article:
When anime was making its big push into the West at the turn of the millennium, consoles filled up with fighters based on beloved series, and InuYasha: A Feudal Fairy Tale is one of the kind that fans have not forgotten. It came out in 2003 under the Bandai banner, that is, at a moment when the PlayStation had long since been passing the torch to its successor the PS2, and yet this game found its audience.

It is a classic **2D fighter** built on the characters from Rumiko Takahashi's series. Instead of trying to compete with technical 3D titles, it bets on what it does best: nice **pixel-art graphics**, a faithful rendering of the beloved heroes and one-on-one fights where timing, combos and knowledge of each fighter's move set matter. For viewers of the series it is a joy to see their favorites dish out special blows drawn directly from the source.

The fact that the game arrived so late in the life of the original PlayStation benefited it in a certain sense, the creators had the console's 2D graphics fully mastered and could squeeze detailed sprites and smooth animation out of the hardware. The result is a title that looks mature visually and respectful of the material it stands on.

To be straight: as a fighter, InuYasha does not rank among the tournament pillars of the genre such as the big series from specialized studios represented. Its value lies elsewhere, in how faithfully it transfers the anime's atmosphere into interactive form and gives fans the chance to control characters they had until then known only from the screen. That is exactly the kind of experience licensed games are meant to provide.

Today it is a collector's item of interest and a lovely reminder of the time when anime and video games were increasingly intertwining and every popular series longed for its own console adaptation.

**Why play:** For fans of InuYasha it is a faithful delight with nice 2D graphics; as a gateway to the fighting genre it will serve rather as a likable curiosity.

playstation__vib-ribbon.teaser: Pioneers of the rhythm genre; stylistically unmistakable.
playstation__vib-ribbon.detail: Masaya Matsuura practically founded the rhythm genre. PaRappa is an adorable rap hit („I gotta believe!“). Vib-Ribbon is minimalist (a vector bunny runs along a line) and could generate levels from your own CD inserted in place of the game disc. Stylistically unmistakable and influential.
playstation__vib-ribbon.article:
Insert your own music CD into the PlayStation and watch brand-new game levels being born from your favorite songs, in 1999 it sounded like magic and to this day it is one of the boldest ideas a rhythm game has ever brought. Vib-Ribbon from the studio **NanaOn-Sha** is proof that sometimes less really is much more.

The game's visuals are radically minimalist: along a single line runs a **vector bunny** named Vibri, rendered as a clean white line on a black background. Your task is to press, at the right moment, buttons corresponding to the obstacles that appear on the line in time with the music. No garish textures, no polygon orgies, just an elegant line, music and a pure gameplay feel. If you make mistakes, Vibri gradually degrades into less advanced forms; when you do well, it evolves.

The trump card that placed Vib-Ribbon beyond all competition was the ability to **generate levels from any music CD**. The game loaded entirely into the console's memory, so you could take the disc out and insert any album of your own, and the game would create a track for it. That meant a practically endless number of levels limited only by your music collection, which was an extraordinarily clever and liberating concept for its time.

Masaya Matsuura, the lead creator behind NanaOn-Sha, is a name that stands at the very origin of the modern rhythm genre, his work gave rise to the charming rap hit PaRappa the Rapper, and Vib-Ribbon is its flip side of the coin: experimental, stylish, unyieldingly itself. Where PaRappa enchanted with colors and humor, Vib-Ribbon bet on pure abstraction.

In its time it was a title cult rather than mass-selling, but its influence and aesthetic daring made it a favorite of critics and players seeking something original. Stylistically it is utterly unmistakable and holds a firm and honorable place in the history of the genre.

**Why play:** A minimalist rhythm gem that conjures a game out of your own music, an unmistakable style and an idea seen once a decade.

playstation__parappa-rapper.article:
„I gotta believe!“ – this line burrowed into the memory of an entire generation of players and became the unofficial motto of a genre that PaRappa the Rapper practically helped invent. The adorable paper-flat pup who learns to rap in order to win over the girl of his dreams is today rightly considered one of the grandfathers of the whole rhythm gaming scene.

The gameplay principle is ingeniously simple: a sequence of buttons runs across the screen, which you have to press in rhythm as your teacher demonstrates them to you, whether it is a karate dog in the dojo, a frog at the flea market or a chicken in the kitchen. Your goal is to repeat their rap part as faithfully as possible. The game rates your accuracy, and based on it the mood of the track and the rating change from „awful“ to „cool“. When you get on the wave and start improvising, the game rewards you and the song literally comes alive.

The visual side is unmistakable: flat, paper characters in a vibrantly colored world created by illustrator Rodney Greenblat gave the game such a distinctive look that it burns into memory instantly. Together with catchy, professionally written rap tracks, a whole emerged that feels fresh and infectiously cheerful even after many years.

Culturally, PaRappa's significance is hard to overstate. It opened the door to the rhythm genre, which later blossomed into forms like Dance Dance Revolution, Guitar Hero or Rock Band. It showed that music and timing can carry an entire game on their own and that cuteness and style are full-fledged gaming values. The creative duo led by Masaya Matsuura thereby steered an entire branch of the gaming industry.

PaRappa remains an icon of the early PlayStation era, a symbol of the time when Sony could afford to release bold and original ideas that had no equal in anything. To this day it is a title that can coax a smile onto your face and set your foot tapping.

**Why play:** A founding legend of the rhythm genre with irresistible style and catchy songs, a joy that ages gracefully.

playstation__intelligent-qube-kurushi.teaser: An abstract puzzle game; tense and unique.
playstation__intelligent-qube-kurushi.detail: Abstract, tense logic: on a large chessboard you mark and destroy rolling cubes before they sweep you off the edge. Accompanied by orchestral music. Unique, stressful in a good way.
playstation__intelligent-qube-kurushi.article:
You stand on a huge chessboard, a grid of stone cubes rolling toward you, and you have only a few seconds before they sweep you over the edge into the void, Intelligent Qube, known in Europe as Kurushi, is one of the most nerve-wracking puzzle games ever to appear on the PlayStation. It was created in 1997 in Sony's workshop in collaboration with the studio G-Artists.

The principle is abstract and at the same time immediately comprehensible: your character moves across a platform onto which rows of cubes roll from the side. Your task is to mark the tiles beneath the floor with the right timing and trap the incoming cubes before they run you over or knock you off the playing field. Some cubes you must destroy, others must not touch the trap, and the black „advantage“ cubes, when used correctly, let you sweep an entire row at once. One mistake in calculation, one bad piece of timing, and the platform beneath you shrinks alarmingly.

What makes Kurushi so exceptional is the combination of cold, geometric abstraction and surprisingly strong emotional tension. The game has no story or colorful environment to build on, it relies purely on the rhythm of thinking under pressure. To this rings a powerful **orchestral accompaniment** that elevates every moment into a little drama. It is stress, but in the best sense of the word: stress that makes you want to come back.

Mechanically it is the pure essence of a puzzle game stripped of all ballast. No distracting elements, just you, the grid of cubes and the ticking clock. This minimalist purity is exactly what fans of the genre prize, the game demands your full concentration and instant spatial reasoning, and it richly rewards that concentration.

Intelligent Qube built up a firm cult reputation as a unique title that resembles nothing else. For players seeking an original brain-teaser with a nerve-shredding atmosphere, it remains a great choice to this day.

**Why play:** A unique, tense puzzle with a hypnotic orchestral accompaniment, stressful in the best sense and utterly its own.

playstation__einhander.teaser: A Square shmup; stylish and technically polished.
playstation__einhander.detail: A rare shmup from Square (famous for their RPGs), a stylish horizontal 2.5D affair with a mechanic for collecting and swapping weapons taken from defeated enemies. Technically and visually refined; a cult favorite among fans of the genre.
playstation__einhander.article:
When a studio famous for its role-playing games suddenly releases a shooter, it pays to take notice, and Einhänder from **Squaresoft** is exactly the kind of case where the experiment turned out better than anyone expected. This rare 1998 action title proved that the makers of Final Fantasy could also craft a devilishly stylish and technically polished shoot 'em up.

Einhänder is a horizontally scrolling **2.5D shmup** in which your ship fights its way through layers of enemies in a darkly industrial, mildly dystopian world. Its core mechanic is brilliantly clever: your fighter is equipped with a movable manipulator arm that lets you **collect weapons from defeated enemies** and attach them to your hull. Each weapon has limited ammunition and different properties, so you are constantly weighing when to deploy a weapon, when to conserve it, and how best to angle it against incoming threats. This dynamic gives the game a tactical depth that most shooters lack.

Technically and visually, Einhänder was a feast for the eyes in its day. Square drew on its experience with pre-rendered and polygonal graphics to create backgrounds and enemies with a remarkable level of detail, smooth animation, and striking effects. The whole thing is rounded out by an atmospheric, electronically tinged soundtrack that underlines the game's cold industrial mood.

The reason it remains a cult title rather than a broad hit is simple: the shmup genre was already niche by the late nineties, and on top of that Einhänder was released only for the Japanese and North American markets, so it reached many European players only by roundabout routes. That makes it all the more prized today among connoisseurs and collectors, who see it as one of the peaks of the genre on the PlayStation.

Einhänder is a reminder of a time when even the biggest studios could afford smaller, ambitious projects outside their main genre, and when such a detour could produce a gem.

**Why play it:** A stylish and technically polished shmup from the masters of the RPG, with a clever weapon-stealing mechanic, a cult gem for fans of the genre.

playstation__command-and-conquer.article:
Tiberium, the Brotherhood of NOD, and the charismatic villain Kane, in the mid-nineties Command & Conquer laid the foundations of the modern real-time strategy, and its console incarnation brought this landmark experience to players without a powerful PC. Together with the Retaliation expansion, it was a hearty serving of strategic meat.

The gameplay is a textbook **RTS**: you harvest rare tiberium, build and defend a base, produce units, and hurl them into battle against the enemy. The game from Westwood Studios pitted the Global Defense Initiative (GDI) against the mysterious, fanatical Brotherhood of NOD in a struggle for control over a strange alien substance. Each side had its own units, tactics, and campaign tone, which gave the game surprising depth and replay value.

What lifted Command & Conquer above the competition was its presentation. Live-action cutscenes with the first-class villain Kane, played by Joseph Kucan, gave the campaign a cinematic swagger and the sense that you were part of a larger conflict. Together with the iconic rock soundtrack, the result defined how strategy should look and sound, and pointed the whole genre forward for years to come.

The PlayStation console version faced the same challenge as other RTS games of the era, controlling an army with a gamepad never reaches the precision of a mouse. Even so it was a worthy effort: the Retaliation expansion added new missions and content, and the whole package opened up this strategy legend to an audience sitting in front of televisions, not just monitors.

Command & Conquer's influence on the genre is enormous; it stood at the birth of an entire family of games, and its world and characters etched themselves into gaming history. The console version is today a testament to a time when even demanding PC genres boldly moved into living rooms.

**Why play it:** A founding RTS legend with the unforgettable Kane and cinematic presentation, on console a dignified gateway to one of the most influential titles in the genre.

playstation__warcraft-ii-dark-saga.article:
Before Warcraft became a phenomenon in the form of an online world, it was first and foremost an outstanding fantasy real-time strategy, and Warcraft II: The Dark Saga brought this Blizzard gem to the PlayStation too, offering orcs, humans, and epic battles right in the living room.

The gameplay foundation is a classic **RTS** set in the rich fantasy world of Azeroth: you build a base, harvest wood and gold, train soldiers, archers, mages, and mighty war machines, and throw them into the fight between the human Alliance and the orcish Horde. Warcraft II stood out for its carefully balanced factions, clear mission design, and an addictive campaign that led players through a richly developed story of a conflict between two irreconcilable races.

The Dark Saga was the console edition, which alongside the original content also included the Beyond the Dark Portal expansion, so players got a hefty load of missions and storytelling. Blizzard was already known for its meticulousness and eye for detail, and Warcraft II is an excellent example of it, its hand-painted 2D graphics, distinctive units, and unforgettable unit quips when clicked gave the game a distinctive and instantly recognizable character.

As with all console strategies of the era, controlling with a gamepad could not match the nimbleness of the mouse that PC strategists were used to. The developers nonetheless tried to adapt the interface, and the overall experience remained a full-fledged one, home players got the chance to experience one of the peaks of the genre without needing an expensive computer.

The significance of Warcraft II is fundamental: it helped establish Blizzard as one of the most respected studios, built the foundations of a fantasy world that would later explode in the form of further games, and became a benchmark for quality fantasy strategy. The Dark Saga is a dignified gateway into this legendary universe.

**Why play it:** A polished fantasy RTS from Blizzard with a rich campaign and an unmistakable world, on console a welcome chance to experience a legend of the genre.

playstation__warhammer-dark-omen.article:
Leading a regiment of Empire knights into battle, watching a line of infantry clash with a horde of the undead, and feeling that every decision about unit placement could mean victory or ruin, Warhammer: Dark Omen brought the atmosphere of Games Workshop's tabletop wargaming to the PlayStation with unexpected gravity and depth.

Unlike classic base-building RTS games, Dark Omen focuses on **battlefield tactics**. You do not build bases or harvest resources, instead you command an army of regiments that you manage, upgrade, and replenish between battles. The clashes themselves then resemble a real battle from a tabletop game: you deploy formations, use terrain, cavalry, artillery, and magic, and try to outflank the enemy or break through his weak point. Unit morale plays a crucial role, and a panicking regiment can drag down an entire line.

The game faithfully conveys the grim, gothic universe of the Warhammer Fantasy world, where the forces of the undead and chaos stand against the Empire. The campaign is guided by a narrative, and the player gradually builds a bond with his units, which remember the experience of previous battles. This continuity gives the campaign weight, losing seasoned veterans hurts more than the fall of anonymous foot soldiers.

Dark Omen was released on both PC and PlayStation and was one of the more ambitious attempts to bring the depth of tabletop strategy into digital form. For players looking for more than brisk clicking, it offered a slower, more thoughtful, and atmospheric experience that rewarded patience and tactical thinking.

Today Dark Omen is prized as one of the more faithful adaptations of the Warhammer world in video game form and a cult item among fans of tactical games and Games Workshop alike. It is a title that, in its approach, was ahead of its time and still holds its distinctive character today.

**Why play it:** An atmospheric, tactically deep battle strategy set in the Warhammer world, for anyone who prefers thoughtful command over brisk clicking.

playstation__front-mission-3.article:
Robots never looked so machine-like yet so human as in **Front Mission 3**. This turn-based tactics game from Squaresoft, released in 1999, put you in the cockpits of combat mechs called **Wanzer** (from the German Wanderpanzer) and told a story that was not afraid of politics, corporate conspiracies, and the gray zones between good and evil.

At the heart of the game is deep mech customization. Each Wanzer is made up of a torso, arms, legs, and weapons, with damage to a specific part having clear consequences, shoot off an enemy's arm and it loses a weapon, destroy its legs and it loses mobility. This modularity turns every battle into a tactical puzzle in which you decide where to aim and what to risk. The **skill** system, which activates randomly depending on your equipment, adds an exciting element of uncertainty.

The storytelling offered unusual finesse: right at the start, a choice between two paths opened up different story lines following other characters and factions. That meant two full-fledged campaigns in one package and a strong reason to replay. The story, set in a tense geopolitical world of the future, tackled themes of weapons of mass destruction and the power of multinational corporations with surprising seriousness.

The **Front Mission** series was always off to the side of Square's mainstream, faithful more to a core of tactics fans, and the third installment is often considered the peak of the classic era. For many players in the West it was their very first encounter with the brand, and that is precisely why it earned a special place in their hearts.

Instead of fast action, it offers a patient, thoughtful war of machines in which technical detail and storytelling go hand in hand. It is a game for those who want not just to pilot mechs but to literally take them apart and reassemble them to their liking.

**Why play it:** Deep mech tactics with a branching story and two campaigns, the peak of the classic Front Mission era.

playstation__vandal-hearts.article:
Blood spraying into the sky in regular geysers, that is how players remembered **Vandal Hearts**, one of the first tactical RPGs that helped this genre break through on the Western PlayStation. In 1996, Konami offered an accessible yet clever gateway into the world of turn-based battles on an isometric grid.

Mechanically, the game stands on the solid foundations of the genre: characters move across a chessboard of terrain, use height and range, and each class has its strengths and weaknesses. The rock-paper-scissors system between units, where swordsmen, archers, and mages counter one another, makes every battle a thinking puzzle. Characters gradually develop into stronger classes, which rewards careful party building.

For its time, the game stood out with fully 3D-rendered battlefields that could be rotated and explored, a rarity on a console in the mid-90s. The story of intrigue, corruption, and a fight against tyranny did not surprise with originality, but it held together and gave the battles meaning. And then there was that unforgettable, slightly over-the-top death animation, in which fountains of blood shot from the fallen, a detail that became the game's signature.

In its day it was one of the few representatives of the tactical RPG available to Western audiences, and so it served many players as a springboard into a genre that bigger titles would later make famous. The game received a sequel and became a solid pillar of Konami's first-PlayStation-era library.

Thanks to its accessible difficulty and understandable rules, it remains an excellent starting point for anyone who wants to taste the charm of turn-based tactics without needless complexity.

**Why play it:** An accessible and clever tactical RPG with fully 3D battlefields, an ideal gateway to the genre, and unforgettable geysers of blood.

playstation__civilization-ii.article:
"Just one more turn" — this phrase has destroyed more nights of sleep than perhaps any other game, and **Civilization II** is its perfect embodiment. The legendary turn-based strategy created by the team around Sid Meier put you in the role of a nation's leader from the dawn of history all the way to the journey to the stars. The PlayStation version brought this gigantic 4X experience to television screens.

The premise is breathtaking in its ambition: you found cities, research a technology tree from the wheel to nuclear power, negotiate and go to war with rival civilizations, and try to lead your people to victory, whether by conquering the world or by elevating science and culture. Every decision has long-term consequences, and every game plays out differently. That is the famous "replayability" that people have demanded of the genre ever since.

**Civilization II** from 1996 was a huge step forward on the PC compared to the original, an isometric view, better graphics, the famous video clips of the **Council of Advisors**, and more sophisticated diplomacy. It was one of the most influential strategies of all time and often appears on lists of the best games in history. The console conversion was a bold attempt to bring a deeply mouse-and-keyboard experience to a controller.

The transfer to PlayStation carried compromises in controls, managing a sprawling empire with a gamepad was never as nimble as with a mouse. Even so it was a remarkable effort to make one of the peaks of PC strategy accessible to console players who otherwise had no way into this world.

Wherever you play it, the core remains the same: a hypnotic loop of planning, expansion, and discovery that can swallow up dozens of hours. It is a monument of the genre whose DNA you will find in every modern strategy.

**Why play it:** One of the most influential 4X titles of all time with endless replayability, and the infamous "just one more turn" syndrome.

playstation__theme-hospital.article:
A patient with a bloated head, a disease called **bloaty head**, and an ambulance that only comes when you pay for more staff, welcome to **Theme Hospital**, where management mixes with pure English humor. This building strategy from Bullfrog Studios, released in 1997, turned running a hospital into a surprisingly fun and witty discipline.

The task is to build and run a hospital: lay out clinics, hire doctors, nurses, and cleaners, treat increasingly absurd invented illnesses, and all the while keep an eye on the budget, patient satisfaction, and the queue at reception. The game masterfully balances a serious economic challenge with comic details, from the loudspeaker announcements to diseases like invisibility or "king complex." This mix turned an otherwise cold simulation into an unforgettable experience.

Bullfrog, under the leadership of **Peter Molyneux**, was in the 90s synonymous with clever and imaginative building games, and **Theme Hospital** was created as a spiritual successor to the successful Theme Park. The team managed to take a dry subject and spice it up with such humor and playability that the game has aged remarkably well. The PlayStation conversion brought the PC experience to console players too, though the controls were adapted to the controller.

The game's legacy is alive to this day, the modern **Two Point Hospital** is openly a tribute to this classic and comes from many of its creators. Few simulations can boast such a faithful and loving continuation decades later.

Beneath the humorous shell hides an honest challenge in planning and optimization that will delight anyone who enjoys watching a well-oiled machine slowly emerge from chaos. Laughter and strategy hand in hand.

**Why play it:** A witty and clever building simulation from the legendary Bullfrog, whose humor and playability age with grace, the roots of the modern Two Point Hospital.

playstation__populous-beginning.article:
Being a god means more than just handing out miracles, in **Populous: The Beginning** it literally means reshaping the very landscape beneath your people's feet. The third installment of Bullfrog's legendary series, released in 1998, took a bold step: it abandoned the bird's-eye view and moved the action into a fully 3D world of round planets that could be rotated and circled.

Unlike its predecessors, where you were an abstract divine force, here you control a **shaman** leading her tribe across a solar system of planets. The famous terrain shaping is still here, raising and lowering the land so your followers have somewhere to build and a way to advance, but directly controllable units, spells, and a tree of divine abilities from firestorms to volcanoes have been added. In terms of genre, the game shifted closer to real-time strategy without losing its iconic soul.

Each planet is a standalone puzzle: you must expand, master magic, and wipe out the enemy tribe before it does the same to you. Manipulating the landscape remains the heart of the experience and still feels unique today, few games give you the power to physically rebuild the world as a tool for victory.

Bullfrog was at that time one of the most imaginative studios of all, and **Populous** itself is considered the founder of the entire "god games" genre. This installment was its ambitious farewell to the era, a bold attempt to carry an aging concept into a three-dimensional future.

The PlayStation conversion let console players too taste the role of a deity, though strategy of this type always suited the mouse better. Even so it remains a fascinating and original title worth discovering.

**Why play it:** A bold 3D return of the founder of "god games," where you literally shape the planet beneath your people's feet, a unique experience from the Bullfrog workshop.

playstation__star-wars-dark-forces.article:
Even before there was a Doom Slayer in a galaxy far, far away, there was **Kyle Katarn**, and **Star Wars: Dark Forces** proved that first-person shooters and Star Wars belong together. This game from LucasArts, released in 1995 (and on PlayStation in 1996), took the template set by Doom and planted it in a beloved world, delighting fans and action players alike.

For its time it was a technically advanced shooter built on the proprietary **Jedi** engine, which enabled what Doom could not, real looking up and down, stairs, bridges, and multi-level environments. As the mercenary Kyle Katarn, the player infiltrated Imperial bases, facing stormtroopers, dark troopers, and the famous mechanical menace. The atmosphere was rounded out by iconic sound design and music from the Star Wars world, thanks to which every shootout reeked of the films.

The story followed Katarn's investigation into the Dark Trooper project, a new generation of Imperial combat units, and slotted into the expanded universe that fans devoured. Kyle Katarn became such a beloved character that he carried on through the entire **Jedi Knight** series and became one of the icons of the gaming Star Wars world.

**Dark Forces** is still prized today as one of the best licensed FPS games of the 90s and as proof that LucasArts could do more than just adventures. It laid the foundations of a beloved series and showed the path that action Star Wars games would take for years to come.

The PlayStation console version brought this experience beyond the PC, though FPS controls on the controller of the day had their limitations. For fans of the galaxy, though, it was an essential stop.

**Why play it:** A technically advanced Star Wars shooter that gave birth to the cult character Kyle Katarn and laid the foundation of the Jedi Knight series, one of the best licensed FPS games of its time.

playstation__star-wars-jedi-power-battle.article:
Igniting a lightsaber, deflecting a volley of blaster fire, and charging side by side with a partner against overwhelming odds, **Star Wars: Jedi Power Battles** bet everything on pure cooperative action from the world of Episode I. Here, in 2000, LucasArts offered an arcade ride in which players became full-blooded Jedi knights.

The game combines an action platformer with beat 'em up combat. You choose one of several Jedi, including **Obi-Wan Kenobi** and **Qui-Gon Jinn**, and battle through levels inspired by the film, slicing up droids, deflecting shots back at enemies, and pulling off acrobatic jumps. The real magic, however, comes out fully with two players, when cooperation becomes the heart of the fun.

For its time it was one of the few games that gave players the chance to feel like a real Jedi with a sword in hand and the Force within reach. The emphasis on flashy duels, blocking, and tossing enemies around made every skirmish a spectacle. The difficulty, however, was notoriously merciless, and falls into the abyss could really torment you.

The game was created at a time when LucasArts was experimenting with all sorts of approaches to the new film trilogy, and **Jedi Power Battles** represented the more action-oriented, more accessible face of this wave. Not everyone will rank it among the brand's peaks, but as a laid-back cooperative ride it had its firm place.

Today it is remembered mainly as a likable piece for two-player play, a title that proved swinging a lightsaber to the rhythm of blaster fire can simply be fun.

**Why play it:** An arcade cooperative action game from the world of Episode I, where you finally get to play as a Jedi knight with a lightsaber, best with two players.

playstation__star-wars-masters-of-teras-.article:
What if Star Wars met Tekken? That is exactly the question **Star Wars: Masters of Teräs Käsi** answered, and the answer was, to put it mildly, controversial. Here, in 1997, LucasArts tried what no one had before: pitting the saga's heroes and villains against each other in a one-on-one 3D fighting game.

The concept sounded enticing. You pick your favorite characters, **Luke Skywalker**, **Leia**, **Han Solo**, **Boba Fett**, or **Darth Vader**, and let them measure their strength in the arena in duels inspired by the fictional martial art Teräs Käsi, thanks to which even ordinary fighters could stand up to lightsaber-wielding Jedi. The character models and backdrops from the Star Wars world looked decent for their time, and the fan appeal was undeniable.

The problem lay in the fighting system itself. The controls felt clumsy, the animations stiff, and the character balance raised eyebrows. Compared to the reigning kings of the genre of the day like Tekken or Soul Blade, the game lagged behind in fluidity and depth, which earned it a rather cool reception from critics. For many it became a textbook example of how a strong license alone is not enough.

Even so, **Masters of Teräs Käsi** earned a peculiar place in the history of Star Wars games, as a bold if botched experiment and as a curiosity that fans still talk about today. The chance to send Vader against Boba Fett had its charm regardless of the reservations.

Today the title is interesting mainly as a historical artifact and a reminder that not every genre attempt from the LucasArts workshop worked out. For collectors and fans of curiosities, though, it is an unavoidable item.

**Why play it:** A curious attempt at a one-on-one Star Wars fighting game, a historically interesting experiment that today attracts more with its fan-favorite roster than with its gameplay.

playstation__star-wars-rebel-assault-ii.article:
A cinematic Hollywood spectacle right on your TV set – that was how **Star Wars: Rebel Assault II: The Hidden Empire** was sold, one of LucasArts' most ambitious attempts to blend game and film. The sequel to the successful original bet everything on live-action video footage with real actors, set within both space and ground-based action scenes.

The gameplay rested on the principle of a rail shooter: the game led you along a predetermined path and your task was to shoot enemies, dodge obstacles and hit your targets in rhythm with the slick animated sequences. It was a style typical of the CD-ROM era, when the enormous capacity of discs allowed games to be filled with pre-rendered videos and live-action footage. The emphasis was clearly on the experience and the spectacle rather than on deep mechanics.

For its time it was a technologically impressive piece – full-color video, a combination of live-action and computer-generated scenes, and an effort to create the feeling that you were right in the middle of your own Star Wars adventure. The story of a secret Imperial project expanded the universe, and fans appreciated the atmosphere that radiated straight out of the films.

With hindsight, **Rebel Assault II** is a typical representative of the short but distinctive era of interactive movies, which quickly faded once real 3D graphics matured. Even so, it remains a valuable reminder of a time when creators tried to blur the line between game and film at any cost.

Today it will be appreciated mainly by nostalgics and collectors who want to taste what the ambitions of a mid-1990s multimedia experience looked like. As a piece of history it has its unquestionable place.

**Why play it:** A showcase interactive movie from the CD-ROM era with live-action video from the Star Wars world – a nostalgic stop in history, when games wanted to become film.

playstation__star-wars-demolition.article:
Imagine a vehicular arena brawl in the style of Twisted Metal – except instead of gloomy streets, you wreak havoc in the middle of the Star Wars galaxy. That is exactly how Star Wars: Demolition came about, one of the most unconventional offshoots of the famous brand on the PlayStation.

Instead of X-wing pilots and Jedi knights, you take the controls of combat machines crewed by characters and vehicles from the Star Wars universe. The game is built on the principle of vehicular combat: in enclosed arenas, armored opponents equipped with firearms and special attacks face off against one another, and the goal is to shoot your opponent to pieces before he does the same to you. The game openly acknowledges its debt to the Twisted Metal series, which makes sense – this type of adrenaline-fueled arena action was very popular in the late 1990s.

The charm of the title lies in how it tries to smuggle the familiar faces and settings of Star Wars into a genre that has nothing to do with the saga. For fans it was either a refreshing trip off the beaten track, or a curiosity that treated the brand rather loosely. Arenas set in familiar locations and the chance to duke it out with characters from the films have their own crazy charm.

From today's perspective, Demolition is interesting mainly as testimony to how eagerly licenses were experimented with at the turn of the millennium – a big brand simply tried to squeeze itself into as many game genres as possible. Not every such attempt has aged gracefully, but the effort at originality is to be commended.

**Why play it:** When you want Star Wars a little differently – without the loftiness, but with engine roar and explosions in the arena – this vehicular brawl will delight you with its unexpected audacity.

playstation__star-trek-invasion.article:
The Star Trek universe usually rests on diplomacy and dialogue – but here you let the phaser cannons do the talking. Star Trek: Invasion is a space action game in which you take the cockpit of a fighter and hurl yourself into battles among the stars under the banner of the Federation.

The core of the game is space combat: arcade-tuned dogfights in space, where you maneuver between enemy ships, lock on targets and switch between weapons and shields. The missions are set in the familiar Trek world with ships and factions that fans know well, and they gradually guide you through a campaign with a narrated story. Unlike the slower strategic Treks, this is the brisk, more action-oriented side of the series, where reflexes matter more than patient tactics.

On the PlayStation it was one of the titles that tried to satisfy fans longing for the feeling of piloting a Starfleet combat vessel themselves. The game benefited from the atmosphere of the universe – from the ship designs, the environments and the sound backdrop that evokes the on-screen source material. The space setting also let the effects of lasers and explosions shine, which looked striking on the console.

Space simulators and arcade fighters formed a distinctive genre at the turn of the millennium, and licensed Treks fit into it naturally – who wouldn't want to defend the Federation single-handedly? The title is thus a reminder of a time when big sci-fi brands were regularly turned into cockpit action.

**Why play it:** For anyone who wanted to enjoy direct first-person action in the Star Trek world from the cockpit of a fighter, instead of forever sitting in a briefing room.

playstation__star-trek-deep-space-nine-f.article:
The Deep Space Nine station was one of the darkest and most complex corners of the Trek universe – and this game tried to turn it into a tense first-person action experience. Star Trek: Deep Space Nine – The Fallen brings the player right into the events surrounding the beloved series as a first-person action shooter.

The game is built on FPS gameplay, but complements it with exploration, the use of the tricorder and interaction with the world in Star Trek style. The player takes on the role of the station's key characters and moves through missions tied to a story rooted in the show's lore. It is therefore not purely mindless action – part of the experience is also solving situations, moving through environments familiar from the source, and an effort to preserve the Trek atmosphere, where violence is the last resort.

On the PlayStation it was an ambitious attempt to transfer an expansive and often philosophical series into a brisker game format. For fans the main draw was that they could step into the shoes of the Deep Space Nine heroes and live out their own adventure in settings they knew intimately from television. The story setting and fidelity to the environment were key to the whole project.

The Fallen is an interesting example of how, at the turn of the millennium, first-person shooters tried to link action with storytelling and a licensed world. It was not always an easy pairing, but the ambition to offer something more than mere shooting is likeable.

**Why play it:** If you enjoy Deep Space Nine and want to explore its world actively, from a first-person perspective, this action game offers you a story-driven trip to the familiar station.

playstation__simcity-2000.article:
An empty green plain, a cursor and you as a mayor with absolute power. SimCity 2000 confronts you with the most enticing question in city-building games: can you build a functioning metropolis from nothing, one that won't go bankrupt, won't bury itself in traffic jams and won't revolt over taxes? The version for the Sony PlayStation brought this cult simulator to the console and opened it up to a whole new generation of players in front of the TV.
