Compared to the original SimCity, the sequel made an enormous leap. Maxis replaced the flat top-down city with an isometric view that gave the metropolis depth and character. Suddenly there were layers: you could dig into the underground, deal with water pipes, the subway and utility networks, watch the terrain with its hills and valleys, and build highways and grade-separated intersections. Separate water management and more sophisticated power systems were added, where you chose between various types of power plants, each with different costs, output and environmental impact.

The core of the gameplay remained faithful to Will Wright's brilliant concept: you zone residential, commercial and industrial areas, supply them with power, connect them with transport and balance the budget among services such as firefighters, police, schools and hospitals. The city lives a life of its own, reacts to your decisions and mercilessly shows you when you overdo the taxes or neglect the infrastructure. Nor are disasters missing, from fires through tornadoes to raids, which can test just how resilient a metropolis you have actually built.

In development terms it was the flagship of the Maxis studio, which practically defined the entire genre of sandbox builders with simulations of all kinds. SimCity 2000 became one of the most successful and most-ported games of its era and was released on a countless range of platforms, from PC through Macintosh and Amiga all the way to consoles including the PlayStation. The console version had to solve control without a mouse, but it managed to preserve both depth and clarity, so you can enjoy full-fat mayoring even with a gamepad.

The influence of this game is still enormous today. SimCity 2000 showed that a strategy without enemies and without winning in the classic sense of the word can be as addictive as anything else, because your opponent is your own inability to keep the system in balance. It inspired countless later city builders and to this day is remembered as one of the peaks of the genre and as a game over which whole nights were lost to budgets and traffic.

For PlayStation players it was a chance to taste a previously mostly-PC genre on a console and in the comfort of the living room. Converting a title built on precise mouse work and lots of menus to a controller was no trivial task, but the result made it possible to immerse yourself in city management even without a desk full of peripherals. Thanks to this, SimCity 2000 retained its reputation as one of the few truly deep builders that could be fully played lying on the couch, thus strengthening its already broad fan base across platforms.

**Why play it:** For the timeless feeling of absolute mayoral power and for that sweet addiction where it's just one more district, one more budget, and suddenly dawn is breaking.

playstation__ace-combat-3-electrosphere.detail: The most ambitious installment on the PS1 both visually and narratively: a futuristic world, anime cutscenes and branching missions. The Japanese version was significantly more extensive than the Western cut, yet even so it astonishes with its atmosphere and technical execution at the end of the console's life.
playstation__ace-combat-3-electrosphere.article:
A fighter jet slices through the futuristic sky, targets light up on the cockpit glass and the voice on the radio drives you toward the next aerial duel. **Ace Combat 3: Electrosphere** by **Namco** pushed the series into the near future and demonstrated what aerial action on the first PlayStation could look like when cutting-edge technology and a sense of style come together.

The game stays faithful to the recipe that made the series famous: it is an **arcade-tuned flight simulator**, where flight physics gives way to the feeling of speed, maneuverability and instant reward. You pilot a whole palette of **futuristic fighters** armed with a cannon and a set of guided and special missiles, lock onto enemies and dodge anti-aircraft fire in missions that lead you over the city, mountains and open sea. The controls are accessible enough for a newcomer to grasp, yet deep enough that masterful flying becomes a real art.

Beyond pure action, **Electrosphere** is marked by a strong emphasis on story and atmosphere. The game takes place in a future where real states have given way to powerful corporations, and you follow the plot through the eyes of a pilot connected to an electronic network. The Japanese version contained extensive story scenes and animated sequences with several branching paths, while the version released in the West was significantly abridged and lost a considerable part of this narrative. This difference remains one of the most discussed topics among fans of the series to this day.

In development terms the game represents the pinnacle of what Namco squeezed out of the PlayStation for the aerial genre. A smooth framerate, cleanly modeled machines and impressive environments showed that the console could sustain fast three-dimensional action without stuttering. **Ace Combat** established itself on this generation as one of the defining aerial brands, and the third installment is eloquent proof of that.

The cultural significance of the series lies in the fact that it managed to bring aerial combat closer to a broad audience that would never have dared to approach a complex PC simulator. **Electrosphere** added to this a bold cyberpunk vision that makes it a unique experiment for its time, one that fans still remember with respect.

**Why play it:** Stylish and fast aerial action with a cyberpunk atmosphere, one of the jewels of the genre on the first PlayStation.

playstation__porsche-challenge.article:
One brand, one car, one goal: the perfect driving feel. Porsche Challenge did not take the path of extensive car rosters or exotic tracks. Instead, it bet everything on a single model of the legendary Porsche Boxster sports car and built a brisk, finely-tuned and surprisingly addictive racing experience around it on the first generation of the Sony PlayStation console.

The gameplay is pleasantly focused and accessible. Concentrating on a single car meant the developers could carefully fine-tune its behavior and responses, so every corner and every braking maneuver has believable weight. The player races on a series of tracks against opponents and gradually gets to know the subtle nuances of the handling. This purity of purpose made Porsche Challenge a title that, while not the most extensive, was precisely polished.

On the early PlayStation the game was among the titles that showcased the console's capabilities in the area of 3D racing. The detailed car model, the smooth sense of speed and the varied environments showed where the genre was heading on the new generation of hardware. The game was also known for the option to customize the color and appearance of the car, as well as the presence of several driver characters with different profiles.

Porsche Challenge came about at a time when the racing genre on the PlayStation was still taking shape and competing for attention with big names. Thanks to its exclusive focus on one of the world's most coveted automakers, it found its fans among players for whom the driving feel mattered more than the number of unlockable cars. For many it was a kind of postcard of the Porsche brand in digital form.

Today the game is remembered as a likeable, if perhaps slightly overlooked, piece of the early PlayStation era. It represents an interesting contrast to the later megalomaniacal racing simulators: it shows that concentrating on one thing and executing it precisely can create a distinctive and memorable experience.

**Why play it:** For the polished driving feel in a single iconic Porsche and a glimpse of what racing looked like at the dawn of the PlayStation era.

playstation__lego-racers.article:
What happens when the world's most famous construction set turns into a racing game? The result is a colorful, playful and surprisingly rich piece that enchanted an entire generation of young players. Lego Racers takes the classic concept of arcade racing with items and wraps it in the unmistakable world of bricks, minifigures and tracks assembled from familiar pieces.

The gameplay draws on the tried-and-tested recipe of arcade kart racing. Players speed around themed tracks, collect upgrades and offensive items and try to overtake their opponents. But Lego Racers adds its own layer of magic: from bricks you can build and customize both your own racer and their vehicle. This possibility of building from bricks fits perfectly with the brand's identity and gives the game a distinctive dimension that sets it apart from the competition.

The game's world is ruled by a character named Rocket Racer, and across the campaign the player fights through various themed environments inspired by classic construction-set lines, from pirates through the Middle Ages to futuristic worlds. Each area has its own visuals and atmosphere, so making your way through the racing championship feels like a journey across an entire box of Lego.

Lego Racers was released in the late 1990s for the PlayStation and personal computers and became one of the most successful and best-remembered video game titles based on the Lego brand from that time. For many children it was one of their first racing games ever, and the combination of accessibility, colorfulness and creative building made it a favorite of family gaming.

The game received a sequel and became a harbinger of the later huge wave of Lego games that dominated the gaming industry in the following decades. In itself it evokes strong nostalgia today: it is a title that managed to connect the joy of building with the joy of racing and to appeal to players of all ages.

**Why play it:** For cheerful, accessible kart racing with the magic of building from bricks, ideal for nostalgic memories as well as family gaming.

playstation__lego-racers-2.article:
After the success of the first installment, the bricks got moving again, and this time much farther from home. **Lego Racers 2** sends players across planets and exotic environments in arcade races, where everything is made of plastic Lego bricks, from the cars through the tracks to the landscape itself.

Compared to the original game, the second installment added a significant element of free movement. Outside the races themselves, you move around the worlds in open zones, complete tasks, collect parts and unlock new routes. The racing core remains arcade and family-friendly, with an emphasis on fun rather than simulation, so even a less experienced player can take the wheel. Building and modifying your own vehicle from bricks is among the most enticing things the series offers.

The game is part of the wave of licensed Lego titles that were created under the banner of Lego Media and related studios at the turn of the millennium, that is, long before the era of the famous action-adventure games by TT Games. It was released for the PlayStation and PC and clearly targeted a younger audience and families, who were drawn by the combination of racing and creative building.

Culturally, this generation of Lego games shows the path the brand was taking before it found its golden format of parodic action-adventures based on movie licenses. **Lego Racers 2** stands in an interesting interim period, when Lego was experimenting with all sorts of genres, from racing through strategy to adventure, searching for what worked best with plastic bricks in digital form.

On the PlayStation the game holds up its fresh, colorful graphics and accessible controls. It is not a title that would break records in difficulty or realism, but that was precisely the intention. It was about the joy of building, discovering colorful worlds and carefree racing that entertains the whole family in front of one screen.

**Why play it:** For players who want a nostalgic family arcade race with a touch of exploration and the magic of building from Lego bricks.

playstation__lego-stunt-rally.article:
What if a game let you not only race, but also build your own crazy track full of loops and jumps? **Lego Stunt Rally** offers exactly that, combining arcade stunt racing with a track editor, where Lego bricks become your own playground.

In terms of gameplay it is a brisk, accessible racing game with an emphasis on tricks, jumps and ramps. Brick-built cars zoom along tracks full of adrenaline elements, and the game's main appeal is that the player is not confined only to pre-made circuits. The built-in editor lets you assemble your own tracks piece by piece, which turns the title into a small creative workshop for anyone who likes to tinker with design.

The game was created at the turn of the millennium as part of the extensive range of licensed Lego games for computers and consoles, released under the banner of Lego Media. It came out for the PlayStation, PC and Game Boy Color, with the individual versions adapted to the capabilities of the given platform. It was one of many attempts to transfer the joy of the construction set into an interactive digital form.

Culturally, **Lego Stunt Rally** fits into a period when the brand was still searching for its signature in video games. The combination of racing and track-building foreshadows what would always be key for Lego games: creativity and playing with bricks. This philosophy then permeated the later, much more famous titles of the TT Games studio.

Both visually and mechanically the game targets a younger and family audience. The controls are simple, the pace cheerful and the overall impression carefree. It is not a game for hardcore racers, but for someone who wants to race casually while building their own world from plastic pieces.

**Why play it:** When you are drawn to arcade stunt racing combined with the joy of building your own tracks from Lego bricks.

playstation__lego-rock-raiders.article:
Beneath the surface of an alien planet, precious energy is mined and your crew of miners in yellow helmets faces rock, lava and underground monsters. **Lego Rock Raiders** brings the construction-set line of the same name into a world of strategy and exploration, where survival underground matters as much as mining.

The game combines strategic and action elements. You command a team of miners, manage the mining of raw materials, build a base and its equipment, and at the same time you must deal with the pitfalls of the underground. On the PlayStation the game is closer to a more action-oriented, more direct approach to controlling units and vehicles than the concurrent computer version offered, which corresponds to the capabilities of the console and its controller.

The title was released in the late 1990s as part of the wave of licensed Lego games and connected with the then-current Rock Raiders product line, that is, a series of construction sets about a mining crew. It was one of Lego's more ambitious attempts at the strategy and building genre, which stood apart from the simpler family racing.

Culturally, **Lego Rock Raiders** is an interesting testament to how broadly the brand was experimenting at the time. Alongside racing and adventure, it also tried the more demanding genre of resource management and strategy, and did so with its own space theme, which had its construction-set source as well as an animated and comic-book expansion.

On the console the game had to cope with how to transfer complex strategic controls to a gamepad. The result is an experience that is somewhat more action-oriented and more straightforward, but still retains a core of building and mining. For fans of bricks and strategy from that time it is a distinctive and today rather forgotten piece.

**Why play it:** If you are interested in an unconventional strategic detour in the history of Lego games, where you mine, build and fight deep beneath the surface of an alien planet.

playstation__ace-combat.detail: The first installment of the cult aerial series (in the West it was released as Air Combat). Arcade-style but stylish aerial dogfights with 3D graphics that amazed in 1995. It laid the foundations for a series that still rules the aerial action genre to this day.

playstation__ace-combat-2.detail: A significant step up from the original: smoother graphics, a bigger arsenal, more elaborate missions and the first hints of a story line and a fictional world that would later make the series famous. A must for fans of aerial arcade action on the PS1.

psp__god-of-war-chains-of-olympus.article:
When Kratos first appeared on a handheld, there were doubts about whether a bloody Greek quest for vengeance could be crammed into the palm of your hand at all. Chains of Olympus scattered those doubts within its first few minutes – and proved that the PSP could handle a full-blooded God of War.

The game faithfully carries over everything that made the series famous: brutal hack & slash combat with the Blades of Chaos, flashy quick-time finishers, puzzles rooted in ancient mythology and a combat system that rewards both rhythm and aggression. Story-wise it is a prequel that reveals Kratos's past in the service of the gods of Olympus, before he becomes the notorious destroyer of the pantheon. Ready at Dawn did extraordinary work with the console's hardware – the graphics, fluidity and scale of the battles looked breathtaking on a handheld device.

It was precisely this technical execution that made Chains of Olympus the benchmark for how a big action franchise should look in pocket form. The game didn't feel like a watered-down excerpt of the home version, but like a true entry in the series, simply in a format you could take anywhere. That made it one of the proofs that the PSP could handle even the most demanding action blockbusters.

Kratos's journey across Olympus also worked as a bridge between the entries in the main series and enriched the game's mythology with new layers. For fans it was a mandatory stop, and for PSP owners one of the best reasons to own the console.

**Why play it:** A full-fledged, technically top-tier God of War on a handheld – brutal action and ancient mythology with no compromises, wherever you please.

psp__god-of-war-ghost-of-sparta.article:
Ready at Dawn had already proven once that Kratos belongs on the PSP too – with Ghost of Sparta they raised the bar even higher and created one of the prettiest and most polished titles on the entire console. The second handheld God of War is a celebration of what can be achieved on a portable device.

The core formula stays true to the series: bloody hack & slash with an emphasis on flashy combat, brutal finishers, puzzles and a journey through an ancient world full of gods and monsters. But Ghost of Sparta deepens Kratos's personal mythology – the story revolves around his past and his family ties, lending the otherwise merciless hero a surprisingly human dimension. The combat system is expanded with new abilities and the game is not shy about epic moments.

On the technical side it is one of the PSP's peaks. The graphics, animation, scope of the locations and the boss battles look as though the console's hardware shouldn't be able to handle them – and yet it all runs smoothly and impressively. Ready at Dawn showed here just how deeply they could reach into the device's capabilities and squeeze the maximum out of it.

Ghost of Sparta thus closes out the handheld God of War duo as a more mature, more grown-up experience that holds up even alongside the home entries. For many players it was the best action game they could experience on the PSP, and proof that big experiences can fit into the palm of your hand.

**Why play it:** The pinnacle of action on the PSP – an even prettier, more epic and more personal Kratos who proves that a handheld can deliver an experience worthy of the big entries.

psp__gta-liberty-city-stories.article:
The prevailing myth said an open-world Grand Theft Auto would never fit on a handheld – Liberty City Stories shot that myth down with a grin. Rockstar transferred an entire living city into the palm of your hand and proved that the freedom of the criminal sandbox doesn't need a television.

The game returns to the Liberty City known from GTA III, only in an earlier time line and with a new protagonist. The player gets what they expect from the series: a sprawling open city where you can complete story missions, steal cars, roam the streets and cause chaos to your heart's content. The missions combine shooting, driving and running errands for various underworld bosses, and it's all held together by the cynical, ironic tone the brand is famous for. All of this ran surprisingly smoothly on the PSP and with the kind of freedom players were used to from the big consoles.

Technically it was a small miracle – a complete 3D open world with traffic, pedestrians and missions that fit onto a handheld device. Liberty City Stories thus served as proof that the PSP is a genuine home console in your pocket, capable of accommodating even the most demanding genres. For Rockstar it meant a successful entry into the world of handheld gaming.

A city full of possibilities, black humor and the trademark GTA gameplay made the title one of the console's must-have pieces. Players could finally take an open world of crime with them anywhere.

**Why play it:** A full-fledged open-world GTA in your pocket – all of Liberty City, the series' freedom and chaos on the go, with no need to sit down in front of a TV.

psp__gta-vice-city-stories.article:
Neon glow of the '80s, palm trees, pink sunsets and synthesizers – Vice City Stories brings to the PSP the most stylish backdrop the Grand Theft Auto series has ever had. Rockstar returned to the beloved city and proved that handheld GTA can be even richer and more ambitious.

The game develops the tried-and-true open-world formula: a sprawling open Vice City, a story campaign, car theft, shootouts and missions for a colorful gallery of underworld characters. Compared with the previous handheld entry, Vice City Stories also adds empire-building elements, where the player expands their own criminal enterprise and acquires property. All of it is wrapped in the unmistakable atmosphere of the eighties, completed by the music, fashion and visual style of the whole era.

Technically it is once again an impressive piece – a complete living city with traffic and missions running smoothly on a handheld console. Vice City Stories builds on the success of Liberty City Stories and pushes handheld GTA a step further both in scope and content. For PSP owners it was further proof that they could experience full-fledged big games on the console.

The combination of a stylish retro backdrop, an open world and the trademark cynical storytelling made Vice City Stories one of the console's most beloved titles. A return to the city of sin in your pocket was a temptation series fans found hard to resist.

**Why play it:** A stylish open-world GTA set against the neon backdrop of the '80s with empire-building elements – all of Vice City on the go, in a form that pushes the handheld series further.

psp__metal-gear-solid-peace-walker.teaser: Almost a mainline entry in the series; base building + co-op.
psp__metal-gear-solid-peace-walker.detail: Almost a mainline entry in the series (Kojima initially wanted to number it as MGS5). Stealth missions, building your own army and base (Mother Base) in the meta game, and excellent co-op. Dense content; later released in an HD collection on consoles.
psp__metal-gear-solid-peace-walker.article:
When Hideo Kojima unveiled Peace Walker, he spoke of it almost as the fifth mainline Metal Gear – and anyone who knows the game knows that wasn't an exaggeration. This 2010 PSP gem from Kojima Productions is so dense and ambitious that it defies everything we usually imagine a handheld game to be.

At its core remains first-class stealth: sneaking, avoiding enemies and cleverly resolving situations, typical of the entire Metal Gear Solid series. But Peace Walker adds a thoughtful meta game to it – building your own army and a base called Mother Base. The soldiers you recruit during missions are managed and developed between individual expeditions, giving rise to a strategic layer that stretches the game to dozens of hours of content. Another big draw is the excellent co-op, thanks to which a number of missions can be tackled with a partner.

Story-wise the game develops the saga of Big Boss and slots into the broader mythological framework of the series that Kojima had been building for years. The density of content, the elaborate base-management system and the emphasis on team play made Peace Walker an exceptionally rich title that felt almost unbelievably vast on a handheld.

The game's significance is also evidenced by the fact that it later made its way into an HD collection on home consoles, where players without a PSP could enjoy it too. Many of its ideas – especially base building – went on to become the foundation of the later Metal Gear Solid V.

**Why play it:** Almost a full-fledged mainline Metal Gear on the PSP – top-tier stealth, building your own army and base, and great co-op in one exceptionally dense package.

psp__daxter.teaser: A beautiful platformer from the world of Jak & Daxter.
psp__daxter.detail: A spin-off from the world of Jak & Daxter in which you play as the chatty pet. A beautiful, finely tuned platformer that makes excellent use of the PSP hardware; one of the console's prettiest games.
psp__daxter.article:
What does a chatty ottsel do when his buddy Jak disappears? He sets off to find him on his own – and out of that came one of the most beautiful and finely tuned platformers on the entire PSP. Daxter, from 2006 by Ready at Dawn, is a spin-off from the world of Jak & Daxter that puts his motor-mouthed pet in the lead role.

The gameplay is a classic 3D platformer: jumping, collecting, combat and exploring varied environments, all interspersed with humor and Daxter's commentary. The player controls him and sets off on his own adventure while searching for the vanished Jak. The game draws on the colorful, playful style of the series and offers brisk, pleasantly accessible action that suits both fans of the original trilogy and newcomers.

Where Daxter truly dazzles is its technical execution. Ready at Dawn – who would later show off their craft with God of War on the PSP as well – squeezed gorgeous graphics, smooth performance and precisely tuned controls out of the console. The game is among the prettiest things ever made on the PSP and again proves just how deeply this group could reach into the hardware's capabilities.

Thanks to the combination of a likable hero, tuned gameplay and terrific presentation, Daxter ranks among the titles worth trying on the console. It is proof that even a supporting character can carry their own game – and be entertaining while doing so.

**Why play it:** One of the prettiest and most finely tuned platformers on the PSP – a colorful adventure with the motor-mouthed Daxter in the lead role and technical excellence from Ready at Dawn.

psp__patapon-1-3.teaser: Rhythm strategy; you beat a drum and command an army. An original.
psp__patapon-1-3.detail: A brilliantly original blend of rhythm and strategy: you drum out commands in rhythm (Pata-Pata-Pata-Pon = march) and your little army of eyeballs obeys, attacks and defends. A hypnotic, addictive, adorable one-of-a-kind with silhouette graphics.
psp__patapon-1-3.article:
Pata-Pata-Pata-Pon. Just four beats on the drum and a whole little army of black eyeballs with a single glowing eye starts to march. Patapon is one of those miracles that could only have come about on the PSP and only in the heads of people who weren't afraid to mix genres that, at first glance, don't belong together at all.

The principle is brilliantly simple and yet deep. You don't command your units directly, but through **rhythm**. Each command is a four-beat sequence of drum hits: Pata-Pata-Pata-Pon means march forward, Pon-Pon-Pata-Pon means attack, Chaka-Chaka-Pata-Pon means defend. When you hold the rhythm long enough and precisely, your army enters a **Fever** state, in which they attack harder, run faster and the whole screen pulses with joy. The moment you lose the rhythm, the combo falls apart and you have to start building the tempo again.

What could have been just a cute little gimmick gradually grows into a surprisingly complex strategy. You gather materials, craft and upgrade units — spearmen, archers, riders on giant beasts — and advance through the world in pursuit of the enemy and the fabled land of Earthend. The second and third entries in the series deepened the mechanics further, adding new classes, heroes and a more elaborate camp system, so the trilogy forms a coherent and ever-richer whole.

The visuals are unmistakable. The flat silhouette style, where tiny black figures move against pastel backdrops, feels like an interactive picture book. The music and sound aren't merely accompaniment — they are the **gameplay itself**, because the whole game is essentially a rhythmic composition you play with your own hands.

Patapon remains one of the most original titles ever released on Sony's handheld, and to this day it has no real equivalent. It's a game that gets into your head, and you'll catch yourself tapping out its rhythms long after switching it off.

**Why play it:** A hypnotic, addictive and adorably original blend of rhythm and strategy you won't find anywhere else — short sessions ideal for handheld play.

psp__locoroco-1-and-2.teaser: An adorable physics platformer; pure joy.
psp__locoroco-1-and-2.detail: An adorable physics platformer where you don't tilt the character but the whole world (with the L/R shoulders), so gelatinous creatures roll toward the goal. Cheerful music in a made-up language and a radiant style. Pure joy.
psp__locoroco-1-and-2.article:
There are games that try to be cool, edgy and grown-up. And then there's LocoRoco, which wants only one thing — to make you smile. And it succeeds at it with complete ease from the very first second.

The premise is delightfully simple and yet brilliant. You don't control the character directly. Instead, you **tilt the whole world** using the L and R shoulder buttons, so the yellow gelatinous blob called LocoRoco rolls, slides and bounces across the landscape according to gravity. A button press makes it hop, gathering fruit makes it grow and split into a swarm of small blobs, which merge back into one big one as needed. The goal is to get from point A to point B, collect as much as possible and soak up that infectious good mood.

The magic of LocoRoco, however, is above all **sensory**. The music sung in a made-up language, joined by the LocoRoco themselves with their chirping voices, is among the most infectious melodies ever heard in gaming history. The radiant, rounded and adorable art style looks like a fairy tale for the youngest, but the level design hides surprisingly clever physics puzzles and secret paths that will please players eager to explore.

The second entry, released two years later, took the proven foundation and added new abilities, more elaborate levels and an even richer spectacle without losing any of the original charm. Together they form a duo that showed the PSP from its friendliest and most playful side.

LocoRoco is proof that joy can be designed. It's not a game about performance or scores — it's a little good-mood generator you return to at exactly those moments when you need the world to light up a little again.

**Why play it:** Pure, unadulterated joy in the form of a physics platformer with infectious music — the perfect cure for a bad mood.

psp__crisis-core-final-fantasy-vii.teaser: A prequel to FF7; an emotional ending.
psp__crisis-core-final-fantasy-vii.detail: A prequel to FF VII with action combat, following Zack Fair. It gives emotional context to the famous story, and its ending strikes every fan of the seventh entry. Highly acclaimed; it received a remake (Reunion).
psp__crisis-core-final-fantasy-vii.article:
Every fan of Final Fantasy VII knows that name, even if they never played the seventh entry itself: Zack Fair. And it is he whom Crisis Core finally gives his own story — and his own, heartbreaking ending.

Crisis Core is a **prequel** to the legendary Final Fantasy VII, set several years before the events of the original game. You play as Zack, a young and promising member of the elite SOLDIER unit under the aegis of the Shinra corporation, and move through a story that fills in the key gaps of the famous legend — you meet Sephiroth in the days when he was still a hero, the mentor Angeal and the tragic background of what happened to the whole world.

The combat system abandoned the classic turns and bet on **real-time action**. Zack attacks, dodges and casts spells on the move, with the whole affair complemented by the original DMW mechanic — a kind of continuously spinning roulette at the edge of the screen that randomly triggers limit attacks, upgrades and memory sequences. Materia, iconic to the entire series, is tracked and combined here to build up Zack's arsenal.

Where Crisis Core truly excels, though, is its **emotional impact**. The game skillfully builds a bond with its hero, so that its conclusion — which fans of the seventh entry somewhat foresee — strikes with unexpected force. Few finales in the history of handheld gaming can leave the player sitting in silence with a lump in their throat.

The title was highly acclaimed and became one of the most important reasons to get a PSP. Its standing was confirmed by the fact that it received a modern remake under the name Crisis Core: Final Fantasy VII Reunion, which brought the story to a new generation of players.

**Why play it:** An indispensable part of the Final Fantasy VII mythology with action combat and an ending that will etch itself into the memory of every fan of the seventh entry.

psp__final-fantasy-tactics-war-of-lions.teaser: The definitive version of the classic tactics; a new translation and cutscenes.
psp__final-fantasy-tactics-war-of-lions.detail: The definitive version of the classic with a new, more beautiful translation (Shakespearean style), added animated cutscenes and characters. A deep job system and a serious story. The best way to experience FFT.
psp__final-fantasy-tactics-war-of-lions.article:
Betrayal, intrigue, a war for the throne and a hero whose name history forgot. Final Fantasy Tactics always ranked among the darkest and deepest stories the series ever produced — and The War of the Lions is the best way to experience it.

This PSP version is the **definitive edition** of the classic from the first PlayStation era. The most striking change is a completely new translation, which abandoned the earlier clumsy style in favor of a lofty, almost **Shakespearean** language that gave the story of the kingdom of Ivalice and the fate of Ramza Beoulve the dignity and weight it deserved. Beautiful animated cinematic sequences and several new characters were also added, among them the iconic Balthier from Final Fantasy XII.

At the heart of the game remains the brilliant **job system**. You train your units in dozens of professions — from knights and dark mages to archers and exotic classes — and each of them unlocks abilities that can be combined across professions. Building a perfectly coordinated team is a joy in its own right here, and the game rewards thinking ahead, knowledge of the terrain and unit positioning.

The battles themselves play out on isometric grids, where terrain height, range, direction of attack and turn order all matter. It's tactics that won't let go — challenging, deep and immensely satisfying the moment you manage to turn a seemingly hopeless situation around with a clever maneuver.

And yet the story never recedes into the background. It's a serious, adult tale of power, faith, class differences and how history is written and rewritten. The combination of top-tier tactics and a strong plot makes this game a lasting peak of the genre.

**Why play it:** The best available version of one of the best tactical RPGs of all time — a deep job system and a serious, beautifully translated story.

psp__castlevania-dracula-x-chronicles.teaser: A Rondo of Blood remake + bonuses (including the original SotN).
psp__castlevania-dracula-x-chronicles.detail: A 3D remake of the legendary Rondo of Blood that additionally includes the original 2D Rondo and the entire Symphony of the Night as unlockable bonuses — three games in one. Enormous value for fans.
psp__castlevania-dracula-x-chronicles.article:
Three Castlevanias for the price of one. That's how you could sum up in a single sentence the package Konami prepared for PSP owners — and it's an offer no fan of whip-armed vampire hunters can refuse.

At the core of The Dracula X Chronicles is a **3D remake** of the legendary Rondo of Blood. This game originally came out only in Japan for the PC Engine and for years remained an almost mythical, unobtainable piece for Western players. The remake brought it into modern form with polygonal graphics and reworked music, while preserving that classic, uncompromising gameplay of the saga — jumps, whips, sub-weapons and precisely placed enemies, where every wrong step means punishment.

The real value of the package, however, lies in its bonuses. You can unlock here the **original 2D Rondo of Blood** in its authentic form, so the legendary Japanese original finally got an official route to Western audiences. And as if that weren't enough, the complete **Symphony of the Night** is hidden here too — probably the most influential Castlevania ever, the game that defined the entire metroidvania subgenre.

It is precisely Symphony of the Night that makes this release an absolute gem. Roaming a sprawling, interconnected castle, collecting weapons and abilities, leveling up and discovering secret rooms — all of it is available on the go, in full glory and with a slightly reworked voice-over.

Together it makes for one of the most generous packages of its time. For a newcomer it's a great introduction to two different faces of the series, and for a veteran a dream come true to have both Rondo and Symphony together in your pocket.

**Why play it:** Three cult Castlevanias in one — a 3D remake of Rondo of Blood plus the original 2D version and the entire Symphony of the Night as a bonus. Enormous value.

psp__persona-3-portable.teaser: The gateway to modern Persona; an addictive daily cycle.
psp__persona-3-portable.detail: The gateway to modern Persona: by day you study and build relationships (Social Links), by night you climb the tower of Tartarus and fight with the help of „Personas“ summoned by an evoker. An addictive daily cycle. The Portable version added a female protagonist. The start of a phenomenon.
psp__persona-3-portable.article:
What would you do if you knew you had only a limited number of days left? Persona 3 mined this existential question for one of the most addictive gameplay loops any JRPG has ever offered — and the portable version took it on the road.

Persona 3 Portable is **the gateway to the modern era** of the Persona series and defines the formula that later entries went on to make famous. The game revolves around a hypnotic **daily cycle**: by day you live the life of an ordinary student — you go to school, study, do sports, and above all build relationships with the people around you through so-called Social Links. By night, during the mysterious Dark Hour, you ascend the endless tower of Tartarus and battle Shadows.

Combat is built on summoning **Personas** — manifestations of the personality that characters call forth with a dramatic gesture of the evoker. Each Persona has its elements, strengths, and weaknesses, and clever exploitation of enemy vulnerabilities is the key to victory. Personas can also be fused to create ever more powerful beings, which lends the system depth and endless room for experimentation.

The brilliant part is how the two layers interlock: the relationships you cultivate by day directly strengthen your Personas in battle. The game thus forces you to manage your time, decide whom to devote yourself to, and live with your choices — because the days really are limited.

The Portable version brought a fundamental new feature in the form of a **female protagonist**, offering fresh dialogue, new Social Links, and different music, adding value even for those who already knew the story. Persona 3 kicked off a phenomenon that turned the series into one of the most beloved names in Japanese RPGs.

**Why play:** The start of the modern Persona phenomenon with an unforgettably addictive daily cycle and a deep combat system — perfect for handheld gaming.

psp__tactics-ogre-let-us-cling-together.teaser: Deep, serious tactics; a peak of the genre.
psp__tactics-ogre-let-us-cling-together.detail: A remake of a classic by Yasumi Matsuno (whose team went on to create FF Tactics). Deep, serious tactics with a branching story about ethnic war and morality (decisions change the plot). For connoisseurs, one of the genre's high points.
psp__tactics-ogre-let-us-cling-together.article:
War has no good and evil sides — only people making terrible decisions. Tactics Ogre takes this truth deadly seriously and puts you before choices that will haunt you long after the credits roll.

This remake of a classic comes from the workshop of **Yasumi Matsuno**, a creator whose team later gave rise to Final Fantasy Tactics as well. The story unfolds in the Valerian archipelago torn apart by an **ethnic war** between rival peoples, following the young Denam, pulled into a cycle of violence and political intrigue. The narrative is mature, grim, and uncompromising — dealing with purges, revenge, collaboration, and the price paid for ideals.

Crucial is the **branching story** system. Your major decisions at key moments change the direction of the whole plot, open different paths, and lead to divergent endings. The game isn't afraid to place you before a moral dilemma where no option is clean, and to make you live with the consequences.

On the tactical side, this is one of the **peaks of the genre**. Battles on an isometric grid demand thinking through positioning, terrain, elements, and the coordination of your entire squad. The remake added modern conveniences such as a system that lets you rewind turns and rethink your strategy, softening the difficulty without stripping away any depth.

For connoisseurs and lovers of the genre, Tactics Ogre is all but mandatory. It's a game that bets not on spectacle but on density — on the strength of its story, the weight of its decisions, and the satisfaction of a perfectly planned battle. It ranks among the very best that tactical RPGs have ever offered.

**Why play:** Deep, serious, morally weighty tactics with a branching story about war and choice — one of the absolute peaks of the genre.

psp__jeanne-d-arc.teaser: Fantasy tactics by Level-5; accessible and beautiful.
psp__jeanne-d-arc.detail: Fantasy tactics by Level-5 (Professor Layton, Ni no Kuni) loosely based on Joan of Arc with a supernatural touch. More accessible and colorful than Tactics Ogre, yet still deep. A beautiful gateway into the genre.
psp__jeanne-d-arc.article:
What if Joan of Arc heard voices because an ancient demonic force had entered her? From this bold idea grew Jeanne d'Arc — fantasy tactics that take a historical legend and dress it in the garb of supernatural adventure.

The game comes from studio **Level-5**, a name known for series such as Professor Layton, Dark Cloud, and later Ni no Kuni. It draws loosely on the Hundred Years' War and the fate of the French heroine, but quickly strikes out on its own path — Jeanne obtains an ancient magical armlet that grants her the power of transformation and the strength to face the supernatural threats standing behind the enemy armies.

As a game, it is a **tactical RPG** on isometric grids, though with a noticeably friendlier approach than the genre's harsher titles. Combat is enriched, for example, by a system where positioning units next to each other lets you chain turns and attacks, rewarding clever placement and creating dynamic chains of action. The transformation mechanic gives key characters a serious extra punch at decisive moments.

Visually, Jeanne d'Arc is **colorful, clean, and beautiful** — it looks like animated anime, with lively characters and brisk cutscenes. The tone is more serious where it should be, but the overall feel is more adventurous and optimistic than that of its grim competitors.

It is precisely in this accessibility that its greatest strength lies. Jeanne d'Arc offers enough depth to satisfy seasoned strategists, yet doesn't intimidate newcomers. It's an ideal gateway for anyone who wants a taste of tactical RPGs and doesn't want to start with the hardest one.

**Why play:** Accessible, colorful, and beautiful fantasy tactics by Level-5 — deep enough for connoisseurs, but a perfect introduction to the genre for newcomers.

psp__ys-seven.teaser: Fast action RPG; superb music and pace.
psp__ys-seven.detail: A fast action RPG with superb rock music and brisk combat. Felghana is a remake of Ys III, Seven a modern party system with three characters. For lovers of action with pace.
psp__ys-seven.article:
Speed. If you had to describe Ys Seven in a single word, that would be it. Falcom's action RPG saga charges forward here to the rhythm of a screaming electric guitar and won't let you catch your breath.

Ys Seven moves the series about the legendary red-haired adventurer Adol Christin toward a modern **party system**. For the first time in the main line, you control a trio of characters at once and switch between the individual heroes on the fly to exploit their different weapons and attack types against the right enemies. Combat is purely action-driven — you dodge, slash, unleash powerful skills and furious ultimate attacks in real time.

Each weapon falls into one of three types that are effective against different kinds of enemies, so constantly switching characters isn't cosmetic but a tactical necessity. Added to this is a dodge-and-block system with a reward for perfect timing, which makes the fighting brisk, fluid, and immensely satisfying.

An inseparable part of the experience is the **music**. Falcom is renowned for its soundtracks and Ys is no exception — energetic rock and metal compositions drive the action forward and can turn even an ordinary fight into an adrenaline ride. It's music you'll remember for years afterward.

The Ys series offers several gems on the PSP. Alongside Seven, which introduced the modern party approach, The Oath in Felghana — an excellent remake of an older entry — also shines here. Together they show why Falcom has earned such a firm and respected place among lovers of action RPGs.

**Why play:** A lightning-fast action RPG with brisk three-character combat and a superb rock soundtrack — adrenaline in your pocket.

psp__ys-oath-in-felghana.article:
Sometimes it's enough to take an old gem, polish it to a dazzling shine, and the world finally notices just how brilliant it always was. That's exactly what Ys: The Oath in Felghana is — a complete overhaul of a classic that turned it into one of the best action RPGs on the PSP.

The Oath in Felghana is a **remake of Ys III** by studio **Falcom**, masters of the action RPG genre. It takes the original adventure of the red-haired hero Adol Christin and dresses him in a modern coat — with beautiful 2D graphics, reworked level design, and a combat system that matches the fast, dynamic style of the series' later entries.

The gameplay is the pure essence of Ys: **fast, fluid, and hard**. You run, jump, slash with your sword, and unleash elemental spells at a hectic pace, with hordes of enemies bearing down on you. Boss fights are among the highlights — they're demanding, requiring you to learn patterns and hone precise reflexes, and the sense of victory is all the sweeter for it. The game isn't among the easiest, but its fairness and instantly responsive controls make every battle a joy.

And then there's the **music**. Falcom soundtracks are legendary and Felghana ranks among the best — thrilling rock and metal compositions that send adrenaline coursing through your blood and turn every fight into a concert. Many fans rank it among the finest game music ever.

Thanks to its compact length, polished gameplay, and gripping pace, Felghana is an ideal entry point into the Ys series as well as a showcase of what a well-crafted action RPG on a handheld console should look like. For lovers of brisk action, it's all but mandatory.

**Why play:** A polished remake of Ys III with brisk, hard action and a superb rock soundtrack — one of the best entry points into the Ys series.

psp__gradius-collection.article:
The spaceship Vic Viper returns, and with it a legend that stood at the birth of an entire genre. **Gradius Collection** is a small treasure for PSP owners: a single UMD disc hides several entries of one of the most influential shoot-'em-up series in history. Konami offered here a portable archive of games that once defined what a proper horizontal shmup means.

At the heart of it all is a brilliant power-up system. You collect orange capsules that advance the indicator on a bar at the bottom of the screen, and you decide for yourself when to take speed, double shot, laser, or the indestructible **Options** — satellites that copy your fire and change the defensive situation beyond recognition. This degree of freedom was revolutionary in the eighties and remains one of the most elegant upgrade systems in games to this day.

Gradius is also famous for its merciless difficulty and iconic bosses — recall just the Gradius brain or the Moai statues spewing rings of energy. The game demands memorization, precision, and a cool head, because a single hit strips you of all your upgrades and sends you back to the start of the section. It's old-school design that rewards patience and repetition.

On the PSP it makes sense for several reasons. The compilation lets you play in shorter bursts, save your progress, and go through the series in the comfort of your pocket. For newcomers it's an ideal gateway into the genre, for veterans a nostalgic ride through the games that influenced practically everything that came after them — from R-Type to modern bullet hell titles.

Gradius Collection is a tribute to a craft that is scarcely made anymore these days: pure, hard, and satisfying action where every advance is hard-won and every completed level a small victory. If you love shmups or want to know them from their roots, this collection belongs in your library.

**Why play:** An essential archive of one of the most influential shoot-'em-up series with a brilliant upgrade system, ideal for short bursts on the go.

psp__wipeout-pure-pulse.article:
Antigravity machines whistling through a tunnel at a speed that blurs the image, plus a bassline that thunders right into your bones — **Wipeout** on the PSP was, from the very first moment, clear proof that Sony's handheld could be as stylish as few pieces of hardware. Pure and, after it, Pulse brought frictionless futuristic racing straight into your pocket, with no compromises in atmosphere.

The Wipeout series was born at studio Psygnosis and, from the mid-nineties, was inseparably bound to the visual identity of the collective **The Designers Republic** and to electronic music. The PSP entries continued in this tradition: sharp graphics, neon tracks, clean typography, and a soundtrack full of dance electronica turned every race into a small audiovisual spectacle.

As a game, it's about racing hovercraft at high speeds, where merely holding the throttle isn't enough. You have to master air brakes into corners, manage your shield energy, collect weapons, and decide whether to fire them at opponents or sacrifice them to top up energy. The tracks are full of jumps, loops, and shortcuts, and at higher speed classes they turn into a test of reflexes on the edge of human ability.

Pure was a launch title that showcased the power of the hardware, while Pulse added more tracks, improved presentation, and online features. Both entries benefited from downloadable content, so you could gradually expand the offering of tracks and music — a pleasantly modern approach to supporting a game for its time.

Wipeout on the PSP remains one of the best calling cards of what the handheld could do: speed, style, and music merged into a hypnotic whole that today holds the mark of a cult classic. For fans of futuristic racing, it's a must.

**Why play:** Stylish and brutally fast antigravity racing with iconic visuals and an electronic soundtrack that made the PSP a fashion accessory.

psp__lumines.teaser: A hypnotic music puzzle; the PSP's flagship.
psp__lumines.detail: A hypnotic music puzzle from the creator of Rez: blocks vanish to the rhythm of the music and a sweeping „time line“, and each pack of levels changes the music and the visuals (synesthesia). A launch title and the PSP's flagship; one of the most addictive puzzles ever.
psp__lumines.article:
There are puzzle games, and then there is **Lumines** — a title that elevated falling blocks into a hypnotic dance ritual. When it came out in 2004 as one of the PSP's launch pieces, it immediately became the console's flagship and one of the most addictive logic games ever. Once you start that rhythm, you won't easily switch it off.

Behind the game stands **Tetsuya Mizuguchi** and studio Q Entertainment — the creator of the cult Rez, obsessed with fusing music, image, and gameplay into a single sensory experience, so-called synesthesia. In Lumines you assemble two-colored square blocks into larger squares, but the key is the sweeping **time line** that erases the formed shapes to the rhythm of the music. Movement, sound, and score pulse here as a single organism.

The brilliance lies in the interconnection with the music. Each pack of levels, a so-called skin, brings its own track, visual style, and tempo of the time line. So you progress not only through visually diverse environments but also along a musical path, where the beat speeds up and every successful merge of blocks adds a sound element to the track. You play and simultaneously co-create the music.

This connection makes Lumines something much more than a Tetris clone. It's a zen affair in which you lose track of time, and at the same time a game with surprising depth for those who want to chase high scores and handle the accelerating tempo. On the PSP's small screen with headphones on, it's an ideal combination.

Lumines kicked off a whole series and became a symbol of what the PSP could be as a platform for smart, stylish, and original games. To this day it counts as one of the best puzzles that ever appeared on a handheld console.

**Why play:** A hypnotic music puzzle from the creator of Rez, where image, sound, and gameplay merge into an addictive synesthetic ride.

psp__mercury-archer-maclean-s-mercury.article:
Forget controlling a character — here you control the whole world. **Archer Maclean's Mercury** is an inventive physics puzzle in which you don't tilt a hero but the playing surface itself, letting a silvery drop of mercury flow across it. It's one of those concepts that sound simple until you sink your teeth into them.

The principle stems from the classic fairground game with a ball in a maze, but Mercury goes much further. Your drop can split into smaller parts, merge back together, change color by passing through colored gates, and every obstacle poses different demands. You must deliver a precisely measured amount of mercury to the goal, avoid falling off the edge, and solve puzzles that combine precision, timing, and a little chemical thinking.

Thanks to this mechanic, the game offers a pleasant difficulty progression. At first you just carefully tilt the surface, later you juggle several separated drops at once, mix colors to meet objectives, and battle both the clock and your own impatience. The name **Archer Maclean** in the title refers to an experienced British developer whose roots reach all the way back to the home-computer era.

On the PSP, Mercury fit perfectly into the philosophy of short but clever time-killing games. It suits a few levels on the bus just as well as a longer, focused session where you try to reach the hundred-percent solution of every map. Visually it's a clean, glossy presentation that captures the bet on mercury as the main star perfectly.

It's a title that reminds you how original handheld puzzle games could be — and how well the PSP served precisely this kind of creative idea.

**Why play:** An original physics puzzle where you tilt the entire surface and guide a splitting drop of mercury — a clever little game ideal for both short and longer sessions.

psp__exit.detail: Clever logic games for downtime: in Mercury you tilt the surface and guide a splitting drop of mercury, Exit is an action puzzle about rescuing people from burning buildings under time pressure.
psp__exit.article:
A burning building, a floor full of terrified people, and a clock ticking relentlessly — **Exit** is an action puzzle in which you become a professional rescuer with a cool head and fast feet. The game from studio Taito (released in some regions under the Ignition label) came out in 2005 and offered a refreshing combination of puzzle and calm under pressure.

You step into the role of the elegant Mr. ESC, a master of escape whose task is to get all the people out of the affected buildings before time runs out. Every level is a small spatial dilemma: you have to find routes, push crates, use elevators, climb ladders, and above all organize the rescued — some can carry objects, others are injured and need help, still others fear fire and won't move on their own.

The charm of Exit lies precisely in this two-layered play. On one side you solve the logic puzzle of how to get through the level at all, on the other you battle the time limit and the spreading danger, so an elegant solution isn't enough — it must also be fast enough. The visual style, with bold outlines and comic-like animation, gives the whole thing a fresh, stylized look.

On the PSP, Exit worked perfectly thanks to levels divided into short, self-contained challenges that could be played one at a time. It was an ideal title for downtime, yet clever enough to keep you around far longer than you'd planned. The game earned critical attention as one of the pleasantly original efforts of the console's early era.

**Why play:** A stylish action puzzle about rescuing people from burning buildings under time pressure — a clever brain-teaser where an elegant solution must also be fast.

psp__monster-hunter-freedom-unite.teaser: Hundreds of hours of hunting; a social phenomenon in Japan.
psp__monster-hunter-freedom-unite.detail: Hundreds of hours of hunting giant beasts, crafting equipment from their parts, and cooperation. In Japan a social phenomenon — people gathered in parks to hunt together, which turned the PSP into a social platform. Deep progression for the patient.
psp__monster-hunter-freedom-unite.article:
Because of this game, people in Japan gathered in parks, at train stations, and in cafés, sitting down together with consoles in hand to hunt giant dragons as a group. **Monster Hunter Freedom Unite** from 2009 wasn't just another action RPG — it was a social phenomenon that turned the PSP into a social platform and defined an entire era of portable hunting.

The gameplay loop is brilliantly simple and yet bottomlessly deep. You head into the wilderness to hunt a monster, wear it down bit by bit in a demanding fight, craft better weapons and armor from its parts, and with your upgraded gear set out after an even bigger and more dangerous creature. No character leveling in the classic sense — your strength is literally tailored from the prey you hunt and from your own skills as a player.

Capcom honed a combat system here built on deliberation and timing. Each of the weapons, from the ponderous great sword to the nimble dual blades or the hunting horn, has its own rhythm, reach, and style, so learning each of them is a long-term project in itself. The fights are slower, tactically demanding, and unforgiving — you have to wind up an attack in advance and pay for a mistake.

The heart of the experience, however, is cooperation. In a party of four hunters who complement one another, the fights take on a completely different dimension, and it is precisely the shared victory over a giant monster after a long battle that kept players going for hundreds of hours. Freedom Unite was moreover packed with content — an enormous amount of quests, monsters, and equipment made it a practically endless title.

It's a game for the patient that doesn't forgive and doesn't pander, but rewards determination like few others. And it's a milestone that showed how a handheld console can bring people together.

**Why play:** Bottomlessly deep hunting of giant beasts with crafting and cooperation that became a social phenomenon in Japan — hundreds of hours for the patient.

psp__dissidia-final-fantasy-012.article:
What happens when you put heroes and villains from the entire history of Final Fantasy into a single arena and let them duke it out in flashy action? You get **Dissidia Final Fantasy** — an unconventional fighting game that Square Enix built as a celebration of its flagship series, and to which an expanded entry subtitled 012 (i.e., Duodecim) was later added.

Dissidia isn't one of the classic fighting games with a plane and a fixed distance. Battles take place in free 3D arenas where characters race through space, run along walls, and attack both at range and up close. At its core is a clever two-layered system: first you use so-called Bravery attacks to strip your opponent of courage points, which you appropriate for yourself, and only then do you convert them into an HP attack that actually drains health. Combat is thus a constant juggling between building an advantage and timing the decisive blow.

For fans of the series, though, it's above all a grand tribute. You step into the role of heroes like Cloud, Squall, Tidus, Cecil, or Lightning and face off against the series' iconic villains, all with respect for their origins, abilities, and personalities. An RPG layer with leveling, equipment, and skill customization weaves around the battles, so it's not just about reflexes but also about building your character.

The 012 entry expanded the whole concept with new fighters, improved the systems, and tied the story into a larger whole, making it the definitive version for those who wanted to get the most out of this crossover celebration. On the PSP it was a technically ambitious title that pushed the console's hardware toward flashy battles full of spells and animation.

**Why play:** A flashy crossover fighting game with heroes from the entire Final Fantasy series and a clever courage system — a tribute for fans and a distinctive action game with RPG depth in its own right.

psp__valkyria-chronicles-ii.teaser: Watercolor tactics; a truly unique style.
psp__valkyria-chronicles-ii.detail: A sequel to the beloved PS3 game with its gorgeous watercolor „CANVAS" style and hybrid turn-based/action combat (you pick a unit, then control it in real time). Stylistically one of a kind.
psp__valkyria-chronicles-ii.article:
A battlefield that looks like a trembling watercolor painting, and tactics that take your breath away — **Valkyria Chronicles II** brought one of the most distinctive visual and gameplay styles of its era to the PSP. This sequel to the beloved PlayStation 3 game proved that the series' uniquely enchanting world works just as well in your pocket.

The first thing that grabs you is the instantly recognizable graphical style called **CANVAS**, which renders the entire game as if it were drawn with watercolor paints and brush strokes. Characters, landscapes, and explosions all have soft, hand-painted outlines, and the whole visual presentation lends the war story an unexpectedly poetic, almost fairy-tale feel. It is one of those cases where the art direction stays with you long after you finish playing.

Mechanically, it is an inventive hybrid of turn-based tactics and real-time action. In the turn-based phase you look down from a bird's-eye view and select the unit you want to move, but the moment you take control, the game switches to an over-the-shoulder view and you guide the unit across the battlefield in real time, aiming and shooting yourself while enemies can fire back at you. This blend of planning and direct action gives the battles a unique flow and tension.

Around the battles unfolds a story set in a military academy, complete with a whole cast of characters, their relationships, and their growth. The second installment tailored its scope and structure to portable play, offering well-paced missions, a deep class and unit-upgrade system, and plenty of content for tactics lovers.

Sega created a title here that defies categorization — it is not quite a classic turn-based game nor pure action, but something in between, wrapped in one of the most beautiful visual styles any strategy game has ever had.

**Why play it:** Stylistically unique tactics in the gorgeous CANVAS watercolor style, with a clever hybrid of turns and real-time action.

psp__ratchet-and-clank-size-matters.article:
A Lombax with a serious arsenal and his little robot buddy set off into your pocket — and, surprisingly, lost almost none of their big-screen charm along the way. **Ratchet & Clank: Size Matters** brought the beloved action-platformer-shooter series to the PSP with the ambition of delivering a full-fledged adventure, not just a trimmed-down side trip.

At the heart of the experience is what always made the series famous: the crazy, inventive arsenal. Ratchet collects and upgrades a whole range of wacky weapons and gadgets, from classic blasters to weapons that turn enemies into something else entirely, and switching between this weapon circus mid-action is half of all the fun. Added to that are platforming sections, puzzles with the likeable Clank, and collectibles that tempt you to explore every corner.

The game combines snappy third-person action with platforming and the humor that was always typical of the brand — a colorful sci-fi world full of jokes, oddball characters, and self-irony. The pacing alternates wild shooting with calmer passages, and it is all held together by the friendly chemistry of the main duo.

The move to a handheld console was a technically ambitious undertaking. The game tried to preserve the visual richness and gameplay of the console entries on a smaller screen and with different controls, making it one of the more impressive platformer titles on the PSP. For fans of the series, it was a welcome chance to take Ratchet along anywhere.

Size Matters is proof that a charismatic brand can work even away from its home hardware, as long as the port is handled with care and respect for what makes the original fun.

**Why play it:** A full-fledged pocket portion of action-platforming with a crazy arsenal and the series' signature humor — Ratchet and Clank in your pocket.

psp__burnout-legends.article:
The crunch of metal, flying glass, and a slow-motion shot of a devastating pileup — **Burnout Legends** delivered exactly the adrenaline-fueled, aggressive driving on the PSP that the series made famous on the big consoles. These are not respectful races decided by tenths of a second, but arcade mayhem where speed is everything and crashes are half the fun.

The Burnout series built its identity on a single bold idea: the more recklessly you drive, the better. You barrel down the wrong side of the road, whiz past opponents by a hair, drift through corners, and by doing all that you fill up your boost, which then launches your car to speeds that blur the world. Legends gathers the best of the previous installments and packages it into portable form, so you get proven tracks, cars, and game modes.

Of course, the iconic **Crash mode** is also here, the pure essence of destruction — you drive a car into a busy intersection and try to cause the biggest chain crash possible, and with it the highest damage. It is a perversely satisfying diversion that turned destruction into a discipline of its own and became one of the hallmarks of the entire series.

On the PSP, the game had to bring this feeling of unbridled speed and destruction to a smaller screen, and it managed to keep the brisk pace and that characteristic tension of driving on the edge, where every mistake ends in a spectacular wreck. Short, intense races and crash challenges also fit playing on the go perfectly.

Burnout Legends is an arcade racer without compromises — no simulation worries, just pure speed, risk, and the joy of a proper collision.

**Why play it:** Aggressive arcade racing full of speed and destruction, including the cult Crash mode, the ideal dose of adrenaline for your pocket.

psp__mega-man-powered-up.article:
Imagine the classic Mega Man from the 8-bit era going through complete plastic surgery into a cute, chubby 3D — while not skipping a single gram of that old devilish difficulty. That is exactly Mega Man Powered Up, a pocket remake of the very first installment from 1987, which Capcom sent to the PSP as a treat for fans and newcomers alike.

The core of the game stays true to the original: you run through short, precisely designed levels, jump over traps, and at the end of each stage a robot boss awaits, whose weapon you gain after defeating him and use against the next enemy. This „rock-paper-scissors" mechanic of choosing the boss order remains one of the cleverest design ideas in action platformers to this day, and Powered Up presents it in a clean, readable form. New compared to the original is the addition of two brand-new bosses, so even seasoned veterans get unfamiliar challenges.

But the biggest draw is elsewhere. After defeating them, you can play as a whole row of robot bosses yourself — each has its own movement, jump, and attack, which fundamentally changes how you approach individual levels. Add to that a full-fledged level editor in which you build, save, and share your own tracks. For its time, it was a surprisingly generous offering of content that turned a tiny remake into a surprisingly addictive little box.

Visually, the game bets on the so-called „super deformed" style with big heads and cute proportions, complemented by new voice acting and light-hearted humor. For some it is a delightful refresh, for others heresy against the austere 8-bit aesthetic — fortunately, a classic „old style" mode in a more faithful retro guise is also available. This option shows how considerately Capcom approached the series' legacy.

Mega Man Powered Up is a showcase of what an honest remake should look like: it respects the source but is not afraid to enrich it with meaningful new features. For PSP owners who love precise, demanding action with perfectly tuned controls, it is one of the best platforming reasons to switch the console on at all.

**Why play it:** A pocket-sized love letter to the 8-bit original, enriched with playable bosses and a level editor — precise action that will please veterans and newcomers alike.

psp__mega-man-maverick-hunter-x.article:
When Mega Man X came out in 1993, it redefined what an action platformer meant — faster, more aggressive, and with a hero who learned new abilities on the fly. More than a decade later, Capcom decided to bring this milestone to the PSP and completely rebuild it in 3D. The result is Mega Man Maverick Hunter X, a remake that does not just want to copy, but to modernize.

The gameplay stays at the series' roots: you control a hunter named X, run through eight sprawling levels in any order, and after defeating each of the bosses — the so-called Mavericks — you gain his weapon, which you then use against other enemies. Added to that is the iconic dash, wall-sliding, and the gradual finding of armor upgrades that make X more powerful and open up new paths in the game. This combination of fluid movement and strategic ordering makes the series a benchmark of the genre.

The remake reworked the graphics into polygonal 3D while keeping the classic 2D side-scrolling view, so it still plays like a true platformer, just in a more modern coat. Voice acting, a reworked soundtrack, and polished animations were added, giving the battles some flair. For the PSP, whose widescreen display suited action like this magnificently, it was a welcome spectacle.

The biggest treat for fans is the unlockable animated film Day of Sigma, which expands the story background of the entire series and sheds light on the relationship between X and his adversary. Added to that is a playable mode as the boss Vile — an alternative perspective that adds value for those who finished the base campaign and want more.

Maverick Hunter X is proof that a well-designed game ages gracefully. If you like fast, technical action where timing and learning enemy weaknesses matter, this pocket version offers one of the best ways to experience the legend of the X series. For many, it remains to this day the best entry point into the entire branch with the letter X in its name.

**Why play it:** A stylish 3D remake of one of the best action platformers of the nineties, plus a bonus film and a playable boss — fast, precise fun for your pocket.

psp__half-minute-hero.teaser: An RPG parody where you save the world in 30 seconds; funny and clever.
psp__half-minute-hero.detail: A brilliant JRPG parody where you have 30 seconds to save the world (you reset the clock at a goddess for money, so you level up and shop frantically). Funny, clever, and confidently different — it mocks conventions, yet is a great game in its own right. A hidden gem.
psp__half-minute-hero.article:
Thirty seconds to save the world. It sounds like a joke, but Half-Minute Hero turned it into one of the most original games ever released on the PSP. This crazy shortcut of the classic JRPG takes all the established conventions of the genre — grinding, shopping, long quests — and compresses them into hectic thirty-second stretches in which you have to manage absolutely everything.

The principle is ingeniously simple and yet insane: you have half a minute before the villain casts a spell of doom. So you level up frantically by defeating enemies, buy equipment, and run toward the goal — and when time runs short, you dash to the Goddess of Time, who resets the clock for you in exchange for money. This loop turns you into a manic optimizer who counts every second and every coin. It is a parody of grinding, but at the same time a surprisingly addictive and clever game in its own right.

Half-Minute Hero came out in 2009 from the Japanese studio Marvelous, and from the outset it does not try to be a grand epic — on the contrary, it takes shots at grandiosity. The visuals bet on a cute retro pixel-art aesthetic whose 8-bit feel perfectly underscores the genre satire. The storytelling is written with wit, and the game pokes fun at clichés about chosen heroes, cursed princesses, and how „epically" the usual JRPG wastes your time.

What elevates the game above a single funny idea is its variety. Alongside the main „Hero 30" mode, it offers other play styles with different mechanics, so the basic idea does not wear thin and takes on new forms. The pace is brisk, the individual „rounds" short, which makes the game an ideal title for a handheld console where you can play anytime and anywhere.

Half-Minute Hero is exactly the kind of hidden gem that genre fans discover with enthusiasm and then recommend to others. It is confidently different, funny, and clever — and at the same time fully functional as a game, not just as a joke. If you love JRPGs and can also laugh at their bad habits, this is a must.

**Why play it:** A brilliant JRPG parody where you save the world in thirty seconds — funny, clever, and surprisingly addictive. A hidden gem of the PSP library.

psp__3rd-birthday.article:
After years, Aya Brea returns, the heroine of the cult Parasite Eve series — but this time in a form few fans would have expected. The 3rd Birthday is an action game with RPG and shooter elements that throws the familiar character into a dark, post-apocalyptic New York infested with monsters.

The core of the gameplay is third-person combat that combines cover, precise aiming, and a key ability called Overdive — Aya can „jump" into the bodies of allied soldiers on the battlefield, thereby instantly changing position, avoiding danger, or attacking from a better angle. This body-switching mechanic gives the battles a tactical dimension rarely seen in the genre, and she uses it both offensively and to survive desperate situations.

The game is production-ambitious: it bets on cinematic cutscenes, elaborate presentation, and the oppressive atmosphere of a ruined metropolis. Visually it was among the best the PSP had to offer at the time and showed how far a handheld console could be technically pushed. Story-wise it builds on the legacy of the Parasite Eve series, though it shifts the genre from the original RPG more toward action — a step that was controversial for some fans, but unmissable.

Between repeated playthroughs and gear collecting hides RPG depth — upgrading weapons and abilities rewards repeated play and experimentation with character builds. The game thus offers both an intense action experience and room for those who want to feel out the system in detail and optimize their Aya for the toughest clashes.

The 3rd Birthday is a title that divided opinions — but few would deny it its boldness and visual machinery. For PSP owners looking for a dark, action-tinged ride with unusual combat mechanics and a strong atmosphere, it is a memorable stop.

**Why play it:** A dark action ride with the legendary Aya Brea and the unique mechanic of jumping into other bodies — a production-ambitious experience for action fans.

psp__silent-hill-origins.article:
Fog-shrouded alleys, a grinding siren, and the feeling that there is always something behind you in that darkness. Silent Hill: Origins brings one of the most famous horror brands into your pocket and proves that psychological terror does not need a big screen to get under your skin.

As a prequel to the legendary first installment, the game follows the story of truck driver Travis Grady, who gets stranded in the cursed town of Silent Hill. The gameplay honors traditional survival horror: you explore oppressive environments, solve logic puzzles, conserve ammunition, and fight for survival against disturbing monsters. This series was never about action as such — the fear stems from atmosphere, sound, and the uncertainty of what lurks around the corner.

The series was made famous by two key things, and Origins preserves them: the terrifying switching between the „normal" and the rusty, bloody „Otherworld," and the unforgettable sound design. Music and ambient sounds are a full-fledged part of the horror in Silent Hill — the crackle of the radio signaling the proximity of an enemy is among the most iconic audio moments in the history of horror games.

Bringing such an atmospheric experience to the PSP was not a self-evident task, and Origins shows that darkness, fog, and dread work even on a small display — perhaps all the more so when you play alone with headphones.
