Orion Prime is an adventure game set in a sci-fi world where the stakes lie not in fast fingers but in atmosphere, exploration and problem-solving. The adventure genre is ideal for the homebrew scene — it doesn't need brutal computing power for smooth scrolling, yet it gives creators room to tell a story, build a mood and polish the audiovisual side to a level of detail often missing from original period titles.

And it's precisely the technical execution that tends to take your breath away with modern homebrew games. Today's authors command knowledge and tools that programmers in the eighties could only dream of, and they can squeeze graphics and sound out of the same chips that feel like little miracles. Orion Prime thus represents not nostalgia for the old but rather proof that the platform still has something to offer when passionate people take it up.

With homebrew titles it's always wise not to bet on made-up figures and awards — the community around the CPC is small and devoted, and the value of these games isn't measured in sales but in the love with which they're made. Orion Prime is exactly such a project: born of enthusiasm for a specific machine and genre, meant for people who can appreciate what it takes to program a full-fledged adventure for a computer from 1984.

For anyone who thinks retro is only about old cassettes, Orion Prime is a small revelation. It shows that "retro" can also be the present tense — that you can make new games for old iron, and that on that iron there's still room for exploratory adventure.

**Why play:** For the experience of a modern sci-fi adventure on the classic Amstrad CPC and for the joy that the eight-bit scene is still creating new, technically polished games.

amstrad-cpc__relentless-various.article:
Not every game on the Amstrad CPC became a legend with its own Wikipedia page — and titles exactly like these formed the backbone of everyday gaming. **Relentless** and similar action games represent that vast, often overlooked layer of the eight-bit library from which hours of fun at the cassette recorder were drawn, without ever heading for the hall of fame.

The action genre was the CPC's home discipline. These were games built on quick reactions, readable challenges and the "just one more try" principle — that feeling when the screen sends you to the eternal hunting grounds, but you press the button again right away, because this time you'll surely make it. It was precisely in this category that an immense number of titles arose, some of which shone while others remained modest but honest pieces.

With games of this type it's fair to admit where verified knowledge ends. Rather than attributing a specific studio, year or sales figures to a title I have no reliable data on, I'd rather highlight what matters: the platform's context. The Amstrad CPC offered, compared to the competition, a distinctive colour palette and decent sound, so even simpler action games on it could feel lively and catchy.

This entry is really a window into a broader phenomenon. The eight-bit era didn't stand only on mega-hits like Renegade or imported arcade conversions — it stood on thousands of smaller games that arose in garages, small studios and the bedrooms of home programmers. Many of them are being discovered today by collectors and emulator archaeologists, who find in them surprising gems as well as instructive dead ends.

And that's precisely the charm of exploring this layer of retro history: you never know exactly whether beneath an unknown title you'll find a forgotten jewel or a quirky experiment. Both have their worth for anyone who wants to understand how varied and wild the eight-bit scene really was.

**Why play:** To discover a lesser-known layer of action games on the Amstrad CPC and to understand that retro history rests not only on famous titles but on hundreds of honest unknowns.

amstrad-cpc__bubble-bobble.article:
Two adorable little dragons that spew bubbles to trap their enemies - and then pop them with a cheerful smack. Bubble Bobble is the essence of cooperative arcade fun, and on the eight-bit Amstrad CPC this immortal hit found its way into many a child's bedroom.

The game is easy to grasp and fiendishly addictive. You control the dragon Bub (and with two players his green companion Bob), work through a hundred single-screen levels and blow bubbles. You trap enemies inside them, then burst the bubble and turn the opponent into fruit or treasure to collect. The game's strength lies in the interplay of two players at a single screen and its surprising depth - hidden bonuses, secret doors and the famous true ending, which you can only reach as a pair.

Bubble Bobble comes from the workshop of the Japanese company Taito and arrived in arcades in 1986. It became one of the most successful and most ported arcade titles of the eighties and gave rise to a whole family of games, including the sequel Rainbow Islands. The characterful dragons Bub and Bob became mascots of the brand.

Culturally, Bubble Bobble is a textbook example of a game that pairs a cute look with mechanics that never grow stale. It defined the notion of what a cheerful cooperative arcade game should look like, and to this day it appears in rankings of the best co-op games ever.

The conversion to the Amstrad CPC, popular especially in Britain, France and Spain, had to respect the possibilities of that eight-bit graphics and sound, so compared to the arcade machine it looks and sounds more modest. Even so, it kept what matters - the catchy gameplay and the joy of playing together as a pair, which makes Bubble Bobble a classic across generations.

**Why play:** For immortal, instantly catchy cooperative two-player fun that still delights decades later.

amstrad-cpc__double-dragon.article:
A pub brawl transferred to the monitor of an eight-bit computer – that's how you could describe the feel of the home conversion of the arcade game **Double Dragon** on the Amstrad CPC. A game that unleashed an entire fashion wave of the beat 'em up genre in the arena of arcades tries to cram its brutal poetry of fists and knees into the modest memory of the British machine. And it's precisely this contrast between the grand original and the possibilities of home hardware that makes this version an interesting chapter of retro history.

The essence stays true to the original: the pair of brothers Billy and Jimmy Lee fight their way through gang-ruled streets to rescue the kidnapped girl Marian. The mechanics rest on punches, kicks and above all on grabbing and using weapons left lying on the ground by enemies – a whip, a barrel, a knife or a crate become a welcome ally in the fight against superior numbers. It was precisely the element of weapons and combat against waves of opponents that set Double Dragon apart from older fighting games and foreshadowed the shape of the genre for years to come.

The development context is to be found in late-eighties Japan, where the studio Technos Japan created the arcade original, which became an instant arcade hit in 1987. Conversions for home microcomputers including the Amstrad CPC were then prepared by British teams, for whom porting arcade titles was daily bread. Eight-bit machines could never offer the smoothness and colour of an arcade board, so the result is always a compromise between ambition and the reality of cassette or diskette.

The cultural significance of Double Dragon is meanwhile indisputable. It became synonymous with the genre, inspired countless imitators, and the cooperative play of two players side by side etched itself into the memory of an entire generation. On the gaming field it foreshadowed later legends like Final Fight or Streets of Rage, and its name embedded itself in pop culture so deeply that it survived in the form of sequels, an animated series and an unfortunately received live-action film.

The Amstrad CPC version is today more a testimony to an age when arcades were moving into children's bedrooms and every decent hit had to come out on all the platforms of the time. For those who remember it, it's a nostalgic recollection; for younger curiosity-seekers, a window into times when a big gaming idea hid behind modest graphics.

**Why play:** For a glimpse into the roots of the beat 'em up genre and a feel for how the eight-bit era recast arcade legends into home bedrooms.

amstrad-cpc__golden-axe.article:
An axe flashes, a roar rings out and another horde of enemies is scattered across the screen – **Golden Axe** on the Amstrad CPC attempts to bring one of the arcades' most famous fantasy brawlers into the innards of the British eight-bit. In the original, Sega offered a world reminiscent of Conan the Barbarian, and it's precisely this rough atmosphere, steeped in sword and magic, that drives the conversion forward despite the technical limits of the home computer.

The game builds on the tried-and-true principle of the beat 'em up genre: the player fights through the ranks of the evil Death Adder's henchmen to avenge the fallen and free the captives. You choose one of three heroes – a barbarian, a dwarf or an amazon – and besides fists and weapons you also have magic at your disposal, whose power grows according to the collected vials of magical essence. A specialty are the ridable beasts, which you can saddle up to breathe fire or club with the tail, something that gave the original an unmistakable flair.

The development framework belongs to Japan's Sega, which released Golden Axe into arcades in 1989 on the powerful System 16 board. Home conversions then arose in Europe, and eight-bit machines like the Amstrad CPC faced a tough task: to imitate a game whose magic lay in speed, large characters and two-player battles at once. The result is therefore necessarily more modest, but the effort to preserve the spirit of the original is evident.

Culturally, Golden Axe ranked alongside Double Dragon and Final Fight among the pillars of the genre and became one of Sega's flagship brands. It received a number of sequels and ports to consoles and to this day belongs among the titles fans associate with the golden era of arcades. The cooperative carnage of two friends side by side defined the weekend afternoons of an entire generation.

On the Amstrad, Golden Axe is more a respectful tribute to the great original than an equal replacement for it. For collectors and nostalgics, though, it's a valuable testimony to how ambitious arcade titles travelled into children's bedrooms and how programmers working with a fraction of an arcade board's power managed to cope with them.

**Why play:** For the raw fantasy atmosphere and the chance to experience an arcade legend from the turn of the eighties and nineties on a classic British eight-bit.

amstrad-cpc__out-run.article:
Wind in your hair, a blonde in the passenger seat and an endless road before the bonnet vanishing over the horizon – **Out Run** is a celebration of freedom behind the wheel, and even its conversion to the Amstrad CPC tries to bring this feeling of a holiday drive to the home computer screen. The original was a revelation in its day, and its name still conjures images of a red Ferrari racing down a coastal road under a blue sky.

The game principle is brilliantly simple: you don't compete with other drivers for position but with relentlessly ticking time. At the end of each stretch the road forks and the player chooses which way to go – this branching structure offers several different destinations and encourages repeated playing. Instead of aggression, style, smoothness and the joy of speed rule here, which made Out Run more a feeling for life than just a racing game.

Behind the original stands the legendary Japanese designer Yu Suzuki and the studio Sega, which released the game into arcades in 1986 in a version with a moving cabinet that tilted according to the curves. This technological and musical timelessness – a soundtrack of licensed-style melodies the player chose by switching the radio – made Out Run the benchmark of so-called arcade racing. Home conversions for the eight-bits including the Amstrad CPC were prepared by European teams and faced the tough task of imitating the original's pseudo-3D scaled graphics.

Out Run's cultural footprint is enormous. It defined an entire subgenre, inspired countless followers, and its aesthetic of a coastal drive into the setting sun became so iconic that the music and visual scene still cite it today. The game received many sequels, and the name Out Run still means a synonym for carefree racing.

On the Amstrad CPC, Out Run is necessarily more modest than the dazzling arcade original, but as a historical document it has its worth. It recalls a time when arcades tried to get into living rooms and when even an eight-bit machine could offer at least a flash of the feeling that you had an open road and the whole summer ahead of you.

**Why play:** For the timeless joy of pure driving and the chance to sample one of the most influential racing titles in history on a home eight-bit.

amstrad-cpc__r-type.article:
Few shooters evoke such a mix of respect and frustration as **R-Type**, and its port to the Amstrad CPC belongs to the legendary chapters of eight-bit history. This horizontal space shooter became famous for its uncompromising difficulty and a design that forces players to learn every level by heart, and it's precisely this demanding nature that made it a cult classic.

The heart of the game is its ingenious weapon mechanic. Besides the chargeable main cannon, the so-called Beam, you have at your disposal a module called the Force – a sturdy satellite that can be attached to the front or rear of the ship, or sent forward as an autonomous weapon. This tactical choice between defence and attack elevated R-Type above the competition, and its battles against monumental bosses, inspired by organic horror, became unforgettable moments.

The original was created by the Japanese company Irem, which brought the game into arcades in 1987. The conversion for European home computers including the Amstrad CPC was then handled by Activision, and the CPC version became famous for how well it managed to convey the atmosphere and difficulty of the original, albeit at the price of a slower pace. For many who remember it, the Amstrad R-Type is precisely a symbol of what an eight-bit machine could handle when a capable programming team came together.

The cultural significance of R-Type is fundamental. The game popularised the mechanic of an attachable support weapon, influenced countless later shooters and became the founder of an entire series that continued long into the 3D era. Its aesthetic, combining machine coldness with biomechanical organicity, etched itself permanently into the genre's memory.

Today R-Type on the Amstrad CPC is prized as one of the better ports of an arcade shooter to an eight-bit and as a tribute to the patience of players who weren't afraid to die again and again. For newcomers it's a hard school; for those who remember, a return to a title that defined what a real challenge means.

**Why play:** For the tactical depth of its weapon system and the honest, uncompromising challenge of one of the most influential shooters of all time.

amstrad-cpc__barbarian-ultimate-warrior.article:
Few games of the eighties caused such an uproar as Barbarian: The Ultimate Warrior. Sword duels, the evil wizard Drax and one utterly unforgettable move that separated an opponent's head from his body turned this game into a scandalous legend of home computers.

The gameplay rests on duels between barbarian warriors armed with swords. The player controlled a set of strikes, slashes, kicks and blocks performed through combinations of joystick and button. The combat had surprising depth; it was about correctly judging distance, timing the attack and the defence. The peak was the famous killing blow that lopped off the opponent's head, whereupon a small goblin dragged the headless body out of the arena. It was precisely this scene that wrote itself into gaming history.

Behind the game stood the British studio Palace Software, and the game also became famous for its iconic cover, on which the muscular Michael Van Wijk and the model Maria Whittaker posed. A media wave erupted around the box art due to its raciness, which paradoxically gave the game enormous publicity. On platforms like the Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum and Commodore 64 it became one of the most-discussed titles of its time.

The cultural significance of Barbarian is twofold. On one hand it was one of the first games to openly bet on violence and blood as a selling point, foreshadowing later debates about video game content. On the other, its combat system influenced a number of later titles. The game also received a sequel and became an immortal icon of the eight-bit era.

Today Barbarian remains a fascinating testimony to an age when home computers were coming of age and weren't afraid to provoke. The duels are still fun, especially against a second player, and that fabled decapitating blow has kept its grotesque appeal. It's a piece of history that has to be experienced.

**Why play:** For legendary sword duels with the notoriously infamous decapitating blow and a piece of gaming history that provoked an entire generation.

amstrad-cpc__daley-thompson-s-decathlon.article:
Do you remember that strange feeling when your thumbs and wrists still ached long after you had put the joystick down? Daley Thompson's Decathlon is exactly the game to blame. It was named after the British Olympic legend, a two-time gold medalist in the decathlon, and built one of the most legendary button-mashing orgies of the eight-bit era around his name.

The premise was brutally simple and all the more addictive for it. Across ten athletic disciplines, from the 100 metre sprint through the long jump and the shot put all the way to the javelin, you had to build up speed by frantically waggling the joystick or hammering the keys, and then press the button at just the right moment to launch or throw. The result was a competition that physically drained you just as much as the virtual athlete on screen. It literally made players sweat at the monitor.

The game was developed by the British publisher Ocean Software, one of the most important European publishers of the eighties, famous for its licensed titles. Decathlon originated on the ZX Spectrum and Commodore 64, and the Amstrad CPC version joined the family of ports that brought this athletic merry-go-round to all the key home computers of the day. It was a clear response to Konami's arcade hit Track & Field, which had kick-started the entire genre of button-bashing sports games.

Culturally, Daley Thompson's Decathlon became a symbol of clashes between schoolmates and friends. Kids invented absurd techniques to make the joystick waggle as fast as possible, from rubbing rulers across it to crushing the stick with both hands, and sometimes they literally sacrificed the hardware in the name of a better time. A wrecked joystick was almost a badge of honour for a true player.

It is precisely in this pure, almost primitive physicality that lies the magic which has survived decades. The game needed no complicated story or elaborate graphics; all it needed was rhythm, reflexes and the desire to beat your friend by a hundredth of a second. It is one of those titles that perfectly captures why retro gaming was so primally joyful.

**Why play it:** If you want to experience the pure, almost physically exhausting arcade fun of the eighties and test just how fast your thumbs can waggle, this is a legendary classic.

msx__metal-gear.detail: The very first Metal Gear and the birth of the whole stealth series — it was created on the MSX2, not on a console. Kojima bet on avoiding enemies instead of direct combat (partly because of hardware limits that could not handle a lot of shooting). A historically priceless foundation of one of the biggest franchises.
msx__metal-gear.article:
A soldier meant to hide rather than shoot — in 1987 that sounded almost like heresy, and yet it was this very idea that gave birth to one of the most influential genres in video game history. **Metal Gear** was not born on a console, as many would expect, but on the Japanese MSX2 computer, with a then still unknown designer named Hideo Kojima at its cradle.

The game's key mechanic came partly out of necessity and partly out of genius. The MSX2 hardware could not render the number of enemies and the amount of gunfire that a classic action game would require, so Kojima turned the problem into a virtue: instead of blasting your way through, you have to **avoid** the enemies. You sneak through the Outer Heaven base, dodge the guards' fields of view, search for cards and items and advance more with your brain than with the trigger. That is how stealth was born as a full-fledged gameplay principle.

For its time it was a remarkably thoughtful design. The game forced you to think about movement, about sound, about where the enemy was looking and when it was safe to slip past. Layered on top were inventory management and the gradual unlocking of new areas, which turned a simple „action“ experience into something far more strategic and tense.

The historical value of Metal Gear can hardly be overstated. It became the cornerstone of a franchise from which the **Metal Gear Solid** phenomenon and Kojima's entire career as one of the world's most acclaimed game authors later grew. The fact that many people first met the later installments or the botched NES conversion only underlines how important it is to return to the original on the MSX2.

Playing the first Metal Gear today means seeing a great idea in its embryonic form — still without cinematic scenes and without fame, but with the pure essence of why it pays to be invisible. It is a lesson in game design written by a man who turned a hardware limitation into a revolution.

**Why play it:** To experience the complete birth of the stealth genre from the hands of Hideo Kojima and to understand how one of the most influential ideas in the history of games arose from a hardware limit.

msx__metal-gear-2-solid-snake.detail: Kojima's sequel (MSX2, Japan only), significantly more sophisticated — radar, sneaking based on sound, a deep story. Years ahead of its time; many of its ideas appeared in Metal Gear Solid eight years later. Long unknown in the West.
msx__metal-gear-2-solid-snake.article:
Three years after the first sneaking mission, Hideo Kojima released a sequel that was so far ahead of its time that the world almost overlooked it. **Metal Gear 2: Solid Snake** came out in 1990 exclusively on the Japanese MSX2 and long remained practically unknown in the West — and yet it carried ideas that a major studio would only grow into eight years later.

Compared to the first game, Kojima pushed stealth an enormous step further. A full-fledged **radar** showing the guards' fields of view was added, and sneaking reacted to **sound** — if you run, the enemy hears you; if you move carefully, you slip through. Snake could crawl crouched, move through more intricate environments and handle situations that demanded genuine tactical thinking. These mechanics became the direct ancestors of what would later make **Metal Gear Solid** famous on the PlayStation.

Not only the gameplay but also the story took a great leap. Metal Gear 2 offered a deep narrative with elaborate characters and themes that reached far beyond the usual standard of action games at the turn of the eighties and nineties. Kojima's flair for serious themes, twists and characters showed itself here in full force — on eight-bit, or rather MSX2, hardware it was a small miracle.

The context of its release is fascinating in itself. While the West got only botched offshoots of the franchise, the true sequel remained locked in Japan on a platform that most players outside Asia never owned. It was only with later re-releases within the Metal Gear Solid series that the game reached a wider audience, which finally understood how mature a title Kojima had created back in 1990.

Today Metal Gear 2 is a mandatory stop for anyone who wants to understand the DNA of the entire series. It is the missing link between the timid first experiment and the grand three-dimensional era — and proof that the best ideas are sometimes born years before the world is able to appreciate them.

**Why play it:** To discover the long-hidden missing link of the Metal Gear series, which was ahead of its time and foreshadowed the mechanics and storytelling of the later Metal Gear Solid.

msx__vampire-killer.detail: The MSX version of the original Castlevania, released alongside the NES version but with differences — you collect keys and explore (more adventure elements). An interesting alternative take on the birth of the series.
msx__vampire-killer.article:
A whip against vampires, Dracula's castle and music you keep humming long after switching off the computer — that sounds like Castlevania, and indeed it is. But **Vampire Killer** on the MSX2 from 1986 is its curiously different twin, released alongside the famous NES version yet going its own way.

While the NES Castlevania is a purely linear platformer where you gnaw your way forward through levels, Vampire Killer adds a noticeable dose of **adventure**. The castle is not just a corridor to fight through — you have to collect **keys** in it, explore rooms and search for the way ahead. This structure changes the pace and the player's mindset: here you discover and think about where to actually go more than you simply react to swooping bats and skeletons.

The core of the experience, however, remains unmistakably Castlevania. You control a whip-wielding hunter, face gothic monsters and advance toward a duel with the lord of darkness. Even back then Konami masterfully built the atmosphere of a horrific mansion and underscored it with music that became one of the hallmarks of the entire franchise.

It is precisely the existence of two different versions of the same game that makes Vampire Killer a fascinating study material. It shows how Konami adapted its design to different platforms and how differently the birth of a single series could look depending on the machine on which the player encountered it. For Castlevania fans it is an alternative view of the very roots.

Today Vampire Killer will be appreciated mainly by someone who enjoys exploration and does not mind a slower, more deliberate rhythm than that of its more action-oriented NES sibling. It is a reminder of an era when a series' identity was still being sought and a single brand could have two quite different souls on two computers.

**Why play it:** For an alternative, more exploration-focused take on the birth of Castlevania, which Konami created for the MSX2 alongside the legendary NES version.

msx__aleste-aleste-2.detail: The MSX2 was a paradise for shoot 'em ups. Aleste (Compile, the roots of the later Power Strike / GG Aleste series) and Space Manbow (Konami) are among the technically best shmups on eight-bit computers — fast, colourful, with terrific music.
msx__aleste-aleste-2.article:
A screen flooded with colourful explosions, a speed that won't let you catch your breath, and music driving you onward — anyone who says eight-bit computers couldn't do a proper shooter has never played **Aleste**. On the MSX2, which turned into a veritable shmup paradise, this series belongs to the absolute technical elite.

Aleste comes from the studio **Compile**, masters of the vertical shooter genre, and its roots later grew into acclaimed lines such as Power Strike and GG Aleste. The gameplay rests on the best of what shmups offer: a constant rain of enemies, weapon upgrades, dense formations you have to weave through, and that intoxicating feeling when the screen explodes and you somehow still miraculously live.

What makes Aleste exceptional is its technical execution on the MSX2 hardware. The game wrung impressive colour and fluidity out of the machine, so that it matched even the better arcade and console shooters of its time. On top of that comes a terrific soundtrack — the audio side was often just as important a weapon as the shooting itself in MSX2 shmups, and Compile knew that well.

The context matters too: the MSX2 became home to an unprecedented number of quality shooters, and Aleste, alongside titles like Konami's Space Manbow, shows just how high the bar lay back then. For fans of the genre this platform is literally a treasure trove, one long forgotten outside Japan and now being rediscovered by collectors and players on emulators alike.

Anyone who loves sharp, uncompromising action and wants to see just how far eight-bit shooters could be pushed will not regret a single second with Aleste. It is pure, fast joy — and at the same time proof that a shmup's greatness is not measured by hardware generation, but by the heart of its creators.

**Why play it:** For one of the technically best and fastest shooters of the eight-bit era, which shows why the MSX2 was a true paradise of the shmup genre.

msx__space-manbow.article:
Space action that races forward on an eight-bit computer so nimbly that you forget which machine you are actually playing on — that is **Space Manbow**, one of the pride of the MSX2 shooter library. Here Konami proved it could do not only sneaking and whips against vampires, but also first-class space barrages.

Space Manbow is a side-scrolling shmup in the best traditions of the genre: you cut your way through waves of enemies, face mighty bosses and rely on quick reflexes as well as mastery of your arsenal. What sets the game apart is its emphasis on a brisk pace and technical flair — it belongs among the titles that squeezed the maximum out of the MSX2, whether in fluidity of movement or in visual effects.

The execution by Konami bears the signature of a studio that at the time ruled the art of arcade action. As with their other MSX projects, the audio side played a crucial role — striking, energetic music that drives the player forward and gives every shoot-out a charge. It is exactly this combination of technical maturity and style that places Space Manbow alongside such gems as Compile's Aleste series.

In a broader context, Space Manbow perfectly illustrates why the MSX2 became a mecca of shooters. The Japanese computer market lived a life of its own, and creators like Konami directed titles here that long remained hidden outside Asia. Today, thanks to emulation and enthusiast communities, these gems come alive again and reach an audience that previously had no chance to know them.

For lovers of space shooters, Space Manbow is a small discovery: a game that has not aged in what matters most for shmups — in speed, challenge and pure adrenaline. A few minutes are enough and you understand why Konami built such a reputation on the MSX2.

**Why play it:** For a brisk, technically polished space shooter from Konami that ranks among the very best the MSX2 shmup library has to offer.

msx__nemesis-2-gradius-2.detail: Konami made exclusive Gradius installments on the MSX (Nemesis 2/3) with their own content and characters, technically top-notch. The original Parodius (a comedic Gradius parody) was born here too. A treasure for fans of Konami shooters.
msx__nemesis-2-gradius-2.article:
While the world played Gradius on consoles and in arcades, MSX owners got something exceptional — **their own, exclusive installments** of this legendary space series that nobody else had. Konami's Nemesis 2 and Nemesis 3 (also known under the Gradius name) were not mere ports but full-fledged games with their own content and characters, created specifically for this platform.

The core of the gameplay remains unmistakably Gradius: you control a fighter, collect icons for gradual upgrades and build your arsenal using the famous power-up system that made the series a benchmark of the genre. Konami, however, added its own story and gameplay elements for the MSX, so owners of these computers were not playing a trimmed-down version but standalone chapters of the saga, of which they were rightly proud.

Technically it was the peak of what the platform could do. Konami was among the developers who knew the MSX hardware to the marrow and could wring fast, legible and visually impressive action out of it. For fans of Konami shooters these installments are a real treasure — a piece of history that exists only here.

And there is one more delicacy: it was on the MSX that the original **Parodius** was born, a mad comedic parody of Gradius where, instead of a serious space battle, you face flying penguins and all manner of visual mischief. It shows Konami's playful side and the fact that the platform was a space for the studio to experiment and poke fun at itself.

For anyone who loves classic horizontal shooters, these MSX exclusives represent a small sanctuary. They are not side products of a big brand, but its distinctive branch — and proof that Gradius also has chapters you can only discover among enthusiasts and collectors loyal to this Japanese computer.

**Why play it:** For the exclusive, technically top-notch installments of the Gradius series that exist only on the MSX, and to discover the roots of Konami's mad Parodius.

msx__parodius.article:
Imagine Gradius as drawn by someone after a sleepless night and a gallon of coffee with a sense of humour — that is exactly Parodius. Konami took its prestigious space shooter and turned it inside out: instead of a cold arsenal of war, flying penguins, giant pandas, dancing girls and a duck named... well, just a duck, come hurtling at you. And yet beneath all that lunacy beats the heart of an honest, tough shmup.

The very first Parodius was born on the MSX, before it became the much more famous arcade and console series. This original MSX version is largely a parody of **Gradius** — it adopts its iconic upgrade system, where you collect capsules and choose from a bar at the bottom whether to invest in speed, missiles, double fire or a force field. That rhythm of deciding „now, or do I wait for a better upgrade?“ is fundamental to the entire school of Konami shooters, and Parodius honours it despite its clown costume.

What makes the game so fresh is the contrast. Visually it is a carnival of colours and witty ideas, musically the creators reached for playful reworkings of classic melodies, but in terms of gameplay the title does not spare you. Enemy formations, narrow flythroughs and bosses demand the same dose of memorisation and precision as any serious shooter of the era. That is precisely the charm: the game pretends to be joking, but in reality it expects full commitment from you.

For the European player, the MSX was a home computer tied mainly to Konami's Japanese output, and Parodius is a beautiful example of why this platform earned its cult status. It was a brand that later grew into a whole line of sequels on arcades, the SNES, the PlayStation and handhelds, and the roots of it all lie right here, in this modest but inventive little MSX gem.

Today the original Parodius is more of a collector's and historical delicacy than an easily accessible title, but for fans of retro shooters it remains a fascinating testament that even the most serious genre can bear a hearty dose of self-irony. It is a love letter to Gradius, written with a smile on its lips and a finger firmly on the trigger.

**Why play it:** If you love classic Konami shooters and want to taste them in their most playful, self-ironic form, here is the start of the entire legendary series.

msx__maze-of-galious.detail: A metroidvania-like adventure (part of the Knightmare series) with exploration of an interconnected castle, two characters and puzzles. Influential and cult; it received a modern fan remake.
msx__maze-of-galious.article:
There are games that were so distinctly ahead of their time that the world only caught up decades later — and The Maze of Galious is exactly such a case. Long before anyone uttered the word „metroidvania“, Konami in 1987 built on the MSX computers a sprawling, interconnected castle full of secret passages, keys and puzzles that you have to gnaw through with your own head.

The game is part of the **Knightmare** series and follows it as its second installment, though it jumps into a completely different genre. Instead of straightforward action you get a world that gradually unlocks: you explore ten „worlds“ connected by a central castle, collecting items and abilities that open up previously inaccessible places. You control two **characters** at once — the knight Popolon and his wife Aphrodite — each with different traits (Aphrodite, for instance, swims better), and the game forces you to switch between them according to the situation.

For its time it was a remarkably rich design. You will find hidden rooms revealed with the help of passwords and items, a boss at the end of each world, and unexpected moments when you must enter a secret code obtained elsewhere in the game. This layer of discovery and logical reasoning makes Galious an experience that rewards curiosity and patience — while also being able to be thoroughly uncompromising, as retro titles tend to be.

The development context is key here: the MSX was Konami's home platform in Japan, and the studio experimented on it with ideas for which there was no room in the arcades. Maze of Galious is a perfect showcase of that creative freedom — an ambitious, thoughtful title that would have been hard to find elsewhere at the time. No wonder it earned a cult reputation and is still cited as one of the forerunners of the whole subgenre of exploratory action-adventures.

The community's love for this game is so strong that a modern fan remake was created, making the work accessible to new generations in today's graphics and with more comfortable controls. That in itself says something about how timeless the underlying design was — if something is still worth rebuilding decades later, it must have been exceptional from the start.

**Why play it:** It is one of the grandfathers of the metroidvania — an exploratory adventure full of secrets and puzzles that was ahead of its time and can still absorb you today.

msx__knightmare.article:
Before Konami launched its most ambitious adventure experiment on the MSX, it all started with anything but pondering over puzzles — it started with gunfire. Knightmare is a vertically scrolling shooter set in a fantasy world where, instead of a spaceship, you pilot the brave knight Popolon facing hordes of monsters in the name of rescuing his beloved.

In terms of gameplay it is brisk action in which you climb up the screen, dodge enemy formations and collect upgrades that change and strengthen your weapon. This combination of fantasy scenery and classic shooter mechanics was refreshing for its time — where most shmups bet on sci-fi, Knightmare offered swords, dragons and a medieval atmosphere without losing the drive of arcade action.

The significance of this game, however, exceeds its own boundaries. Knightmare kick-started an entire series of the same name whose later installments aimed at a completely different genre: the second installment, **The Maze of Galious**, turned into an exploratory action-adventure with puzzles, making the brand one of the most interesting in the MSX library. The first Knightmare thus stands at the beginning of this remarkable family line as its action cornerstone.

The MSX was, especially in Japan, a showcase for Konami, and titles like Knightmare show why this platform won such a strong position among collectors and retro enthusiasts. The studio poured ideas, colourful worlds and soundtracks into it that managed to wring more out of a home computer than one would expect, building a reputation that accompanies it to this day.

For today's player, Knightmare is an interesting intersection — a relatively accessible, cleanly playable shooter that also serves as a gateway into a broader universe. If you enjoy discovering the roots of famous series and tasting what fantasy action looked like in the mid-eighties, it is a title worth getting to know.

**Why play it:** A fantasy-set vertical shooter that stands at the beginning of the famous Knightmare series and shows Konami's action face on the MSX.

msx__salamander.article:
When Gradius decided to break out of line a little, Salamander was born — and fans of space shooters still know to this day why they remember it. This Konami classic took the proven foundation and dared to change the rules: it combines both horizontally and vertically scrolling levels and offers the option to play with two players at once, which made it a small revolution within the series.

The MSX version brought this action to the Japanese home computer, and with it the characteristic organic, almost biological-looking environments after which the game was named. Instead of a purely technical space, you gnaw your way through tunnels full of pulsating matter, seas of fire and giant enemies that seem more like living creatures than machines. This aesthetic gave Salamander its own, unmistakable face.

In terms of gameplay it is a proper challenge in the best tradition of Konami shooters. You collect upgrades, strengthen your fire, dodge through narrow passages between enemies and learn the level layouts by heart, because one careless moment means an explosion. It is precisely this blend of instant reaction and gradual memorisation that makes the genre so addictive — and Salamander masters it with grace.

Konami was among the most prominent studios on the MSX, and conversions of its arcade hits were a great draw for owners of these computers, especially in Japan. Salamander is a good example of this: a brand born in the arcades found its way into living rooms too, and every such conversion helped build the MSX's reputation as a platform with an exceptionally strong offering of action titles.

Today Salamander is part of the broader legacy of the Gradius universe, which lives on in compilations and in players' memories of the golden era of shooters. For anyone who wants to understand where the quality bar of this genre came from, getting acquainted with this game is practically a duty.

**Why play it:** A classic Gradius spin-off with organic aesthetics and two-player co-op — one of the defining shooters of the genre's golden era.

msx__king-s-valley-ii.detail: Logic classics. King's Valley II is a puzzle-platformer with a level editor (early moddability), Eggerland is the predecessor of Adventures of Lolo (HAL). Clever logic.
msx__king-s-valley-ii.article:
Sometimes it is not about reflexes, but about whether you can piece together a path out of a maze in your head. King's Valley II asks exactly that of the player — it is a logic platformer where success depends not on the speed of your fingers, but on clever planning of how to reach the goal through piles of obstacles, traps and enemies hidden in ancient corridors.

In 1988 Konami put something into it that was extraordinarily progressive for its time: a **level editor**. Players could thus design their own puzzles and share the experience beyond the pre-made content — an early form of what we today call modding and user creation. This feature extended the game's lifespan by orders of magnitude and made it one of the most interesting logic titles in the entire MSX library.

Each level is essentially a standalone logic task: you must weigh the order of steps, use the environment to your advantage and find the sequence of moves that leads you to the exit without getting stuck or dying. That moment when the solution you have been searching for for minutes finally clicks into place in your head is exactly the kind of satisfaction for which people love puzzle games.

It is worth mentioning that this line of logic classics belongs to the best the MSX offered. Alongside King's Valley II there is, for instance, Eggerland from the studio **HAL**, the predecessor of the famous Adventures of Lolo series — proof that the Japanese computer scene of the late eighties could produce clever, elegant brain-teasers that hold up to this day.

For today's player, King's Valley II is a reminder of a time when even small home computers did not stand in the way of big ideas. The level editor, thoughtful design and pure logic make it a title you will appreciate if you enjoy thinking over movement and are looking for something in retro that will tax the brain instead of the thumbs.

**Why play it:** A clever logic platformer with a pioneering level editor — for anyone who prefers thinking to reflexes.

msx__eggerland-lolo.article:
Before the adorable blue ball of yarn named Lolo became a star on Nintendo's consoles, he lived his first life on Japanese home computers as Eggerland – and it was here that one of the most elegant puzzle concepts of the 1980s was born. HAL created a game where you neither shoot nor jump: here, you think.

The principle is brilliantly simple yet endlessly variable. In every single-screen room you have to collect all the hearts, which unlocks the chest and the exit, but the path leads through enemies that behave according to fixed rules and stones that can be pushed. Your job is to find the exact sequence of steps that will guide you through the task without getting stuck in an unsolvable position – one wrong move and the room is lost.

The magic of Eggerland lies in how it makes so much out of so little. A handful of game elements combine into hundreds of ingenious puzzles, where every enemy works like a cog in a clockwork mechanism. That feeling when, after several failed attempts, you finally see through the solution and the whole room „clicks“ into place is utterly addictive, and it is the reason this brand has survived for decades.

Eggerland is the direct predecessor of the **Adventures of Lolo** series, which HAL later made famous mainly on the NES and Game Boy. This turned a Japanese computer title into a worldwide phenomenon, and Lolo joined the ranks of recognizable puzzle-game icons. With this style of clever, accessible design, HAL built a reputation that followed it into later, far more famous projects.

For retro enthusiasts, Eggerland is a fascinating look into the roots of the entire „sokoban-like“ puzzle subgenre with enemies. It is pure, focused fun that doesn't try to dazzle with graphics but relies on the timeless power of a well-designed puzzle – and in that, it is practically unrivaled.

**Why play:** The roots of the famous Lolo series and one of the most elegant puzzle concepts of its era, where every room is a perfectly tuned brain-teaser.

msx__penguin-adventure.article:
Few games hold as much history within them as Penguin Adventure – this colorful platformer for the MSX is one of the first titles worked on by a young designer whose name would later circle the entire gaming world: Hideo Kojima. Yes, the future creator of Metal Gear got his start, among other things, with the story of a brave penguin.

The game follows the action title Antarctic Adventure and pushes it further – a simple run becomes a fuller-fledged adventure. You guide the penguin Penta across levels in which you run forward, jump, dodge obstacles and enemies, and collect items. Compared to its predecessor, it adds more variety, shops, upgrades, and even hidden elements and surprises that make each playthrough a little richer.

For its time, this was a remarkably brisk and charming game. Pseudo-3D running into the depth of the screen, cheerful graphics, and catchy music made it a pleasantly accessible title that can nonetheless put up a challenge – and what is especially interesting, it hides alternate endings and unexpected moments that reward the player for exploring. These little touches hinted at a creative eye for detail that was only just beginning to develop at Konami at the time.

The context of its creation is crucial here. Konami was one of the leading studios on the MSX, and Penguin Adventure is a beautiful example of how, on this platform, even budding authors got room to work – authors who would later transform the entire industry. For fans of Kojima's work, this game is thus a fascinating first piece in the mosaic of one of the most influential game designers of all time.

Today Penguin Adventure remains a beloved piece of MSX history – a game that is fun in its own right but at the same time carries the mark of something greater. It is a reminder of an era when great talents were only just being born from seemingly innocent stories about penguins.

**Why play:** A charming retro platformer with hidden surprises, plus one of Hideo Kojima's early titles – a piece of gaming history in an adorable package.

msx__usas.article:
Konami never skimped on colors or ideas on the MSX, and Usas is a shining example – an action platformer that takes you on an adventurous quest for treasure in a spirit that not even cinematic seekers of lost arks would shy away from. It is a title that bets on brisk action, exploration, and the visual richness typical of the studio's best output of the time.

Mechanically, you get a platformer with an emphasis on movement, jumping, and combat, interspersed with searching for paths and items across various exotic environments. You progress through levels, face enemies and bosses, and collect what moves you forward – a combination typical of the action platformers of the era, but Usas dresses it in an above-average attractive coat thanks to vibrant graphics and a catchy soundtrack that Konami was renowned for on the MSX.

What stands out in the game is precisely that craftsmanship. Konami knew how to pull colorful, detailed worlds and dynamic music out of the MSX at a time when many other titles on home computers felt modest. Usas thus ranks among the titles that helped define how „luxurious“ an MSX game could look and sound, reinforcing the platform's reputation as a home of quality Japanese action gaming.

For the European player, this type of game was often more of an exotic curiosity – the MSX never spread as widely here as elsewhere, and titles like Usas remained the domain of enthusiasts and collectors. All the more magical, then, is discovering them today, when they can be reached more easily and one can see with their own eyes what treasures were hidden on this platform.

Usas is thus a game for those who want to enjoy honest retro action with a touch of adventure while also tasting the characteristic signature of Konami from its MSX era. It is not a title chasing revolution, but it is a polished piece of craftsmanship that represents its time with honor.

**Why play:** A colorful and brisk action platformer with an adventurous atmosphere that shows just how great MSX games from Konami could look and sound.

msx__sd-snatcher.detail: An RPG version of Kojima's cyberpunk Snatcher (see PC Engine), with turn-based combat that targets body parts. MSX2/Japan only (fan translation). A treasure for fans of Kojima and cyberpunk.
msx__sd-snatcher.article:
If there is a game worth digging out an old MSX2 for, it is SD Snatcher – a cyberpunk gem from the workshop of Hideo Kojima that takes the dark world of his adventure Snatcher and reclothes it in the guise of a full-fledged RPG. The result is a title that fans consider one of the most valuable treasures of the entire platform.

Released in 1990, SD Snatcher reworks Kojima's cyberpunk detective story into a role-playing form with an adorable „super deformed“ visual style that contrasts with the serious, adult story about androids passing themselves off as humans. The most interesting part, however, is the combat: the turn-based system lets you **target specific body parts** of enemies, giving battles a tactical depth you wouldn't expect from a game like this. This mechanic makes combat more than just an exchange of blows – it is a little strategic puzzle.

Story-wise it ties into the world of Snatcher, which later earned its fame on, among others, the PC Engine console, and it bears all the marks of Kojima's storytelling: a strong atmosphere, characterful figures, and a noir cyberpunk mood inspired by the classics of the genre. For anyone who loves Kojima's later work, it is fascinating to watch how, even here on the MSX2, he was honing his sense for cinematic storytelling and an elaborate world.

The catch is availability. SD Snatcher was released only on the MSX2 and only in Japan, so for Western players it was long practically unreachable – until the community took it up and created a fan-made English translation that opened the game to the rest of the world. It is precisely thanks to this fan devotion that we can even get to know this hidden gem today.

In the end, SD Snatcher is exactly the kind of game that makes digging through MSX2 history worthwhile: an ambitious, auteur title from one of the most significant game creators, combining a clever combat system with an unmistakable cyberpunk atmosphere.

**Why play:** Kojima's cyberpunk treasure in an RPG coat with tactical targeting of body parts – a must for fans of Snatcher and dark sci-fi alike.

msx__ys-i-and-ii.detail: The MSX2 version of the action RPGs. Ys with its „bump“ combat and phenomenal music, Xak (Micro Cabin) as another quality action RPG. The MSX2 had a strong RPG library, especially in Japan.
msx__ys-i-and-ii.article:
There are soundtracks that stay in your head for years and heroes who write themselves into the history of the genre – and the Ys series offers both. The MSX2 version of Ys I & II brought to Japanese home computers an action RPG that became one of the pillars of the entire genre and to this day ranks among the platform's most valuable titles.

The heart of Ys is its unmistakable **„bump“ combat system**: there is no attack button, instead you simply ram into enemies at the right angle and off-center. It sounds absurdly simple, but in reality it is a surprisingly fluid and satisfying system that keeps the action brisk and uninterrupted. Together with rapid progression and an immersive adventure, this creates a sense of constant forward motion that set Ys apart from the slower, more static RPGs of its time.

On the MSX2 the game shone on the technical side too – and above all musically. The soundtrack of the Ys series is legendary, full of energetic melodies that perfectly underscore the pace of the action, and it is precisely the music that is one of the main reasons fans still cherish this brand so much. The MSX2 version brought this phenomenal sound to home computers and helped cement the series' reputation as one of the best in the field.

The MSX2 had, especially in Japan, an exceptionally strong RPG library, and Ys held an honored place within it alongside other quality action RPGs such as Xak by the Micro Cabin studio. This wave of home-computer RPGs showed that the action take on the genre had its firm place, and it laid the groundwork for the long and successful future the Ys series still enjoys today on modern platforms.

For the Western player these MSX2 versions were long an exotic curiosity, which makes it all the more fascinating to return to them and see where one of the longest-living action RPG series of all was born. Ys I & II is a gateway into a world that hasn't stopped growing since its inception.

**Why play:** The roots of a legendary action RPG series with its unmistakable „bump“ combat and phenomenal music – one of the gems of the Japanese MSX2 library.

msx__xak.article:
There is a handful of Japanese action RPGs that Western players know mainly by hearsay — and Xak is one of them. At first glance it looks like a Zelda clone, but a few minutes are enough to realize it is a carefully built fantasy world with its own mythology, in which humans, demons, and gods intermingle.

Xak: The Art of Visual Stage is built on a top-down view and real-time combat. The hero Latok moves through the landscape, swings his sword, and gradually grows stronger, but the essential thing is the atmosphere — the colorful town, dialogues with NPCs, the music, and the overall sense of adventure that was top-tier on the MSX2. Unlike purely action titles, story and the gradual unveiling of the world of Xak also play a role here.

The MSX2 was an ideal platform for this type of game: more colors, better scrolling, and better sound than the base MSX. Xak used this to the fullest and could visually measure up to the best that was being created on Japanese home computers at the time. For local players it was a brand that earned sequels and ports to other systems.

It is important to grasp the context. While Nintendo and Sega dominated in the West, the Japanese computer scene around the MSX, PC-88, and similar machines had its own stars and its own genre conventions. Action RPGs like Xak were among the pillars of this culture, and to this day collectors and retro-game fans seek them out as testimony to a parallel gaming history that reached us only in fragments.

If you are drawn to discovering titles outside the mainstream and want to see what a Japanese action RPG looked like at the peak of the MSX2's capabilities, Xak is exactly the kind of game worth getting to know — not least because of an atmosphere that ages surprisingly well.

**Why play:** For an atmospheric Japanese action RPG on the MSX2 that reveals a parallel gaming history most Western players largely missed.

msx__pleasure-hearts.article:
Some games are remembered only by a narrow circle of enthusiasts, and that is precisely where the magic of discovery lies. Pleasure Hearts is a shmup for the MSX, that is, a classic shooter in which what matters above all are reflexes, reading enemy patterns, and that unmistakable feeling when the screen fills with fire and you slip through a gap at the last moment.

The shmup genre was both popular and demanding on the MSX — the hardware had its limits, so authors had to cleverly manage movement, the number of objects on screen, and colors. You can recognize good shooters on this platform by how elegantly they work around these limits while maintaining the brisk pace that defines the genre.

The essence of the experience remains timeless: you advance through waves of enemies, collect weapon upgrades, and head toward bosses who test whether you've learned their attacks. It is pure arcade fun, where every single run counts and where the urge to „get it next time“ drives the player ever onward.

With less-documented titles like this one, it is good to approach the experience with an open mind — without the grand expectations set by a brand's fame, but with respect for what the MSX scene achieved. It is precisely here that games are hidden which never reached large print runs or reviews in foreign magazines, and yet offer an honest genre portion.

If you like old shooters and enjoy digging through the MSX catalog beyond the best-known names, Pleasure Hearts is exactly the kind of discovery that retro gaming is ultimately all about.

**Why play:** For an honest MSX shooter and the joy of discovering titles that stayed out of the main spotlight.

msx__pampas-and-selene.article:
That the retro scene is alive is proven by Pampas & Selene — a modern homebrew metroidvania for the MSX that came about long after this platform's commercial era. It is loving proof that old machines still inspire new authors to honest craftsmanship.

Metroidvania means an interconnected world that opens up gradually depending on what abilities you gain. You return to previously inaccessible places, work out where you can finally reach with a new skill, and the map unravels before you like a puzzle. Pampas & Selene carries this principle over to the MSX with a feel for what the platform can handle and with a design that already knows how the genre works in its modern form.

The advantage of contemporary homebrew is that creators combine period aesthetic sensibility with today's game-design knowledge. The result tends to be a game that looks and sounds like it's from an eighties MSX, but controls and flows more pleasantly than we remember many period titles doing. It is nostalgia without needless frustration.

Such projects also carry cultural significance: they keep the platform alive, give collectors new physical cartridges, and give the community a reason to gather. The MSX still has devoted fans in Japan, Europe, and elsewhere, and it is precisely homebrew titles that form a bridge between memories and an active present.

If you're curious what a modern loving letter to an old platform sounds like and want a metroidvania in an authentic MSX coat, Pampas & Selene is a great example of the fact that retro is not just the past but also living creation.

**Why play:** For a modern metroidvania in authentic MSX garb that combines period aesthetics with today's feel for design.

msx__uridium-various-homebrew.article:
Under the banner of Uridium / various homebrew hides an interesting chapter in the life of the MSX: games that arrived on the platform from other machines or came about within today's home scene. It is a reminder that gaming classics often live many lives across hardware.

Uridium is a legendary action shooter originating on eight-bit home computers, famous for its brisk side-scrolling over the surface of giant spaceships and combat with enemies capped off by an adrenaline-fueled landing. Its DNA — speed, precision, and readable action design — is exactly what makes the genre timeless fun, no matter which machine you play it on.

The „various homebrew“ category then shows the second dimension of the MSX: an active community that keeps creating, porting, and experimenting for the platform. These projects tend to be the work of enthusiasts who want to test the limits of the hardware while enriching the library with titles that weren't here before. It is a scene built on sharing and the joy of creation.

This is precisely where the magic of retro computers lies. They are not frozen museum exhibits — they are living platforms on which something is still happening. For players this means that the MSX catalog is not closed but still growing, and that alongside period classics you can also stumble upon fresh action gems.

If you enjoy fast arcade action and at the same time root for the idea that old machines have something to offer even today, this blend of ports and homebrew is an ideal entry point into the living MSX culture.

**Why play:** For fast arcade action and a look into the living MSX scene, where classics meet modern homebrew creation.

msx__nobunaga-s-ambition.article:
Before strategy games became a global phenomenon, Koei was building in Japan a genre that combined history with deep tactics. Nobunaga's Ambition is its flagship — a historical strategy set in the Sengoku period, when Japan was torn apart by the wars of feuding feudal lords.

The game casts you in the role of a daimyo who must unify the country under his rule. You manage provinces, tend to harvests and the economy, recruit and train armies, forge alliances, and lead campaigns against your neighbors. It is a combination of economy, diplomacy, and military strategy — a genre that Koei helped define and that earned the label of historical 4X strategy.

On the MSX this was an ambitious affair: managing a sprawling map and many variables on an eight-bit machine required patience and strategic thinking, but the reward was the feeling that you were truly writing history. The turn-based pace gave room to ponder every decision, which made playing more of a long-term campaign than quick entertainment.

The cultural significance of Nobunaga's Ambition is enormous. With this series Koei built an entire tradition of historical strategies that continues to this day and has inspired dozens of other games. Together with Romance of the Three Kingdoms, these were titles that showed video games can also be educational and that history can be excellent game material.

If you're drawn to deep turn-based strategy with a historical flavor and don't mind a slower, deliberate pace, Nobunaga's Ambition is one of the cornerstones of the entire genre.

**Why play:** For a deep historical 4X strategy from Koei that helped shape the genre and lets you rewrite the history of feudal Japan.

msx__romance-of-three-kingdoms.article:
Three kingdoms, countless generals, and the fate of all China in your hands — Romance of the Three Kingdoms by Koei brings the famous historical saga into the form of a deep turn-based strategy. It is one of the pillars of the genre that the studio helped to shape.

The source is the classic Chinese epic about the fall of the Han dynasty and the struggle of powerful factions for supremacy. In the game you take on the role of a warlord, manage provinces, look after the economy and population, recruit and promote generals, and lead campaigns as well as diplomatic negotiations. The key role is played precisely by the characters — every general has his abilities, and acquiring and using them is at the heart of the whole experience.

On the MSX this was a demanding but rewarding discipline. The turn-based pace gave room to plan carefully, weigh risks, and watch how your decisions play out across the map of a divided China. It is a strategy in which patience and prudence win, not quick fingers — and therein lies its enduring appeal.

Koei built this brand into a long-lived series that is still released today and, alongside Nobunaga's Ambition, defined the shape of historical 4X strategies. The significance of these games goes beyond play: for many players they were also a gateway to an interest in Chinese history and literature, which is a rare merit for a video game.

If you like well-thought-out turn-based strategies with a rich historical backdrop and want to get to know the roots of the whole genre, Romance of the Three Kingdoms is a mandatory stop.

**Why play:** For a deep historical strategy based on the famous Chinese epic that, together with Nobunaga's, laid the foundations of Koei's 4X genre.

msx__aleste-daisenpuu.article:
When you say top-tier shmup on the MSX, sooner or later the name Aleste comes up. This series from the Compile studio is among the best that the vertical-shooter genre offered on the eight-bit and sixteen-bit scenes, and to this day it is a benchmark of quality.

Aleste (known in some markets also under the name Daisenpuu within the broader family of Compile shooters) is built on brisk action, an elaborate weapon-upgrade system, and level design that pushes the player forward without overwhelming them. Compile had an extraordinary feel for shooters — their games flowed smoothly, rewarded mastery of the mechanics, and had just the right difficulty curve that made you try again and again.

On the MSX2 the series managed to take advantage of the platform's better graphical capabilities and offer visuals and a pace that had nothing to be ashamed of next to console competition. The work with colors, scrolling, and music was top-tier and made Aleste one of the titles for which fans remember the platform with love.

Compile became so famous for its shmups that its legacy lives on — over the years the Aleste series received a number of sequels and modern compilations that bring it back to new generations. This is testament to how strong a mark the studio left on the genre.

If you want to understand why shooter fans have such a bond with the Compile brand and are looking for fast, polished action on the MSX, Aleste is the best possible choice.

**Why play:** For a polished vertical shooter from the masters at Compile that ranks among the absolute best shmups on the MSX.

msx__pac-man.article:
A yellow circle with an insatiable appetite, four ghosts and a maze full of dots – **Pac-Man** is quite possibly the most iconic video game in history, and its presence on the MSX platform shows just how deeply this craze burrowed into the home computers of the 1980s. The moment that unmistakable pellet-munching sound rings out, it's clear you're sitting down to one of the games that defined the very concept of a video game.

The mechanics remain a model of elegance to this day. The player navigates Pac-Man through a maze, eating dots and dodging four ghosts, each with its own distinct movement personality. The key element is the large energizers in the corners – eat one and the roles reverse, letting you hunt the ghosts for a short while yourself. This simple loop of tension and reward proved so addictive that it laid the foundations for the design of countless later games.

The original was created by the Japanese company Namco and designer Toru Iwatani, who released the game in 1980 with the goal of appealing to a female audience too, in arcades still dominated by shooters. Pac-Man came to the MSX – the standard of Japanese home computers from the first half of the 1980s – as a natural choice: the MSX was close to the arcade world and maze games suited it well. The home version offered the comfort of playing on your own screen without having to keep feeding coins into a cabinet.

Pac-Man's cultural impact is almost unprecedented. He became the first video game character to break into the mainstream, adorning T-shirts, cartoon series and even a hit song, and to this day serves as a universal symbol of the entire medium. He laid the groundwork for a whole line of sequels, and his silhouette ranks among the most recognizable icons in all of pop culture.

On the MSX, Pac-Man is exactly what it should be – an accessible, instantly graspable classic that anyone can pick up and that, even after decades, rarely gets boring. Whether you're an old-timer or a curious newcomer, it makes for the ideal gateway into video game history.

**Why play:** To encounter the very bedrock of the whole medium – a game whose simple perfection holds up even after more than four decades.

msx__konami-s-soccer.article:
There are games that defined an entire genre on a specific platform, and Konami's Soccer is exactly such a title for the Japanese computer standard MSX. In an era when virtual football was still finding its feet, this piece from the masters at Konami brought a surprisingly nimble and tangible football experience straight into the living room.

The player viewed the pitch from a side-on, slightly top-down angle and controlled a single player on their team, while the computer directed the rest of the teammates. Passes, the timing of shots and the sharp reflexes needed to outwit your opponent were all crucial. For its time it offered fluid movement and tangible responsiveness, making it one of the more enjoyable football games of the 8-bit era. The title's strength lay in the duel between two players, where a calm match quickly turned into a heated battle for prestige.

Behind the game stood the Japanese studio Konami, which in the 1980s belonged to the absolute elite and released a whole range of cult titles on the MSX, from Metal Gear to the Gradius series. Konami's Soccer fit into their strategy of offering quality, easily accessible games for a wide audience on the MSX, and football was a logical choice for mass entertainment.

The MSX was a fascinating platform, a standard championed by ASCII and Microsoft that caught on most in Japan but also had its loyal players in Europe and South America. It was here that a whole generation of games was born, many of which are now sought-after collector's treasures, and Konami's sports titles hold a firm place among them.

Today, Konami's Soccer feels like a milestone that shows how the tradition of Japanese football games was born, a tradition that would culminate in the great series that came later. It's a glimpse into a time when virtual football was still learning to walk, yet already had a clear appetite for the competitive spirit between two players at a single keyboard.

**Why play:** It's a nimble and surprisingly fun slice of football history on the MSX, ideal for a duel between two players who want to remember how virtual pitches were born.

msx__aleste-2.article:
When you think of the technical peak of 8-bit shooters, most people picture consoles or arcades. But Aleste 2 proves that even the MSX2 computer could conjure up a vertical shmup that had nothing to be ashamed of and that ranks among the very best this platform offered in the field of action.

As with any proper top-down shooter, here too you fly through a wave of enemies, dodge dense hellfire and collect weapon upgrades that turn your ship into a mincer spewing out death. Aleste 2 stands out for its pace, gorgeous graphics that exploit the MSX2's capabilities, and an elaborate armament system that forces players to choose which type of firepower best suits the situation at hand. It's a title that rewards precision, memory for enemy layouts and a cool head in the middle of chaos.

The Aleste series is the work of the Japanese studio Compile, one of the most respected shooter developers of the 1980s and 1990s. Compile built a reputation as masters of the shmup genre, and their Aleste brand appeared on a whole range of platforms in various forms. Compile would later be behind the Puyo Puyo phenomenon too, so this was a studio with an extraordinary feel for gameplay.

The MSX2 was an enhanced version of the MSX standard with significantly better graphical capabilities, and it was titles like Aleste 2 that showed what this platform could do when capable programmers took it on. In the Japanese scene, the Aleste series was among the flagships that demonstrated that a home computer could rival dedicated gaming systems.

Today, Aleste 2 is a sought-after title among shmup fans and MSX collectors alike, and a reminder of a time when the Japanese gaming scene churned out one vertical shooter after another. For lovers of the genre it's a mandatory stop and proof that big action doesn't need big hardware, but above all big talent on the developers' side.

**Why play:** It's one of the technically finest shooters on the MSX2 from the legendary studio Compile, ideal for anyone who loves fast vertical action and dodging bullets.

colecovision__donkey-kong.detail: The bundled Donkey Kong was the killer app that sold the console — its faithfulness to the arcade original was staggering for 1982 and far beyond the capabilities of the Atari 2600. A symbol of why the ColecoVision succeeded (albeit briefly).
colecovision__donkey-kong.article:
Consoles don't sell themselves — games sell them. And for the ColecoVision, the decisive draw was the bundled Donkey Kong, the killer app that gave people a reason to reach for this console in particular.

Donkey Kong is an arcade classic from 1982 in which, as Mario (then still called Jumpman), you climb up a girder structure, dodge tumbling barrels and try to rescue a kidnapped girl from the clutches of a giant gorilla. A simple idea with brilliant execution — the interplay of jumping, timing and rising difficulty makes Donkey Kong one of the cornerstones of the entire platformer genre.

On the ColecoVision, it was staggering for 1982 just how faithful the port was to the arcade original. The fidelity of both graphics and gameplay far exceeded the capabilities of the then-dominant Atari 2600, and this very difference was the key selling point for Coleco. Players saw that on this console they could have the arcade at home in a quality they couldn't get anywhere else.

Donkey Kong is also a symbol of why the ColecoVision succeeded — albeit only briefly, before the great video game crash of the mid-1980s swept the market away. For Nintendo it was the game that kicked off the era of characters like Mario, and thereby indirectly one of the most influential careers in the history of the medium.

If you want to understand why the fight over home ports of arcade games was so crucial in the 1980s, and play a timeless platforming classic while you're at it, the ColecoVision version is the ideal entry point.

**Why play:** For a timeless arcade classic and a killer app that, through its faithfulness to the original, sold the entire ColecoVision.

colecovision__donkey-kong-junior.article:
A sequel in which the roles are reversed — that's Donkey Kong Junior. This time you don't play as the hero catching the gorilla, but as the gorilla's son, who sets out to rescue his imprisoned father from Mario's hands. It's one of the few cases where the previous hero becomes the villain.

Gameplay is built on climbing vines and chains, leaping between them and evading enemies who try to stop Junior from making his way up. Compared to the original Donkey Kong, there's a greater emphasis on vertical movement and grabbing onto creeping plants, which brings its own rhythm and a different pace than jumping over barrels in the first installment.

The ColecoVision built its reputation precisely on faithful ports of arcade classics, and Donkey Kong Junior fits neatly into this lineage. The console had the power to bring the arcade experience home more convincingly than the competition, and for players that meant being able to have their favorite cabinets in the living room.

From a historical perspective, Donkey Kong Junior is also interesting for how Nintendo experimented with its early characters before they became icons. The Donkey Kong series helped build brands back then that remain among the most valuable in the gaming industry to this day.

If you like classic platformers and want to get to know an unconventional take on the famous hero-and-gorilla duo, Donkey Kong Junior on the ColecoVision offers an honest arcade portion with its own distinctive mechanics.

**Why play:** For an unconventional sequel to a famous arcade game with an emphasis on climbing, in the faithful form the ColecoVision knew how to deliver.

colecovision__lady-bug.detail: Maze and arcade classics in which the ColecoVision excelled thanks to faithful ports. Lady Bug is an enhanced Pac-Man style, Mr. Do! a digging arcade game, Pepper II a chase with area-filling.
colecovision__lady-bug.article:
The ColecoVision won players' hearts as a machine for faithful arcade ports, and Lady Bug is one of the titles that reputation rests on. It's a maze chase in the spirit of Pac-Man, but with its own idea that sets it apart from the crowd of imitations.

You know the basic principle: you move through a maze, collect points and avoid enemies. But Lady Bug adds rotating gates through which you can redirect both yourself and your pursuers, creating an extra layer of tactics — it's not just about escaping, but also about cleverly rearranging the paths to cut enemies off. This small innovation gives the game a fresh charge.

For 1982–1983, this was exactly the kind of arcade classic the ColecoVision excelled at. The console handled faithful ports of maze and arcade games better than the competition, and Lady Bug, together with titles like Mr. Do! or Pepper II, formed a category that gave the platform its reputation as a home for quality cabinet conversions.

The magic of this generation of games lies in their simplicity and instant comprehensibility. You learn the controls within seconds, but mastering a higher score takes practice, sharp reflexes and an understanding of enemy behavior. It's a pure arcade experience that never ages, because it rests on the timeless contest between the player and their own high score.

If you like maze classics and want to see how the Pac-Man genre could be pushed a step further, Lady Bug on the ColecoVision is an excellent and still enjoyable choice.

**Why play:** For a clever maze chase with rotating gates that shows why the ColecoVision was the king of faithful arcade ports.

colecovision__mr-do.article:
