Because Bombic is a community homebrew work, I do not have verified information about its author, year of release or any achievements, and so I do not state them. What is certain, however, is that it is a title built on a tried-and-true and always functional principle, available thanks to the open nature of TIC-80. If you are looking for a game you will laugh at with friends, here it is.

**Why play:** A bomberman-like party arcade on TIC-80, built on the immortal mechanic of placing bombs — ideal fuel for chaotic evenings with friends around one screen.

tic-80__escape.article:
A jump, a fall, precise timing and the satisfying feeling when you finally conquer that damned passage. The platformer is perhaps the oldest language in which video games speak to us, and ESCAPE is its dialect on the TIC-80 fantasy console. The escape written into the very name is a challenge here for your fingers and your patience alike.

TIC-80 is an open-source fantasy console in the spirit of PICO-8 — a virtual machine that deliberately ties creators' hands with low resolution, a limited palette and compact code. For a platformer it is a blessing. The genre was never built on graphical opulence, but on the precision of controls, the legibility of the environment and that intangible feeling that in English is called game feel. And it is born precisely within the tight boundaries where every pixel must serve the gameplay.

With platformers of this type one rule usually holds: a simple premise, increasing difficulty. You are driven forward by the desire to get further, to conquer the passage on which you just came to grief. You jump over chasms, avoid traps and look for a way through the level that tests your reflexes as well as your ability to read the layout. Every successfully managed stretch brings that small but genuine joy of an overcome obstacle — the fuel that has been driving platformer players for decades.

Culturally, platformers are a pillar of the entire medium. From arcade machines through eight-bit home computers all the way to the independent scene — this genre never died out, it merely transformed. Community games on TIC-80 are its current chapter, written by enthusiasts who love the pure mechanic of jumping and running. The open nature of the platform meanwhile ensures that these games reach everyone who has the desire.

Because ESCAPE is a homebrew title, I do not have verified data about the author, year of creation or awards, and so I will not make them up. I will rely on the essence: it is a platformer within the elegant limitations of TIC-80, accessible and instantly playable. If you enjoy challenges that are about precision and perseverance, this escape is worth a try.

**Why play:** A pure platformer on TIC-80, where it is about precise jumps and perseverance — for anyone who loves that old-fashioned joy of an overcome obstacle.

tic-80__sumico.article:
What if mathematics became a game that truly makes your brain burn? Sumico is a logic game for the TIC-80 fantasy console and builds on an idea that connects numbers, addition and finding a way through a maze of values. It is the type of puzzle that looks innocent but can keep you at it for long minutes.

TIC-80 is an open-source fantasy console, a sibling of the popular PICO-8. It offers creators an environment with intentional limitations — low resolution, a modest palette and compact code. For a logic game it is ideal ground. The puzzle genre never needed graphical splendor, just a clear idea and clean execution. And the small screen forces the creator into the most comprehensible possible presentation of the rules.

With numerical logic games, which Sumico by all appearances is, it is usually about assembling the required result from the available values and operations — connecting numbers on the playing field so that their sum matches the given goal. You set the pace yourself, you need no reflexes, just the ability to think steps ahead and look for the most elegant path to a solution. It is precisely that moment when the last piece clicks into place in your head and the puzzle unravels that makes this type of game such pleasantly addictive fun.

Culturally, logic games based on numbers are proof that fun and exercising the brain need not be opposites. From paper sudoku to digital puzzles — this branch of the genre has its faithful audience who seek out challenges built on pure reasoning. The community around TIC-80 gives such titles an open and accessible home, where the idea counts more than the budget.

Because this is a community homebrew work, I do not have verified data about the author, release date or awards available, and so I do not make it up. What is certain, however: Sumico is an accessible, instantly playable logic game within the frugal boundaries of TIC-80. If you enjoy racking your brains over numbers and looking for elegant solutions, this little challenge will grab you.

**Why play:** A numerical logic game on TIC-80 that turns mathematics into an addictive puzzle — for lovers of quiet challenges where cool reasoning wins.

tic-80__robomania.article:
Robots, action and a brisk pace — Robomania is an action game for the TIC-80 fantasy console, that open virtual machine where strict technical limitations give birth to surprisingly lively fun. The theme alone promises movement, reflexes and the adrenaline spark we expect from a good arcade game.

TIC-80 is an open-source counterpart to the more popular PICO-8 and shares the same philosophy: deliberately tie the creator's hands with low resolution, a limited palette and compact code, so that pure creativity rises to the surface. For an action game this is an ideal environment. The genre never rested on graphical splendor, but on the instant readability of what happens on screen, snappy controls and a pace that keeps the player in constant tension.

With action titles of this kind it usually holds true that reaction and movement play the leading role. You react to what happens on screen, dodge threats, strike at the right moment and try to stay alive amid the growing chaos. The magic lies in immediacy — you grasp it within seconds, but mastering it takes practice and a cool head. It is precisely that directness that makes arcade action a timeless form of fun we love to return to.

Culturally, action arcades are the backbone of all gaming history. From arcade halls through eight-bit computers to today's independent scene — this genre never aged, it only changed its costumes. The community around TIC-80 keeps it alive in its purest form, and the open nature of the platform ensures the game reaches anyone eager to have a blast.

Because Robomania is a community homebrew title, I have no verified data about its author, year of creation or any awards, so I won't state any — I'd rather stick to what is certain. And what is certain is that this is an accessible, instantly playable action game within the elegant confines of TIC-80. If you're looking for a quick dose of arcade excitement with a robot theme, it's worth trying.

**Why play:** Snappy arcade action on TIC-80 with a robot theme — an instantly playable dose of reflexes and adrenaline in the spirit of timeless arcade classics.

tic-80__bunny-maze.article:
A rabbit, a maze and a path that needs to be figured out — Bunny Maze is a puzzle game for the TIC-80 fantasy console that bets on one of the oldest and friendliest forms of puzzle there is. Finding the right route through a labyrinth is a challenge as old as gaming itself, and yet it still works.

TIC-80 is an open-source fantasy console in the spirit of PICO-8 — a virtual machine that deliberately limits creators' options with low resolution, a modest palette and compact code. For a maze puzzle game this is an ideal environment. The puzzle genre never needed splendor, just a clear idea and clean execution, and the tiny screen steers the creator toward the most intelligible presentation of rules and map layout.

With maze puzzle games the principle tends to be immediately understandable: you have a starting point, a goal and a tangle of paths between them. The task is to find the right route, often with regard to obstacles, item collection or the order in which you must pass through individual points. You set the pace yourself, no stress from a timer — just you, your spatial imagination and the satisfaction of the moment when the knotted path finally unravels. With a cute rabbit in the lead role, it's also a game that suits younger players.

Culturally, mazes belong to the very foundations of human playfulness, from ancient myths through paper puzzles to digital brain-teasers. The community around TIC-80 carries this timeless form into a modern, accessible coat and proves that good puzzle fun needs nothing more than clever design. The openness of the platform meanwhile means the game truly reaches everyone.

Because Bunny Maze is a homebrew title, I have no verified information about its author, release date or awards, so I won't make any up. I'll rely on what is certain: this is a friendly, instantly playable puzzle game within the economical confines of TIC-80. If you enjoy calm brain-teasers where you search for a path instead of fights, this rabbit will gladly guide you.

**Why play:** A friendly maze puzzle game on TIC-80 with a cute rabbit — calm, stress-free fun for lovers of finding the right path and for younger players too.

tic-80__knight-s-quest.article:
A knight, a tight pixel dungeon and a sword that is all that stands between you and doom. Knight's Quest is an action-adventure for TIC-80, a fantasy console in the form of a single piece of code, and from the very first screen it bets on the pure essence of the genre: explore, fight, survive. No sprawling tutorials, no cutscenes. Just you, the blade and a labyrinth that scattered its enemies knowing it wants to get you.

Mechanically the game stands on the interplay of action and discovery. You advance through connected rooms, hack down opponents in real time and search for the way onward — keys, switches, hidden passages. This loop is as old as dungeons themselves, but that is precisely its strength: it is immediately readable and immediately playable. The player knows what to do before they've had time to read the controls, and with a good action-adventure that's half the battle.

TIC-80 as a platform lends itself to this approach. It is a deliberately limited environment — a fixed palette, small resolution, compact code — where the creator cannot hide a weak idea behind effects. Every pixel and every enemy formation must have a purpose. Knight's Quest thus belongs to the tradition of fantasy consoles (PICO-8, TIC-80), where developers return to the roots of the 8-bit era not out of nostalgia, but because limitations force honest design.

Culturally it's a nice illustration of what today's fantasy-console scene lives on. Instead of chasing realism, it bets on the density of the experience: a short, focused adventure you understand in a second and that still manages to occupy you. It's the gaming equivalent of a short story — nothing extra, everything in its place.

The atmosphere of a knightly quest is universal precisely because it is archetypal. A castle, a dungeon, a monster, a hero with a sword — these images work across generations, and Knight's Quest serves them in the most digestible form. Anyone who likes old-school action-adventures and just wants to play something straightforward for a while will find exactly that here.

**Why play:** If you like straightforward fantasy adventure with a sword and dungeons, Knight's Quest offers the pure essence of the genre in the economical coat of TIC-80.

tic-80__tic-tank.article:
A tank in the middle of the battlefield, its barrel aimed at approaching enemies and the only question that counts: who fires first. Tic Tank is an action shooter for TIC-80, built on one of the oldest and most addictive gaming ideas of all — drive the machine, aim, fire and don't get destroyed. It's a genre that has worked since the arcade machines of the seventies, and Tic Tank proves its charm hasn't faded.

At its core is combat in a confined space. You control a tank, rotate, maneuver and eliminate opponents before they manage to do the same to you. Tank action has its specific tactics: it matters what angle, what position, when to pull back and when to push. The machine's slower movement makes it a game of anticipation, not blind reflexes — and that's exactly what sets it apart from ordinary fast shooters.

TIC-80, on which the game runs, is an open-source fantasy console with deliberately modest specs. Low resolution and a limited palette force the creator to place readability and playability above effects. The tank, the projectile and the explosion must be recognizable at first glance here, and this visual clarity is actually a tribute to the classic arcades from which the genre sprang.

Culturally, Tic Tank claims a place in the long line of tank games whose roots reach back to titles like Combat on the Atari or arcade battles. On the modern homebrew scene of fantasy consoles such a return is natural: the genre is simple enough to fit into a tight environment, and fun enough not to age. It's the kind of game you understand immediately and with which you spend more time than you expected.

For the player it's a clear offer — short, intense action with no unnecessary fuss. You get in, you fire and you're in. No learning, no warm-ups. Just the pure pleasure of a well-aimed shot and the satisfaction when the last enemy vanishes in a cloud of pixels.

**Why play:** Tic Tank is a fast tank arcade game that honors the roots of the genre — ideal when you want simple, instantly readable action for a few minutes or longer.

tic-80__ascii-game.article:
A screen full of letters, digits and symbols, where every character hides an enemy, a treasure or death. ASCII Game is a roguelike for TIC-80 that proudly claims the purest form of the genre — the one in which text characters make up the graphics and the player's imagination does the rest. It's a return to roots that reach all the way back to the legendary Rogue from the turn of the seventies and eighties.

The roguelike stands on several firm pillars, and ASCII Game serves them without compromise: procedurally generated levels, so no two expeditions are the same, and permanent death, which lends weight to every decision. When you fall, it's over — no loading right before the mistake. This cruelty is precisely what makes the genre one great school of caution and planning, where even a step into a side corridor can be fatal.

The choice of ASCII aesthetics is not a whim but a creed. Text graphics are an abstract language the player must read and interpret — a letter means an enemy, a symbol means an item — and it's precisely this mental work that is part of the experience. TIC-80 as an economical fantasy console suits this conception ideally: on minimal resources it builds a game that plays out mainly in the head.

Culturally, ASCII Game is a tribute to the whole tradition from which games like NetHack, Angband or modern takes on the genre grew. The roguelike had enormous influence — its principles (random generation, permadeath) today seep into countless titles across platforms. ASCII Game doesn't water these principles down; on the contrary, it returns them to their original, harshest form.

For the player this means a challenge, not a stroll. You will die, learn and come back, because every new expedition offers a different layout of danger. It's a game for someone who isn't looking for spectacle but for depth — and who knows that the best graphics are the ones you imagine yourself.

**Why play:** If you love hard, thoroughbred roguelikes with procedural dungeons and permadeath, ASCII Game returns you to the roots of the genre in its most honest textual form.

tic-80__skip-ahead.article:
A jump, an abyss underfoot and a platform waiting exactly where you must land — or you won't land at all. Skip Ahead is a platformer for TIC-80, a genre as old as video games themselves, and it immediately makes clear what it cares about: movement, timing and that sweet feeling when a series of jumps lands exactly as it should.

A platformer lives or dies on character control, and that's exactly where the decision is made. Skip Ahead builds on precise jumps, reading the placement of platforms and gradually mastering harder passages. The title hints at the pace — it's about not stopping, reading the route ahead and overcoming obstacles in a fluid rhythm. A good platformer is at its core the music of movement, and this game tries to hit that melody.

TIC-80, on which Skip Ahead runs, is an open-source fantasy console with firmly set limits — small resolution, limited palette, compact code. For a platformer that's actually an advantage: readable level design, clearly recognizable platforms and enemies matter more than effects. The player must know at first glance where they can and cannot go, and the economical aesthetic lends itself to that.

Culturally, Skip Ahead joins the endless line of platformers stretching from the eight-bit era to today's indie scene. It's perhaps the most patiently tested genre in the history of the medium — and fantasy consoles like TIC-80 revive it precisely because every good idea in level design stands out on a limited canvas. The jump is the universal language of video games, and this game speaks it fluently.

For the player it's an offer of instant fun with a growing challenge. You start with a simple jump, but soon you catch yourself repeating the same passage until you master it perfectly. That repetition isn't frustration — it's the essence of the genre, that little triumph when you finally reach the spot you failed to reach so many times.

**Why play:** Skip Ahead is a pure platformer about precise jumps and timing — for anyone who likes it when a character's movement is a joy in itself.

tic-80__card-quest.article:
A deck of cards instead of a sword and shield, and yet an equally merciless dungeon where one bad hand can mean the end. Card Quest is a card roguelike for TIC-80 that combines two things which belong together more and more these days: the tactical depth of card games and the ruthless randomness of a roguelike adventure. The result is a game about thinking, risk and luck at the right moment.

Mechanically this means your actions — attacks, defense, abilities — come in the form of cards you draw and play in turns. Added to this are roguelike principles: procedural progression, where paths and encounters change with every attempt, and permanent death, which lends weight to every decision. You must weigh which card to play now and which to save, because a second chance may not come. It's a game of chess into which fate has stirred randomness.

TIC-80 as an economical fantasy console suits such a genre. A card roguelike doesn't need grand graphics — it needs a clear interface, readable cards and an obvious game state. The limited environment forces the creator to focus on exactly this, on the mechanics themselves and their clarity, which is the most important thing in a card game.

Culturally, Card Quest rides the wave that the deck-building roguelike genre set in motion in recent years and that showed how splendidly cards and procedural dungeons complement each other. The principle is elegant: the deck you build during the expedition is at once your strength and your fate. On the homebrew scene of fantasy consoles it's a natural choice — the genre is mainly about systems, and those fit even into the smallest code.

For the player it's an addictive loop of trial and error. You lose, learn how to build your turns better and throw yourself in again. Every expedition is different, every hand a new puzzle. It's a game for someone who likes their brain working at full tilt and where even a loss is a lesson for next time.

**Why play:** Card Quest combines the tactics of card battles with the ruthlessness of a roguelike — ideal for players who enjoy building a deck and taking a risk with every turn.

game-boy__super-mario-land.detail: The very first portable Mario and one of the Game Boy's launch titles. The foreign kingdom of Sarasaland, with a submarine and a plane instead of the Mushroom Kingdom. Small, snappy, historic.

game-boy__kirby-s-dream-land.detail: The debut of the pink Kirby — you inhale enemies and float through the air. Still without copy abilities, but an adorable and perfectly accessible start to the series.

nes__super-mario-bros-2.detail: The American sequel (a reworked Doki Doki Panic): instead of jumping on enemies you pull up vegetables and throw them, and for the first time you pick from four characters with different abilities. Unusual, but charming and distinctive to this day.

nes__teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles-ii-arc.detail: Konami's port of the famous arcade game — four ninja turtles mow down the Foot Clan across New York. Great co-op, faithful animations from the cartoon, one of the best licensed games on the NES.

nes__teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles-iii-ma.detail: An improved sequel to the arcade beat 'em up made directly for the NES — more levels, more attacks, still top-notch co-op. Technically it pushes the console to its limits.

nes__ice-climber.detail: Popo and Nana climb icy mountains, smash ceilings with a hammer and dodge polar bears. A basic Nintendo classic, known today mainly thanks to Smash Bros.

nes__balloon-fight.detail: You fly on balloons and try to pop the opponents above you. Momentum-based physics and a great two-player mode make it a small timeless gem (created by Iwata).

nes__duck-hunt.detail: The iconic light-gun shooter with the Zapper — you shoot down ducks and the laughing dog mocks you when you miss. A symbol of the NES era.

nes__metal-gear.detail: Kojima's original founded the stealth genre: instead of shooting you sneak, avoid guards and figure out how to get through unnoticed. The NES version has its flaws, but it's historically pivotal.

nes__gradius.detail: A horizontal shooter that defined the weapon-upgrade system (you collect capsules and choose upgrades from a bar). Legendary difficulty and the famous Konami code.

nes__ghosts-n-goblins.detail: The knight Arthur in his boxers against hordes of the undead — notoriously punishing difficulty and the need to beat the game twice. Frustrating and addictive at the same time.

snes__teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles-iv-tu.detail: One of the best arcade beat 'em ups ever, in an enhanced form on the SNES: throwing enemies "into the screen", time travel and superb co-op. An absolute classic.

snes__final-fight.detail: The console version of the legendary arcade brawler — Haggar, Cody and Guy clean up Mad Gear's grip on Metro City. A defining title of the genre (this is where Guy from Street Fighter comes from).

snes__super-mario-all-stars.detail: A collection of remasters of SMB 1–3 and Lost Levels in 16-bit graphics and with a save system. The best way to play the entire golden era of Mario all in one place.

snes__r-type-iii-third-lightning.detail: A gorgeous 16-bit horizontal shooter with the iconic "Force" module and three weapon types. Tough, but top-tier both visually and in gameplay.

snes__final-fantasy-mystic-quest.detail: A simplified JRPG aimed at beginners — more straightforward combat and a streamlined map. Fans of the series argue about it, but as an entry point to the genre it works great.

mega-drive__splatterhouse-2.detail: A gory horror beat 'em up: wearing the Terror Mask you fight through walls of flesh and monsters to save your girlfriend. An unusually brutal atmosphere for the Mega Drive.

mega-drive__splatterhouse-3.detail: The third game adds time-based branching and more open levels — you defend your own house against a horde. The peak of the horror series on consoles.

mega-drive__sonic-spinball.detail: Sonic as a pinball ball across multi-level tables full of enemies. An unconventional spin-off of the series — chaotic, but fun.

mega-drive__zero-wing.detail: A decent horizontal shooter from Toaplan, immortal mainly thanks to its comically translated intro "All your base are belong to us" — one of the first internet memes.

playstation__wipeout-2097.detail: Futuristic hovercraft racing at a fierce pace, with weapons and a legendary electronic soundtrack (Chemical Brothers, Prodigy). An icon of the early PS1-era style.

playstation__wip3out.detail: A polished third installment with Designers Republic's clean design and smoother handling. The pinnacle of the series on the PS1.

playstation__medievil.detail: The skeleton Sir Daniel Fortesque returns from the dead to atone for an ancient lie. A Tim Burton-esque gothic atmosphere, humor and honest hack-and-slash. A cult PS1 gem.

playstation__resident-evil-director-s-cu.detail: An expanded version of the original that founded the survival horror genre — a mansion full of zombies, puzzles and a shortage of ammo. The roots of the entire series (we also have RE2 and RE3).

nds__999-nine-hours-nine-persons-nine-do.article: A gripping escape-room visual novel — nine people trapped on a ship solve puzzles and a dark secret. A genre icon that brilliantly uses both DS screens.

nds__dragon-quest-v-hand-of-heavenly-bri.article: A remake of the beloved JRPG following three generations of the hero's family, with monster-catching into your party. Considered by many the best Dragon Quest ever.

3ds__legend-of-zelda-majora-s-mask-3d.article: An enhanced remake of the dark, time-obsessed Zelda — three days until the end of the world and transforming masks. The most atmospheric entry in the series, now in your pocket.

3ds__kirby-planet-robobot.article: Kirby with a robotic mech that copies the abilities of enemies and machines alike. One of the most polished and inventive 2D Kirby games.

master-system__sonic-hedgehog-2.article: The 8-bit sequel with Tails, its own levels, and an infamously brutal ending. A completely different game from the 16-bit version — and magical in its own way.

master-system__zillion.article: Metroid-style action based on an anime — you explore an enemy base, crack codes, and free allies. An underrated Master System gem.

saturn__sonic-jam.article: A collection of the classic Mega Drive Sonics plus a 3D „Sonic World“ hub to explore. The best way to play the old hedgehogs on the Saturn.

saturn__fighting-vipers.article: A 3D fighter from the makers of Virtua Fighter — armored fighters in fenced-in arenas. A snappier, more freewheeling sibling of VF.

arcade__space-invaders.article: The forefather of all shooters: you destroy advancing rows of aliens that speed up with every kill. The game that sparked the entire gaming boom and remains a symbol of video games to this day.

arcade__missile-command.article: With a trackball you defend six cities from a rain of ballistic missiles. A tense, oppressive Cold War classic that you always lose in the end.

arcade__xevious.article: A vertical shooter with two types of weapons — for aerial targets and for ground targets alike. A mysterious atmosphere and an enormous influence on the whole shmup genre.

arcade__dragon-s-lair.article: A laserdisc cartoon game with animation by Don Bluth — the knight Dirk rescues the princess. You control it through quick reactions at the right moment. A visual phenomenon of the 1980s.

arcade__marble-madness.article: You roll a marble through isometric mazes against the clock, over chasms and past enemies using a trackball. A classic that was unusual both in style and technology.

arcade__paperboy.article: You deliver newspapers by bike down a suburban street — hitting subscribers' mailboxes and dodging obstacles. A cult oddity with its handlebar controller.

arcade__contra.article: The arcade original of the famous run & gun action — two commandos mow down an alien invasion. This is where the legendary (and even harder) NES version comes from.

arcade__double-dragon.article: The founder of the modern beat 'em up: brothers Billy and Jimmy Lee against the Black Warriors gang. Two-player co-op defined the entire genre.

arcade__golden-axe.article: A fantasy brawler with a barbarian, a dwarf and an amazon — riding dragons, magic potions and a two-player rampage. A Sega arcade classic.

neogeo__king-of-monsters.article: Wrestling with giant monsters in Godzilla style — you level entire cities and grapple with other kaiju. A bombastic two-player brawl.

neogeo__viewpoint.article: An isometric shooter with a fascinating 3D perspective, an acid-jazz soundtrack and brutal difficulty. Visually one of the most beautiful games on the Neo Geo.

neogeo__fatal-fury-3-road-to-final-victo.article: An SNK fighter with a three-lane system for dodging into the foreground and background. The direct predecessor of the Garou series, with the stylish characters of Southtown.

cps__mega-man-power-battle.article: An arcade spin-off of Mega Man: boss battles from the classic series one after another, playable by two. Fast, nostalgic action for fans of the Blue Bomber.

cps__mercs.article: Vertical commando action (Senjou no Ookami II) — you fight your way through jungles and bases to free the hostages. Brisk, explosive CPS.

cps__magic-sword.article: You climb a fifty-floor tower full of monsters and free allies who then watch your back. A gorgeous Capcom fantasy action game.

msx__goonies.article: A Konami platformer based on the film — you lead the gang of Goonies through caves and free your friends. Absolutely a cult title on the MSX.

msx__zanac.article: A fast vertical shooter with clever adaptive difficulty — the game reacts to your play style. Compile at its very best.

msx__antarctic-adventure.article: A cute penguin runs and leaps over icy crevasses around Antarctica. An early Konami classic and one of the mascots of the MSX era.

c64__m-u-l-e.article: A legendary economic strategy for four players — you colonize a planet, mine, trade, and both compete and must cooperate at the same time. A timeless multiplayer design.

c64__archon-light-and-dark.article: Chess where capturing a square is decided by an action duel in an arena. A brilliant hybrid of turn-based strategy and arcade, complete with a day-and-night cycle.

c64__defender-of-crown-2.article: Knightly strategy in medieval England — you conquer castles, joust in tournaments and fight with swords. An icon of the „interactive film“ of its era.

amiga__super-stardust.article: Asteroids in gorgeous 3D-rendered graphics with bonus tunnel stages taken at full throttle. A technical pride of the Amiga.

amiga__moonstone-hard-days-knight.article: Brutal fantasy action with blood spraying across the screen — you journey after the moonstone and quarter giants and rivals alike. A cult favorite for its uncompromising nature.

amiga__hunter.article: An open military sandbox on islands — you drive, fly, swim and complete missions however you like. A forerunner of modern open-world games, and this was back in 1991.

game-boy-color__rayman.article: A prized port of Rayman on the Game Boy Color — a surprisingly sprawling and colorful 2D platformer with smooth animation. One of the console's technical and gameplay highlights.

game-boy-color__mega-man-xtreme.article: Pocket-sized Mega Man X — reworked stages and bosses from the SNES titles X1/X2 on the GBC. Precise jumping and shooting, complete with the wall dash.

game-boy-color__mega-man-xtreme-2.article: An improved sequel with elements from X3/X4, playable X and Zero, and upgrades. Great on-the-go action for fans of the X series.

game-boy-color__blaster-master-enemy-bel.article: A well-crafted successor to the NES classic — you alternate between driving a tank through side-scrolling levels and top-down foot sections. Sunsoft in fine form.

game-boy-color__bomberman-max-red-blue-c.article: The best Bomberman on the GBC — alongside the classic maze, it adds collecting „Charabom“ creatures and branching levels. Two versions for trading.

game-boy-color__grand-theft-auto.article: A cult curiosity — the entire original top-down GTA squeezed into a handheld console, complete with cars, missions and chaos. Technically remarkable.

game-boy-color__perfect-dark.article: A companion to the N64 version from Rare — a mix of stealth action and top-down minigames. Linking to the N64 via cable unlocked bonuses. Decent pocket espionage.

game-boy-color__tony-hawk-s-pro-skater.article: A surprisingly solid port of the skateboarding series on the GBC — tricks, combos and maps work better on the small console than you'd expect. Addictive.

game-boy-color__croc.article: A charming 2D platformer starring Croc the crocodile, retelling the 3D original in handheld form. A solid platformer for the GBC.

game-boy-color__turok-2-seeds-of-evil.article: Pocket action based on the N64 hit — more of a 2D/isometric shooter than an FPS, but with dinosaurs and exotic weapons. A decent adaptation.

game-boy-color__alone-in-dark-new-nightm.article: A survival horror on a handheld console — you explore a dark house, solve puzzles and fight monsters with a flashlight and weapons. An ambitious piece on the GBC.

game-boy-color__disney-s-aladdin.article: A colorful platformer based on the film — Aladdin jumps, throws apples and slides across Agrabah. A pleasant Disney platformer.

game-boy-color__tarzan.article: A platformer based on the animated Tarzan — you swing on vines and slide through the jungle. Solid licensed fun for younger players.

game-boy-color__legend-of-river-king-2.article: An unusual fishing RPG from the creators of Harvest Moon — you roam the landscape, catch fish and rescue your sister. A calm, addictive chill-out with a cult fanbase.
